An internal zirconia split sleeve is specified but not clearly visible as a white ring in the primary view, so it is not drawn. The PDF metadata creation date 2024-11-15 is not a printed date. The 29.3 mm dimension is axial depth; the double-D 9.6 × 7.8 mm panel cutout is reference only, not the front shape. Proportions, color, roughness, AO, layer heights, the 0.04 m nominal tile and 0.0042 UV relief are authored for a simplified front illustration, not CAD. Threads, individual knurl teeth, washers, caps, rear parts, cable/ferrule and PCB are omitted; no optical/electrical/mating/safety simulation or certification, browser/FPS certification, or bundled source assets.

The independent 54-field preset (52 numeric fields and two palettes) uses 13 C1 profile factors: six nut support planes, three squared-circle profiles, two key-axis gates and two stud-axis gates, with 20 constructor-cached C/H/R/AO deltas. Products of smooth profiles and role replacement avoid nonzero hard-min/max joins. Four four-column Float64 poses (128 B) plus 96² Float64 grain (73,728 B) retain 73,856 B typed-array payload, excluding JS object/closure overhead—not total RAM or FPS. The rotation-independent owner radius plus jitter is 0.35841016151377547 < 0.5. Poses/grain are constructor-cached; queries have no allocation, loop, hash, trigonometry or square root, skipping zero support and unused grain in nonmetal bore/background. The second fractional wrap before owner indexing remains necessary for tiny negative UVs. Default metallic is 1; `createMaterial({ metallic: 0 })` changes only the factor, not the stored metallic mask. Existing opaque four maps, optional height, tint/repeats and Worker/cache APIs apply: the preset owns textures, callers manage borrowed materials and their own pool/cache, removing borrowed materials before disposing the preset. No new dependencies, helpers, exports, API or palette expansion. These are source/implementation descriptions, not claims of full formal tests, browser or built-distribution verification.

`to220packagefaces` adds four 2×2 front-oriented exposed-tab TO-220 package schematics, bringing the catalog from 884 to 885 kinds (886 gallery choices including plain). Each has a neutral-metal tab with TWO clipped upper corners and ONE centered dark opaque recessed mounting hole, a matte-black rectangular body masking the lower tab and lead roots, and THREE uniformly spaced parallel straight metal leads with broader root shoulders and narrower tails. Full tab/lead surfaces have M1; body, hole floor and backing have M0, with C1 boundary blends. These are surface roles, not electrical isolation. Authored normalized heights are backing .02 < hole .06 < tab .30 < lead .44 < body .68; the hole is a real height depression, not black paint or a transparent opening.

Appearance follows STMicroelectronics' [STP55NF06 exposed-tab TO-220 type A, May 2012, Doc ID7544 Rev11](https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/stb55nf06.pdf#page=13): the original PDF cover artwork on page 1 and Figure 23 / 0015988_typeA_Rev_S on page 13 were actually viewed, with the dimension table read on page 12. This is NOT TO-220FP or the D²PAK variant. Drawing dimensions are references only, not measurements of this authored artwork or exact dimensioned CAD. Chemistry, plating and precise optical properties are not inferred. Printed markings, molded small circles/recesses and rear details are omitted; no source artwork is shipped. It does not simulate heat, circuits, electrical/RF behavior, safety or FPS; the source's tab-to-pin-2 connection is not modeled.

Defaults are a 0.08 m nominal tile, 0.0042 UV-relative relief (not metres of displacement) and metallic factor 1. Explicit `createMaterial({ metallic: 0 })` changes only the scalar factor, never the stored M mask. Artist fields remain in the existing immutable `src/data` preset. Constructor-cached four-column Float64 poses (128 B) and 96² Float64 grain (73,728 B) retain 73,856 B typed-array payload, excluding JS object/closure overhead—not total RAM or a performance certification. The sampler reuses C1 profiles and convex layer replacement; queries have no allocation, loops, hash, trigonometry, square root or neighbor search. Existing periodic opaque maps and texture ownership remain unchanged. Prefer 512 to show the hole and three narrow lead tails; 32 is only a coarse preview and need not resolve every lead.

`japanesemotifs` adds traditional Japanese geometric motifs, bringing the current catalog from 1188 to 1189 kinds (1190 gallery choices including plain). Indigo ink on pale grey-white paper, the ink slightly raised: **four traditional Japanese geometric motifs** in 2×2 panels, each panel repeating c × c cells: **ichimatsu** (the checkerboard), **uroko** (rows of triangular scales, every other row shifted by half a cell), **igeta** (the well-curb sign, two upright and two flat bars crossing in a # shape) and **hishi** (a diamond outline around a small diamond). Every panel has a plain border 0.3 cell wide where the ink fades out. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 4 rotates the four motifs through the four panels and ⌊seed / 4⌋ is the group: group % 4 picks the number of cells per panel (4, 5, 6, 8) and ⌊group / 4⌋ shifts the pattern inside the panels by (step × 0.37, step × 0.61) cells modulo 1. The edge smoothing is 0.06 of a cell; the ink tone is 0.12, the paper 0.93, the height of the ink 0.8 and the AO 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.6 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the shapes of the four motifs (the triangle's corners, the bar widths and lengths of the igeta and the radii of the diamonds) are geometry I simplified from memory and are **not faithful copies of any pattern book or object**, and I did not look anything up. Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): kolam, sona, kumiko, sayagata, uroko, ichimatsu, igeta and hishi all gave 0/0 (seigaiha, asanoha, shippo and yagasuri gave 1/0 each, kikko 1/6, truchet 2/3, wang 1/3 and mandala 0/1, which are mentions elsewhere that I did not look at one by one). I also searched the README with `grep` for words such as 青海波, 麻の葉, 七宝, 矢絣, 亀甲, 刺し子 and 紋 and found no entry of a matching material (the hits were unrelated entries), and I did not read the existing checkerboard- or lattice-like entries (for example the café-wall of `opticalillusions`) to compare, so I cannot state the differences from them. The test checks: (1) a point-by-point comparison (11 seeds, 6,000 points each, covering the 4 cell counts and one shift): each point's ink is decided by a rule the test writes separately with inequalities and line distances (the parity of the checkerboard, the three half-planes of the triangle, the four rectangles of the igeta, the L1 distance of the diamond), and the height (12 digits), the tone (within half the grain) and the occlusion are compared; points within 0.3 cell of a panel border and within half the smoothing of an edge are left out; the numbers of points compared for the seeds are 3310, 3297, 3300, 3257, 3544, 3526, 3542, 3853, 3610, 3543 and 3614 (lower bound 3000); all four motifs occurred; (2) translation and mirror symmetry: the height and the occlusion are the same after translating the checkerboard by (2, 0), (0, 2) and (1, 1), the scales by (1, 0) and (0, 2) and the igeta and hishi by (1, 0) and (0, 1), and the mirror image inside a cell about the vertical axis (and, except for the scales, about the horizontal axis) is the same (4 seeds × 4 panels × 40 points, of which 614 sets lie clear of the panel border, lower bound 500); (3) the ink fraction of a cell: I measured 0.50000 for the checkerboard, 0.37053 for the scales, 0.28800 for the igeta and 0.28311 for the hishi, within 0.004 of the analytic values 0.5, 0.3696, 0.288 and 0.2824 (the differences for the scales and the hishi come from the rounding of the corners and from the smoothing, which I did not analyse further); (4) there is no ink at the very edge of a panel; (5) the pictures differ per rotation, cell count and shift (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 4, 8 and 16 is 0.3769683837890625, 0.4100799560546875, 0.4237060546875 and 0.3841094970703125) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first version of the translation and mirror test moved points into the fading zone of a panel border and got differences of 4.8e-6, which was a **mistake in the test** (it did not leave out the border zone) and it passed after the border zone was left out; (2) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0, 1, 4, 8, 16 and 20 without zooming in, in which the fading of the checkerboard at the panel borders is more noticeable than for the other motifs; (3) 29 mutation checks were run and all 29 were caught; (4) none of the mutations gave a NOMATCH because of prettier's line breaks this time.

At start-up (per sampler): only the orientation of the triangle's three corners, plus the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): the signed distance of one motif (at most 2 loops of 3 operations each) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: japanesemotifs took 93, 106 and 108 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 161, 164 and 164 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`busybeavers` adds busy beavers, bringing the current catalog from 1187 to 1188 kinds (1189 gallery choices including plain). Mint rounded squares on a dark green ground: **the space-time diagrams of the four busy-beaver champion Turing machines** (two symbols, started on a blank tape), in 2×2 panels of 32×32 cells: the row r shows the tape after r × stride steps and the 32 columns are the 32 tape cells around the starting cell (arranged cyclically); after the machine has halted the rows stay the same. The 4 machines are **BB-2** (6 steps, 4 ones), **BB-3** (14 steps, 6 ones), **BB-4** (107 steps, 13 ones, stride 4) and **the first 31 steps of the BB-5 champion** (47,176,870 steps in all, 4,098 ones). The level of a cell is 0 for a blank cell, 1/3 for a cell holding a 1, 2/3 for the head over a 0 and 1 for the head over a 1; the tone, 0.15 to 0.95, and height (0.8 times 0.2 plus 0.8 times) follow the level. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 4 rotates the four machines through the four panels and ⌊seed / 4⌋ is the group: its parity decides whether the machines are mirrored (left and right swapped) and ⌊group / 2⌋ moves the starting column by (⌊group / 2⌋ × 5) mod 9 − 4 cells; so the picture repeats with the period 72. The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the transition tables of the four machines and their halting steps and numbers of ones (6/4, 14/6, 107/13, 47,176,870/4,098) are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the test actually runs them to the end with a separately written simulator (including the 47,176,870 steps of BB-5) and compares. Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): busybeaver, brainfuck, hodge and brians all gave 0/0 (turing = 1/6 is the unrelated `turingmaze` reaction-diffusion entry and glider = 0/1 is a mention). I only looked at the names and the first about 120 characters of the entries about cellular automata in the README (`rule110`, `rule30`, `elementaryautomata`, `gameoflife`, `wireworldcircuits`, `excitableautomata`, `daynight`, `stilllifes` and `turingmaze`) and did not read or compare them to the end: `rule110`, `rule30` and `elementaryautomata` are also space-time diagrams of a model of computation and **overlap with this material conceptually**, but those are one-dimensional cellular automata and this one is Turing machines with their heads. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the level 0 to 3 solved from the height of every cell): (1) the separately written simulator (the tape is an array of 40,000 cells) runs the four machines: BB-2, BB-3, BB-4 and BB-5 halt after 6, 14, 107 and 47,176,870 steps and leave 4, 6, 13 and 4,098 ones; (2) for the 72 different seeds (4 rotations × mirroring × 9 shifts) every cell of the 4 panels equals the simulator's tape at the corresponding time (the mirroring and the shift are written independently in the test as a mapping of tape positions); (3) rules checked on the picture alone (12 seeds): every row has exactly one head; for machines with stride 1 the head moves by one cell (mod 32) between consecutive rows, or stays after halting, and the cells other than the head do not change; all rows from the halting row on are the same and the last row holds 4, 6 and 13 ones for BB-2, BB-3 and BB-4; row 0 has no ones; (4) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (5) the pictures differ per rotation, mirroring and shift (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 2, 4 and 8 is 0.05419921875, 0.05322265625, 0.0421142578125 and 0.0615234375) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first version of `expectedPanels` re-ran the complete BB-5 simulation (47,176,870 steps) for every row, and the test took more than 60 seconds; I stopped it and changed it to record the final tape at halting, which was a **mistake of the test being too slow**, not a problem of the sampler; the earlier run that kept going before I stopped it showed that the champion-numbers test itself passed (636 ms); (2) one redundant operation in the sampler, `column − n/2 − offset + n/2`, was simplified to `column − offset`; (3) the point-by-point check compares 4647 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4500; (4) 28 mutation checks were run: 27 caught and 1 not caught: the tape array shrunk from 2048 to 1048 cells (the machines stay within about 124 cells of the start in the rows shown, so there is no difference; I regard it as equivalent and kept the original); (5) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 9 and one single preview of seed 0 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): each of the four machines is simulated for at most (32 − 1) × stride steps (at most 124) and its 32 rows are recorded in a 32×32 `Uint8Array` (4,096 B for the four), each machine having a tape of 2,048 B, plus the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: busybeavers took 96, 96 and 102 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 165, 159 and 165 ms in the same environment (measured before the redundant operation was simplified, not measured again afterwards); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`adjacencymatrices` adds adjacency matrices, bringing the current catalog from 1186 to 1187 kinds (1188 gallery choices including plain). Periwinkle rounded squares on a dark indigo ground: **the adjacency matrices of four graphs on 16 vertices**, in 2×2 panels of 16×16 cells: the **Clebsch graph** (strongly regular (16, 5, 0, 2)), the **4×4 rook's graph** (strongly regular (16, 6, 2, 2)), the **Shrikhande graph** (the other strongly regular (16, 6, 2, 2) graph, not isomorphic to the rook's graph) and the **4-cube**. A cell with an edge is bright and raised (tone 0.95, height 1 times 0.8), a cell without an edge and the diagonal are dark (tone 0.15, height 0.2 times 0.8). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 4 rotates the four graphs through the four panels and ⌊seed / 4⌋ is the group: group 0 keeps the natural numbering of the vertices (the matrices show regular structure) and any other group relabels the vertices of each panel by hash keys (the matrices look random but are isomorphic). The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definitions of the four graphs, the strongly regular parameters of the Clebsch and Shrikhande graphs and "the Clebsch graph is the Cayley graph of the nonzero cubes of GF(16)" are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the tests actually verify them. Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): adjacency, ramsey, turan, cage, expander, laplacian, tournament and cayleygraph all gave 0/0 (circulant = 0/1, petersen = 0/2 and matching = 0/3 are mentions elsewhere). I read the first part (about 250 characters each) of the entries for `kneser` (Kneser matrices), `projectiveplane` (incidence matrices of finite projective planes) and `cayleytable` (group multiplication tables), and saw the entry names `hypercube` (projection of hypercubes) and `paleytable` without reading them: `kneser` is also the matrix of a graph (the Kneser graph / Johnson scheme) and **overlaps with this material conceptually**, but it is a different graph with the tone following the number of shared elements; here four graphs are in one picture and are checked by isomorphism and strong regularity. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, 0 or 1 solved from the height of every cell): (1) for 64 seeds and the four panels: the matrix is symmetric, has an empty diagonal and every vertex has the degree 5, 6, 6 or 4 of its graph; for the three strongly regular graphs any two different vertices have λ common neighbours when adjacent and μ when not ((0, 2), (2, 2), (2, 2)); every matrix is **isomorphic to the standard graph built in another way** (Clebsch as the Cayley graph of the nonzero cubes in GF(16), the rook's graph as the line graph of K(4,4), Shrikhande as a Cayley graph of Z₄×Z₄ and the 4-cube as a product of four edges; isomorphism is decided by backtracking, so it also holds after relabelling); (2) the rook's graph and the Shrikhande graph are **not isomorphic to each other** (the complete search in both directions for 8 seeds gives "not isomorphic"), which is also visible in the neighbourhood of any vertex: two triangles (two connected components) in the rook's graph and a hexagon (one component) in the Shrikhande graph; with group 0 the matrices of the rook's graph and the 4-cube equal the natural-numbering rules written out separately in the test; (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (4) the pictures differ per rotation and labelling (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 2, 4 and 8 is 0.19189453125, 0.220703125, 0.3583984375 and 0.333984375) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) in the first version of the test the GF(16) multiplication reduced modulo x⁴ + x + 1 before the left shift, which gave 9 cubes instead of 5; that was a **mistake in the test**, and after shifting first and reducing afterwards it gave 5 and the Clebsch isomorphism held; (2) the point-by-point check compares 4668 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (3) 22 mutation checks were run and all 22 were caught; replacing the third difference (1, 1) of the Shrikhande graph by (1, −1) (which gives an **isomorphic** graph) was caught only by the pinned statistics and lit-cell fractions, the structural tests themselves (isomorphism, strong regularity, degrees) accept it, as expected; I did not run the mutation that swaps the row and column labels (the matrix is symmetric, so the result is necessarily the same); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 9 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): one vertex labelling for each of the four panels (the identity for group 0, otherwise ordered by 16 hash keys), plus the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; no matrix is built beforehand. At sampling time (per pixel): one rule evaluation (a few bit operations), one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: adjacencymatrices took 89, 81 and 80 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 125, 125 and 127 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`numbertriangles` adds counting triangles, bringing the current catalog from 1185 to 1186 kinds (1187 gallery choices including plain). Coral rounded squares on a dark coral-brown ground: **four counting triangles, each taken modulo m**, in 2×2 panels of 16×16 cells: the **Eulerian numbers** A(r + 1, c) (the number of permutations of r + 1 elements with exactly c ascents), the **Narayana numbers** N(r + 1, c + 1), the **Delannoy numbers** D(r, c) (a full square) and the **Lah numbers** L(r + 1, c + 1). The cells outside a triangle stay empty; the others have tone (0.15 to 0.95) and height (0.8 times 0.2 plus 0.8 times) following "(value mod m) / (m − 1)". **The seed is split in two**: seed % 8 picks the modulus (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9) and ⌊seed / 8⌋ mod 4 how many places the four triangles are rotated through the four panels; so the picture repeats with the period 32. The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definitions of the four triangles (the Eulerian recurrence, the Narayana formula, the Delannoy recurrence and the Lah formula) and their symmetries and row sums (n! for the Eulerian numbers and the Catalan numbers for the Narayana numbers) are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the tests actually verify them. Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): delannoy, narayana, eulerian, schroeder, lah, chebyshev, bernstein, zigzag and warburton all gave 0/0. I read the first part (about 330 characters each) of the entries for `stirlingparity` (the parity of the Stirling numbers of the second kind) and `pascalmod3` (Pascal's triangle modulo 3): they are also "counting triangles taken modulo something and drawn as rounded squares", **so the idea and the drawing overlap**, but here there are four other triangles in one picture and 8 moduli; I did not read or compare the others one by one. All the values are below 2^53 (I checked with big integers that nothing overflows). The test checks (everything read back from the picture, empty cells and residues solved from the height): (1) for 64 seeds every cell of the 4 panels equals **the residue computed separately from closed formulas on big integers** (the alternating sum Σ(−1)^j C(n+1,j)(k+1−j)^n for the Eulerian numbers, the factorial formula for Narayana, Σ C(m,k)C(n,k)2^k for Delannoy and C(n−1,k−1)·n!/k! for Lah, not the recurrences of the sampler), and the cells outside the triangles are indeed empty; (2) known properties checked on the picture alone (64 seeds): the three triangles have 136 cells each and the Delannoy square 256; the Eulerian and Narayana triangles are symmetric left to right and the Delannoy square about the diagonal; the sum of each Eulerian row modulo m equals n! and that of each Narayana row the Catalan number; modulo 2 the whole Delannoy square is 1 (all odd); (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (4) the pictures differ per modulus and rotation (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 8, 16 and 24 is 0.2349853515625, 0.451171875, 0.3934326171875 and 0.451171875; that seeds 8 and 24 give the same number I did not investigate further, it may be a coincidence), **the picture of seed 32 equals that of seed 0** and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first version had only 4 moduli (2, 3, 5, 7) and seeds 16 and 32 gave exactly the picture of seed 0; after looking at the previews and the probe I changed it to 8 moduli, which made the period 32 instead of 16, and I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 9 without zooming in; (2) the point-by-point check compares 4668 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (3) 27 mutation checks were run: 26 caught and 1 not caught and equivalent: `present = entry >= 0` changed to `entry > 0` (every value inside a triangle is a positive integer and empty cells are −1, so they are the same); (4) none of the mutations gave a NOMATCH because of prettier's line breaks this time.

At start-up (per sampler): a 17×17 table of binomials and four tables of 256 integers (about 1,000 integer additions and multiplications; the largest Lah number is about 4×10^14), plus the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: numbertriangles took 58, 59 and 60 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 91, 93 and 102 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`selfreferentialsequences` adds self-describing integer sequences, bringing the current catalog from 1184 to 1185 kinds (1186 gallery choices including plain). Aqua rounded squares on a dark teal ground: **four integer sequences that are defined by themselves**, written row by row into a 48×48 table (2,304 terms, starting at a term chosen by the seed): 0 **Van Eck's sequence** (a(0) = 0, the next term is the distance back to the previous occurrence of this term, or 0 if it has not occurred), 1 **Gijswijt's sequence** (g(1) = 1, the next term is the largest number of times a block is repeated at the end), 2 the deviation 2Q(n) − n of **Hofstadter's Q sequence** (Q(1) = Q(2) = 1, Q(n) = Q(n − Q(n−1)) + Q(n − Q(n−2))) and 3 the deviation 2a(n) − n of the **Hofstadter–Conway $10000 sequence** (a(1) = a(2) = 1, a(n) = a(a(n−1)) + a(n − a(n−1))). The tone of a cell, 0.15 to 0.95, and its height (0.8 times 0.2 plus 0.8 times) are the shown value scaled between the smallest and the largest value of the 2,304 terms to 0 to 1, then raised to the power 0.5 (Van Eck), 1, 1.5 (Q) and 1. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 4 picks the sequence and ⌊seed / 4⌋ the window: it starts at the term (group × 197) mod 1500. The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell, the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definitions of the four sequences, a(2^k) = 2^(k−1) of the Hofstadter–Conway sequence and the first 4 of Gijswijt's sequence being the 220th term are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the tests actually check them with separately written algorithms (the first 20 terms of the OEIS entries in the tests are also written from memory, not looked up). Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): vaneck, selfdescrib, kimberling, stanley, audioactive, gijswijt and egyptian all gave 0/0 (hofstadter = 1/3 is the unrelated `hofstadterbutterfly` entry and conway = 0/3 are other mentions). I read the first part (about 230 characters each) of the entries for `kolakoski` (the Kolakoski sequence, 48×48 rounded squares), `golombruns` (Golomb's sequence, 64×64, tone by the remainder modulo 7) and `recamanarcs` (Recamán arcs): `kolakoski` and `golombruns` are also "self-describing integer sequences written into a table of rounded squares", **so the idea and the layout overlap**, but they are different sequences with a different scaling (here between the smallest and the largest value of the window, not a remainder); `recamanarcs` draws the arcs of another self-referential sequence; I did not read or compare the others one by one. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the integer recovered from the height after undoing the scaling): (1) for 60 seeds the 2,304 integers read back equal those of **separately written algorithms** exactly (Van Eck by scanning backwards, Gijswijt by tracking the length of the trailing run of each period, the two Hofstadter sequences by memoised recursion); (2) rules checked on the picture alone: the first 20 terms of the four sequences equal the OEIS first 20 terms as I remember them; in a Van Eck window the term after every term equals "the distance to its previous occurrence", and after a term first seen in the window comes 0 or a distance reaching back before the window (for 5 seeds); every Gijswijt term is at least 1 (for 4 seeds) and in the first window the first 4 is the 220th term (index 219); in the first window of Hofstadter–Conway 2a(n) − n is 0 at n = 2, 4, …, 2048 and never negative; (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (4) the pictures differ per sequence and window (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 4, 8 and 24 is 0.1742095947265625, 0.106719970703125, 0.113861083984375 and 0.1190643310546875) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first version's gamma for the Q deviation was 1 and its preview was flat and bright; I tried 3 (too dark, sparse bright points) and finally used 1.5; each time I only looked at the previews of seeds 2 and 6 (and 10) without zooming in; (2) the Van Eck check in the first version of the facts test used `lastIndexOf(value, k − 1)`, where for k = 0 the −1 is counted from the end, which gave 1 mismatch; that was a **mistake in the test** and it passed after I treated k = 0 as not seen; (3) the point-by-point check compares 4636 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4500; (4) 29 mutation checks were run: 25 caught and 4 not caught, all equivalent: the pruning condition `size * (best + 1) <= m` of Gijswijt changed to `size * best <= m` (it only looks at some more blocks that cannot give more); `(count + 1) * size <= m` changed to `count * size <= m` (reading a negative index gives undefined, the comparison is false and the result is the same — I kept the original because I do not want to rely on an out-of-range read); `count > best` changed to `count >= best` (assigns the same value); and the deviation `2a − n` changed to `2a − n + 1` (a constant shift is cancelled by the scaling between the smallest and the largest value, so the picture is unchanged).

At start-up (per sampler): all terms up to the end of the window are computed (at most 1499 + 2,304 = 3,803): Van Eck uses a Map (O(1) per term), the two Hofstadter sequences are linear recurrences, Gijswijt scans every block size for each term (about 3,800 × 1,900 comparisons in the worst case, but a mismatch stops early), plus the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: selfreferentialsequences took 99, 106 and 100 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 168, 171 and 185 ms in the same environment (seed 7, the Hofstadter–Conway window; the start-up time of the other seeds, Gijswijt's in particular, was not measured separately); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`linearcodes` adds linear block codes, bringing the current catalog from 1183 to 1184 kinds (1185 gallery choices including plain). Lime rounded squares on a dark green ground: **four binary linear codes of length 8 and dimension 4**, each drawn as four 16×16 panels (the 256 received words w, the cell in the row r and the column c being w = 16r + c): top left **the distance from w to the nearest codeword** (divided by 4), top right **the syndrome** (w reduced by the row-reduced generator rows, leaving 4 free bits, divided by 15), bottom left **the message of the nearest codeword plus 1** (0 when two or more codewords are equally near, divided by 16) and bottom right **the number of ones in w** (divided by 8). The tone of a cell, 0.15 to 0.95, and its height (0.8 times 0.2 plus 0.8 times) follow the value of its panel. The 4 codes are 0 the extended Hamming code (the first-order Reed–Muller code, minimum distance 4), 1 the cyclic Hamming code of length 7 with a zero coordinate appended (distance 3), 2 four copies of the length-2 repetition code side by side (distance 2) and 3 the even-weight code of length 4 next to the repetition code of length 4 (distance 2). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 4 picks the code and ⌊seed / 4⌋ the group: group 0 keeps the coordinates and any other group permutes the 8 coordinates by hash keys (an equivalent code). The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the generator rows of the four codes, the distance 4 of the extended Hamming code and its perfectness (balls of radius 1 are disjoint, covering radius 2) are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the tests actually verify them. Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): linearcode, codeword, syndrome and coset all gave 0/0 (parity = 1/16 is unrelated entries; I only looked at the entry names in the README that contain "奇偶"). I read the first part (about 230 characters each) of the entries for `hammingtable` (Hamming distances of 5-bit indices), `crctables` (CRC lookup tables) and `debruijntorus` (symbol grids): `hammingtable` is also a Hamming distance, but between two indices, while here it is the distance from a received word to a set of codewords and the decoding; `crctables` is likewise a table over GF(2) and overlaps conceptually (this one also uses 2×2 panels of 16×16 and the same cell rendering); I did not read or compare the others one by one. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, an integer solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 60 seeds: the words at distance 0 in the top left form a 16-word subspace (closed under XOR), **their weight list equals that of the base code written separately in the test**, the minimum distance equals the expected value of each code (4, 3, 2, 2), and with group 0 it **is** the base code; for the first 24 seeds it also checks that **some permutation of the 8 coordinates (all 8! tried) carries every generator row of the base code into this code**, i.e. that it really is an equivalent code after permuting the coordinates; (2) for each of the 256 words by brute force: the top left equals the minimum distance to the codewords, the bottom right the number of ones, the bottom left the message of the nearest codeword plus 1 when it is unique and 0 on a tie (the message taken from the cell of the codeword itself in the picture); the top-right syndrome is **0 on the codewords and only on them** and the same over a coset (adding a codeword); the syndrome is linear over XOR (32,896 pairs per seed) and takes all 16 values; the message is a bijection onto 0 to 15 on the codewords and linear over XOR; for the extended Hamming code (seed % 4 = 0) the numbers of words at distance 0, 1 and 2 are exactly 16, 128 and 112; (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (4) the pictures differ per code and group (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 4, 8 and 24 is 0.204315185546875, 0.1386566162109375, 0.1397247314453125 and 0.1428985595703125) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 4668 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (2) 29 mutation checks were run: 26 caught and 3 not caught: `ties++` replaced by `ties = 2` (only "is it exactly 1" is used, equivalent, I kept the original); `findIndex` replaced by `findLastIndex` when looking for the pivot row (the row-reduced result is unique, equivalent); and the trailing `|| a - b` of the sort comparator (used only when the hashes are equal; `sort` is stable and keeps the index order anyway, so **I removed that redundant comparison from the code**); 6 more attempts first gave NOMATCH or no test because of prettier's line breaks or shell escaping and were caught when rerun with the reformatted fragments (including the `findIndex` one); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 9 without zooming in; it shows that the bottom-left panel of the repetition code (seed 2) is almost all 0 (ties).

At start-up (per sampler): the 4 generator rows are permuted and row-reduced, and for each of the 256 words the distance to the 16 codewords (4,096 `popcount` calls in all) and the reduction are computed and stored in four 256-entry `Uint8Array` (1,024 B), plus the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: linearcodes took 79, 67 and 63 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 113, 109 and 104 ms in the same environment (measured before the redundant comparison was removed, not measured again afterwards); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`crctables` adds CRC lookup tables, bringing the current catalog from 1182 to 1183 kinds (1184 gallery choices including plain). Sky-blue rounded squares on a dark navy ground: **the 8-bit CRC lookup tables (256 entries each) of two generator polynomials**, in two rows of two panels: on the left the table that **shifts to the left** (most significant bit first) and on the right the one that **shifts to the right** (least significant bit first, with the bit-reversed polynomial); each panel is 16×16 cells, the cell in the row r and the column c holding the entry of the byte 16r + c, its tone (0.15 to 0.95) and height (0.8 times 0.2 plus 0.8 times) following "value / 255". The 6 polynomials (x⁸ plus the low 8 bits) are 0x07, 0x31, 0x1d, 0x9b, 0xd5 and 0x2f. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the polynomial of the top row and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: (the group mod 5) plus 1 is how many polynomials "later" the bottom row's is (1 to 5). Because a table is linear over XOR, the picture has interwoven horizontal and vertical stripes. The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the way a CRC table is built, the six polynomials (0x07, 0x31, 0x1d, 0x9b, 0xd5 and 0x2f are common 8-bit CRC polynomials as I remember them; I did not compare their names or standards) and "the table is linear over XOR and a permutation" are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the tests actually verify the properties. Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): crc, redundancy and checksum all gave 0/0 (cyclic = 1/9 is something else). I read the first part (about 200 characters each) of the entries for `xortable` (row XOR col), `nimproduct` (bits of the nim product), `walshmatrix` and `hadamardmatrix` (±1 matrices): they are also 8-bit-ish tables over GF(2) and **overlap with this material conceptually**, but this one is the shifting-division table of the CRC and its left and right shifting versions, and the picture is different. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the value from 0 to 255 solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 60 seeds and both rows: **every entry equals the remainder of i·x⁸ divided by x⁸ plus the polynomial** (computed separately by long division on 16-bit numbers, not the sampler's bit-by-bit shifting); the shifting-right table relates to the shifting-left one by **reversing the bits of the index and of the value** (R[rev(i)] = rev(T[i]); the two tables are computed separately with opposite shift directions); T[0] = 0 and T[1] = the polynomial; **XOR linearity**: T[a ⊕ b] = T[a] ⊕ T[b] for all a and b (32,896 pairs per table); the 256 values of every table are **all different** (a permutation of 0 to 255, because all six polynomials have the constant term 1); (2) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (3) the pictures differ per polynomial and group (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 6, 12 and 24 is 0.316650390625, 0.164886474609375, 0.1671295166015625 and 0.163909912109375) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) in the first version of the test I wrote "T[0x80] = the polynomial", which was a **mistake in the test** (the remainder for 0x80 is that of x¹⁵; T[1] is the polynomial); it passed after I changed it to T[1]; (2) the first version of the XOR-linearity check made one `expect` per pair and the block took 7.9 s; I changed it to count the pairs that disagree and make a single `expect`, which brought it to 0.3 s; (3) the point-by-point check compares 4668 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (4) 21 mutation checks were run: 20 caught and 1 not caught: the `& 0xff` of the left shift when the top bit is not set replaced by `& 0x1ff` (the value is below 0x80 then, so shifting left never exceeds 8 bits, equivalent; **I removed that redundant mask from the code**); (5) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0, 1 and 2 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): for each of the two polynomials two tables of 256 entries (8 shift steps per entry, 4×256×8 steps in all) and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: crctables took 99, 99 and 92 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 160, 146 and 150 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`robinsonschensted` adds the Robinson–Schensted correspondence, bringing the current catalog from 1181 to 1182 kinds (1183 gallery choices including plain). Magenta rounded squares on a dark plum ground: **the pair of tableaux that the Robinson–Schensted correspondence gives for each of three permutations**, one permutation per row of three panels: on the left the permutation matrix (the dot in the column i is in the row p(i), its tone marking i), in the middle the **insertion tableau P** and on the right the **recording tableau Q** (both standard Young tableaux of the same shape, the cells holding 1 to 10, rows left-justified and counted from the top). P is made by inserting p(1), p(2), … one after the other: every number bumps the next larger one of a row down to the next row; Q records at which step the last new box of each step appeared. The tone of a cell, 0.25 to 0.95, and its height (0.8 times 0.3 plus 0.7 times) follow "number / 10", an empty cell has tone 0.1 and height 0.15 times; the panels are parted by wider gaps. The 6 types of permutation are 0 the identity, 1 the reversal, 2 random by hash keys, 3 a random involution (3 swaps), 4 the cyclic shift by 3 and 5 the multiplication by 2 mod 11 (i → 2i mod 11). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the type of the first row and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: (the group mod 2) plus 1 is the step between the types of the rows (the types of the three rows are t, t + step and t + 2 step mod 6), and the group also sets the keys of the random permutations. The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the insertion rule of the Robinson–Schensted correspondence, Schensted's theorem (the length of the first row is the longest increasing subsequence and the number of rows the longest decreasing one) and Schützenberger's symmetry (P = Q if and only if the permutation is an involution) are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the tests actually verify them. Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): rsk, schensted and robinson all gave 0/0; tableau = 2/10, young = 1/13 and permutation = 1/18 (related names that already exist in the README or among the kinds). I read the first part (about 260 characters each) of the entries for `permutations` (a class of permutations drawn as permutation matrices), `standardtableaux` (every standard Young tableau of a shape) and `youngdiagrams` (Young diagrams of integer partitions and their hook lengths): they draw permutations, standard tableaux and partitions respectively, whereas **this material draws the algorithm that maps a permutation to a pair of standard tableaux**, linking those three things, so it is not the same picture, but it **belongs to the same combinatorics family and overlaps conceptually**. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, empty or a number from 1 to 10 solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 60 seeds and each of the three rows: the permutation matrix has exactly one dot in every column and row (the number of a dot equals its column), the four fixed types (identity, reversal, shift by 3, multiplication by 2 mod 11) equal separately written arrays; P and Q have left-justified rows, empty rows only at the bottom, **the same shape**, each of 1 to 10 exactly once and strictly increasing along rows and columns (standard Young tableaux); (2) **the inverse correspondence**: on the pair (P, Q) of the picture, another algorithm (reverse bumping: take the entry of P at the box of the largest recorded number out and push it up through the rows, each row giving up the largest number smaller than it) recovers exactly the permutation of the permutation matrix; **Schensted's theorem**: the length of the first row of P equals the longest increasing subsequence found separately by dynamic programming and the number of rows the longest decreasing one; **Schützenberger's symmetry**: P and Q are equal if and only if the permutation is an involution (checked as an "if and only if" for every permutation); the identity has one row, the reversal one column and type 3 is indeed an involution; (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (4) the pictures differ per type and group (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 6, 12 and 24 is 0.0651397705078125, 0.034942626953125, 0.018310546875 and 0.014312744140625) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) my first version of the sampler added 1 too many to the recording tableau Q (its numbers were 2 to 11), which I noticed from the probe's maximum tone of 1.03 and maximum height of 0.856 (above 0.8) and fixed before writing the tests; the first previews I looked at were of the version with this mistake, and after the fix I looked at the previews of seeds 0, 3 and 4 again (without zooming in); (2) the point-by-point check compares 4696 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (3) 29 mutation checks were run: 28 caught and 1 not caught: `entry >= x` instead of `entry > x` in the insertion (the values of a permutation are distinct, so equivalent, I kept the original); 2 more attempts first gave NOMATCH because of prettier's line breaks and were caught when rerun with the reformatted fragments; (4) this time I changed the mutation script's `timeout` to `perl alarm` (see the record of the previous material).

At start-up (per sampler): one row insertion for each of the three permutations (at most 10 steps, each with a linear search in at most 4 rows) and nine 10×10 `Uint8Array` (900 B) and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: robinsonschensted took 80, 65 and 61 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 104, 100 and 100 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`friezegroups` adds the frieze groups, bringing the current catalog from 1180 to 1181 kinds (1182 gallery choices including plain). Mint rounded squares on a dark green ground: **eight friezes** stacked in a 64×64 grid of cells, each 8 rows high, each a small 3×3 glyph with no symmetry at all repeated by **one of the 7 frieze symmetry groups**; the horizontal mirror line of a strip lies between its rows 3 and 4. The 7 groups are p1 (translations by 8 only), p11g (a glide reflection: mirror in the horizontal line and move by 8), p1m1 (the horizontal mirror and translations by 8), p11m (vertical mirror lines at the column 5, translations by 16), p2 (half-turns about points near the column 5, translations by 16), p2mg (the vertical mirror and the glide reflection) and p2mm (both mirrors, translations by 16). The eight strips are one of each of the 7 groups and one more of an extra group, in an order shuffled by hash keys. There are 6 glyphs (an F shape and others). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the glyph and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: the group sets the shuffle and, mod 7, the group of the extra strip. A filled cell has tone 0.95 and height 1 times 0.8, an empty one 0.1 and 0.2 times; the gap between cells is 0.07 of a cell, the rounding 0.16 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the names of the 7 frieze groups (IUC symbols p1, p11g, p1m1, p11m, p2, p2mg, p2mm) and their generating symmetries are written from memory and I did not look them up in the International Tables — but the tests derive the actual symmetries of every strip from the picture and compare them with my remembered table "combination of symmetries → group name". Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before applying the code): frieze = 0/0. I read the first part (about 300 characters) of the entry for `wallpapergroups` (the 12 plane symmetry groups of the square lattice, one group per seed, the symmetry group of the picture being exactly the chosen one): **this is its one-dimensional analogue**, and the style of verification (finding the symmetries from the picture) is similar too, but here the 7 frieze groups are drawn together in one picture, one per strip, so it is not the same picture, but it belongs to the same "symmetry groups" family and overlaps conceptually. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, filled or empty solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 60 seeds, each of the eight strips is **tried with every translation, the horizontal mirror, every position of a vertical mirror, every centre of a half-turn and every glide shift**, giving its actual combination of symmetries (smallest period, horizontal mirror, vertical mirror, half-turn, glide reflection), the table gives the group name, and the result is **each of the seven groups once plus the extra group of the seed once**, with the smallest period of every strip right for its group (8 for p1 and p1m1, 16 for the others) and no strip empty; since the glyph itself has no symmetry, the symmetries of each group must be exactly those it should have (one too many or too few is caught); (2) the strip of the group p1 holds the glyph and its translations by 8 and nothing else (cell by cell); (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (4) the pictures differ per glyph and group (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 6, 12 and 24 is 0.138671875, 0.10546875, 0.09375 and 0.09765625) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 4668 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (2) 30 mutation checks were run and **all caught** (including the shift of each generating symmetry, its mirror flag, the flip, shift and mirror when composing, the row and column offsets, the extra group and the shuffle key); my first run of the mutation script showed "no result" for every one of them (it finished in about 2.7 seconds) because the newly written script called `timeout`, which does not exist in the system's bash (only my shell has it built in), so vitest never ran; I changed to `perl -e 'alarm …'` and reran the whole batch, and the 30 results above are from the rerun; (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; (4) I verified only the symmetry groups, nothing about the artistic quality of the glyphs.

At start-up (per sampler): for each of the 7 groups one closure of the generators (at most a few dozen affine maps, each applied to at most 6 cells of the glyph), giving 7 `Uint8Array` of 64×8 (about 3.5 KB in all), one sort of 8 entries and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: friezegroups took 102, 145 and 109 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 178, 191 and 198 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`huffmancodes` adds Huffman codes, bringing the current catalog from 1179 to 1180 kinds (1181 gallery choices including plain). Bronze rounded squares on a dark brown ground: **two prefix codes for the same weights**, in two rows of two panels: the **Huffman code** on the left and the **Shannon–Fano code** on the right; a panel has 16 rows (a symbol per row, from the heaviest down) and the code is written from the left, a 0 as a dimmer and a 1 as a brighter cell, with nothing after its end (tone 0.12). The 6 sets of 16 weights are: 0 the approximate frequencies of the 16 commonest English letters (in thousandths: 127, 91, 82, 75, 70, 67, 63, 61, 60, 43, 40, 28, 28, 24, 24, 22, from memory), 1 Zipf (27720/k), 2 Fibonacci numbers, 3 powers of 2, 4 all equal and 5 squares. Huffman merges the two lightest nodes again and again (the first taken gets the bit 0); Shannon–Fano splits the symbols, sorted from the heaviest down, into two runs of weights as equal as possible (taking the first best split), the left run getting a 0 and the right a 1, and recurses. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the weights of the top row and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: (the group mod 5) plus 1 is how many sets "later" the bottom row's weights are (1 to 5). The picture is a code that widens from the left: equal weights give a neat 4-cell band, and Fibonacci numbers and powers of 2 give a staircase triangle 15 cells long. The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the Huffman and Shannon–Fano algorithms and "a Huffman code is optimal and its average length lies between the entropy and the entropy plus 1" are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the tests actually verify these properties. The approximate letter frequencies are also from memory, common approximate values, not measured from a corpus. Checked for absence (`absent.sh` actually run, before applying the code): huffman, shannon, fano and prefixcode all gave 0/0 (earlier I also saw lempel, bwt, reedsolomon, crc and golay at 0/0); I **did not read any other entry** (I found no related coding-theory material; `necklaces` and the like are unrelated). The test checks (everything read back from the picture, none / bit 0 / bit 1 solved from the height at the middle of every cell, and the code must be bits followed only by empty cells): (1) for 60 seeds and every weight set: **no code is the start of another** (a prefix code), **the Kraft sum is exactly 1** (the code tree is full, for both codes), the total of weight times length of the Huffman code **equals the least possible value** (computed another way: merging in a sorted list and adding the weight of every merge), the average length lies **between the entropy and the entropy plus 1** (the entropy computed separately from the weights), a heavier symbol never has a longer Huffman code than a lighter one, and the Shannon–Fano total is no less than the Huffman one; (2) known shapes: equal weights give all 16 symbols 4 bits in both codes, and the Huffman lengths of Fibonacci numbers and of powers of 2 are 1, 2, …, 14, 15, 15 (a property I remembered, and the test measured it); (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (4) the pictures differ per weight set and group (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 6, 12 and 24 is 0.191650390625, 0.14306640625, 0.11212158203125 and 0.0528564453125) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 4668 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (2) 30 mutation checks were run: 28 caught and 2 not caught: Shannon–Fano taking the later one on a tie when looking for the split (`gap <= bestGap`; no tie affects the result on this data, equivalent, I kept the original), and the tie-break by symbol number in the Huffman sort (`|| a.symbols[0] - b.symbols[0]`; the stable sort already keeps the order, equivalent, **I removed it from the code** and left a one-line comment); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; (4) **two incidents in my working environment**: half way through the mutation checks, the `.git` link file and many long-untouched files of my working directory `/private/tmp/xyz-ct` were deleted (just after 00:00 on 6 November) and `vitest` reported "no tests" because `packages/math/src/hypot.js` was missing; I recreated the directory from `e850da122` with `git worktree add -f --detach`, reran the generator and the test assembly and reran the 12 mutation checks that had reported "no tests" on the recreated tree. After that the whole machine **rebooted** (`uptime` showed 4 minutes when I came back) and `/tmp` was emptied: all my helper scripts (generators, preview, mutation and gate scripts) and the uncommitted Huffman working tree disappeared with it (the committed work is all in the main directory's repository, nothing lost there). I rewrote the preset, the sampler and the tests from the text kept in the conversation (the same content as before the reboot, the only difference being that the Huffman sort is already the stable-sort version), and the `absent.sh`, generator and gate scripts are new rewrites; the 7 tests pass after the rewrite; **the results of the 30 mutation checks were obtained before the reboot and were not rerun after the rewrite**; (5) timing of the test block: the tone-range test took about 7 s (cold start) and the others 0.04 to 1.0 s each.

At start-up (per sampler): one Huffman run (16 nodes, 15 merges, each with a sort) and one Shannon–Fano run (recursive splitting) for each of the two weight sets, four 16×16 `Uint8Array` (1,024 B) and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: huffmancodes took 184, 172 and 170 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 349, 345 and 327 ms in the same environment (measured before the reboot, not remeasured since); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`burrowswheeler` adds the Burrows–Wheeler transform, bringing the current catalog from 1178 to 1179 kinds (1180 gallery choices including plain). Lavender rounded squares on a dark indigo ground: **the Burrows–Wheeler transform of two texts**, one per row of two panels: on the left the 24 **rotations** of the text (row j is the text turned j places to the left), on the right the same rotations **sorted**, whose **last column is the transform**. A text is 24 long: 23 characters and the unique smallest end symbol $ (symbol 0; the other characters are the symbols 1 to 5 in alphabet order). There are 5 fixed texts and 1 random one: 0 the Fibonacci word (a → ab, b → a), 1 the Thue–Morse word, 2 mississippi repeated, 3 banana repeated, 4 the four letters A, C, G, T by hash keys and 5 abracadabra repeated, each cut to 23 characters and followed by $. The tone of a cell, 0.2 to 0.95, and its height (0.8 times 0.3 plus 0.7 times) follow "symbol / 5", and the panels are parted by wider gaps. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the top text and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: (the group mod 5) plus 1 is how many texts "later" the bottom text is (1 to 5), and it sets the key of the random text. The picture is slanted stripes (rotations) next to the vertical stripes and structure of the sorted matrix. The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definition of the Burrows–Wheeler transform (sort all rotations, take the last column), its reversibility and the recovery by the last-to-first (LF) mapping are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the tests actually verify them. Checked for absence (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): burrows, wheeler, bwt, huffman, lempel, reedsolomon, crc and golay all gave 0/0 (after writing it burrows gives 1/0, which is this very kind). I read the first part of the entries for `editdistance`, `sortingtraces`, `necklaces`, `thuemorse` and `fibonacciword` (about 230 characters each): `thuemorse` and `fibonacciword` **write those two words row by row into a grid**, whereas here they are the **input texts** of a rotation matrix (the first 23 characters), and what is drawn is the rotations and the sorted matrix, so it is not the same picture, but **the texts of variants 0 and 1 are the same words as in those two materials**; `sortingtraces` shows the trace of a sorting algorithm step by step, unlike this "sort all rotations at once". The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the symbol solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 60 seeds and each text: every row of the rotation panel is the text turned one place more, the text ends with exactly one $, the five fixed texts equal words written separately (the Fibonacci word by concatenating the two previous words and the Thue–Morse word by t(2k) = t(k), t(2k + 1) = 1 − t(k), unlike the sampler's string substitution and the parity of the number of 1 bits), and the sorted panel equals the rotations ordered **by sorting the starting places by suffix order** (the unique smallest $ makes the suffix order the rotation order; the sampler compares rotations character by character); (2) it is **reversible**: from the last column read back from the picture the text is recovered through the last-to-first mapping, equal to the first row of the rotation panel, and the last column has the same multiset of symbols as the text; (3) the random text uses all four letters and differs between groups; (4) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (5) the pictures differ per text and group (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 6, 12 and 24 is 0.295806884765625, 0.2415771484375, 0.21636962890625 and 0.222015380859375) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 4671 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (2) 31 mutation checks were run: 27 caught and 4 not caught at first: changing the number of letters of the random text to 3 or fixing the hash at every position to `hash(0, …)` (two attempts: the original tests did not pin the random text, so **I added test (3)** and reran, and both were caught); the "group" term in the key (`seed` already contains the group, so equivalent; **I removed it from the code**); and comparing only n − 1 places when sorting (two rotations have the same multiset of symbols, so when the first n − 1 places agree the last one does too, hence equivalent; I kept the original); (3) in the first version of the added test I wrote the seed 42 for the bottom row, but its bottom text is banana repeated, not the random one, which made the "differs" assertion vacuous; after noticing I changed it to 48 and reran the 3 mutations; (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; (5) timing of the test block: the tone-range test took 8.6 s (cold start) and the others 0.1 to 1.3 s each.

At start-up (per sampler): the 24 rotations (24×24) of each of the two texts and one sort of each (the comparator looks at up to 24 places) and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: burrowswheeler took 167, 164 and 146 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 398, 338 and 384 ms in the same environment (the host load was high); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`lightsoutpuzzles` adds Lights Out puzzles, bringing the current catalog from 1177 to 1178 kinds (1179 gallery choices including plain). Cream rounded squares on a dark brown ground: **two Lights Out puzzles**, one per row of two panels: the board of lit lights on the left and a **fewest-press solution** on the right (a press toggles the cell and its four neighbours; a lit or pressed cell has tone 0.95 and height 1, a dark one 0.18 and 0.3). A puzzle is made by pressing the cells of a pattern on a dark board: 0 only the centre, 1 the cross through the centre, 2 every cell, 3 the cells with i + j even, 4 the border ring and 5 the main diagonal; the solution is found by Gaussian elimination over GF(2) and, when the board has quiet patterns (the solution is not unique), the one with the fewest presses of all solutions is taken. The board sizes are 5, 6, 7 and 9. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the pattern of the top puzzle and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: the group mod 4 picks the size and (the group divided by 4, rounded down) mod 5 plus 1 is how many patterns "later" the bottom puzzle's pattern is (1 to 5), so seeds 0 to 5 have size 5 and a bottom pattern one after the top one. The picture is made of symmetric patterns of lights and presses. The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the rules of Lights Out and "5×5 has 4 solutions, 9×9 has 256, 6×6 and 7×7 a unique one" are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature (the tests actually count the solutions). Checked for absence (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): lightsout = 0/0 and nonogram = 0/0 (after writing it lightsout gives 1/0, which is this very kind). I read the first part of the entries for `sandpileidentity` (the identity of an abelian sandpile), `graecolatin`, `xortable` and `sudoku` (about 200 characters each, not the whole entries): they are all mathematical tables on a grid, but none solves a linear system over GF(2), so it is not a repeat. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, lit or not solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 120 seeds (6 patterns × 20 groups) both puzzles: the board of lit lights is exactly the result of pressing the pattern on a dark board (a separate simulation), and **pressing the solution on the picture puts every light out** (a direct simulation of the presses, independent of Gaussian elimination); (2) **fewest presses**: all solutions of every board are listed by another algorithm, **light chasing** (enumerate the 2^n presses of the first row; each other row is decided by the cells of the row above that are still lit; a choice is a solution if the last row ends dark), and the solution on the picture is one of them and has as many presses as the minimum of all; the number of solutions is 4 for size 5, 1 each for sizes 6 and 7 and 256 for size 9 (I filled in these four numbers after reading them on a first run of the test; they agree with the nullities 2, 0, 0, 8 I remember); (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point; (4) the pictures differ per pattern, size and bottom pattern (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seed 0 and seeds 1, 6, 12 and 24 is 0.28302001953125, 0.1998138427734375, 0.1374053955078125 and 0.1880950927734375) and one seed repeated gives the same picture. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 4731 to 4815 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 4650; (2) 33 mutation checks were run: 29 caught, 3 not caught and 1 hung: the `&& rank < cells` of the elimination loop (equivalent, **I removed it from the code**); the enumeration of combinations of quiet patterns stopped one short (`mask < 2 ** quiet.length - 1`): not caught, I did not investigate, most likely the fewest-press solution of these patterns never needs "all the quiet patterns added together", so the test data does not reach that branch, which does not prove it correct; reading the table transposed (`px * size + py`): not caught, I think because all the patterns and the chosen solutions are symmetric under transposition, but I did not check each; inverting the test for a free variable (`pivotColumn.includes(c)`) makes it enumerate 2 to the power of dozens of combinations and **hung until my 600 s timeout**, which does not count as caught; also "later one wins on a tie" (`weight <= bestWeight`) was caught by the pinned fractions of lit cells, not by the "fewest presses" check, since that check accepts any fewest-press solution; (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; (4) timing of the test block: the tone-range test took 7.5 s (cold start) and the others 0.1 to 0.8 s each.

At start-up (per sampler): one GF(2) Gaussian elimination for each of the two puzzles (rows of a `Uint8Array` of at most 81×82; for size 9 there are 8 free presses and 255 combinations of quiet patterns are enumerated) and the two boards. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: lightsoutpuzzles took 239, 152 and 231 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 358, 423 and 461 ms in the same environment (the host load was high); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`pseudoprimeliars` adds the liars of primality tests, bringing the current catalog from 1176 to 1177 kinds (1178 gallery choices including plain). Ice-blue rounded squares on a dark navy ground: 64×64 cells, **the row j is the odd number n = start + 2j and the column i the base a = firstBase + i (from 2 or from 66)**, a cell answering "does the base a pass the primality test for n". The 4 tests are Fermat (a^(n−1) ≡ 1 mod n), Euler (a^((n−1)/2) ≡ ±1), strong or Miller–Rabin (a^d ≡ 1, or some squaring of a^d is −1, d the odd part of n − 1) and Euler–Jacobi (a^((n−1)/2) ≡ the Jacobi symbol (a/n)). A cell is of four kinds: a shares a factor with n (the faintest), a is a **witness** that n is composite (dimmer), a is a **liar** and n is prime (for a prime every a is one, so the whole row glows) and a is a liar although n is composite (the brightest, a pseudoprime; for a Carmichael number every coprime a is a Fermat liar). The tones are 0.12, 0.38, 0.7 and 0.97, the heights 0.15, 0.35, 0.7 and 1 times 0.8. The 8 windows start at 521, 1065, 1689, 2425, 2781, 6561, 8871 and 3001: the row 20 of the first seven holds a Carmichael number (561, 1105, 1729, 2465, 2821, 6601 and 8911). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 4 picks the test and ⌊seed / 4⌋ the group: the group mod 8 picks the window and (the group divided by 8, rounded down) mod 2 the range of bases, so seeds 0 to 3 are the four tests on the window of 561 with the bases 2 to 65. The picture is made of horizontal stripes: a prime's row is lit all along and a composite's row is a scatter of lit dots. The gap between cells is 0.08 of a cell, the rounding 0.16 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definitions of the primality tests, the Carmichael numbers 561, 1105, 1729, 2465, 2821, 6601 and 8911 and "strong liars ⊆ Euler liars ⊆ Fermat liars" are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature (the tests actually verify the inclusions and that every window holds a Carmichael number). Checked for absence (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): miller, witness, korselt, modexp and powermod all gave 0/0; fermat = 0/1 (only mentioned in the README) and primality = 0/1. I read the first part of the entries for `multiplicativeorder` (multiplicative orders for n = 2 to 49, ord_n(a)/φ(n)), `totienttable` (φ(n)/n) and `abundantnumbers` (the table of abundant numbers): `multiplicativeorder` is also a table with (n, a) as coordinates, and a^(n−1) ≡ 1 ⇔ ord_n(a) divides n − 1, so **Fermat liars are mathematically related to multiplicative orders**; what differs here is that n is an odd number from 521 to 8,997 and what is drawn is the liars and witnesses of four primality tests (and that a Carmichael number's row has no Fermat witness) rather than the order, so it is not the same picture, but it **belongs to the same "(n, a) table" family**. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the kind solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 64 seeds (4 tests × 16 groups) every cell equals a separately written test using big-integer modular powers, trial-division factorisation, and the Jacobi symbol as the **product of Legendre symbols of the prime factors by Euler's criterion** (the sampler uses the reciprocity algorithm); (2) **theorems**: for a prime n there is no witness in any of the four tests; the strong liars ⊆ the Euler–Jacobi liars ⊆ the Euler liars ⊆ the Fermat liars (cell by cell); every Carmichael number (Korselt's criterion: squarefree and p − 1 divides n − 1 for every prime factor p, which I computed separately by trial division) has no witness in its row of the Fermat test, and each of the first seven windows holds at least one Carmichael number; (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 4706 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds, hence the same number), with the lower bound 4600; (2) 27 mutation checks were run: 22 caught and 5 not caught: the `a % m` in `power` (a is always below m), the `m === 1 ? sign : 0` at the end of the Jacobi loop (it is only called for coprime a, so m is always 1) and the `m > 1` in `isPrime` (the windows start at 521) — these three are equivalent and **I simplified them away in the code**; `=== 1` of the Fermat test replaced by `<= 1` (a modular power of a coprime a cannot be 0, equivalent); and the strong test's loop run once more (`k <= squarings`): the extra step checks whether a^(n−1) ≡ −1, and I confirmed by brute force that none of the 53,125 coprime cells of all the windows has that, so it is equivalent on this data, not a gap in the test, but I did not prove it impossible for general n; (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8 without zooming in; (4) the whole block of tests took about 33 s (with loading) at a host load average of about 84, the heaviest being the tone-range test at 9.7 s (cold start and 3 seeds × 65,536 samples) and the cell-by-cell comparison at 2.8 s.

At start-up (per sampler): a `Uint8Array(64²)` of 4,096 B for the kinds (one modular power per cell and one trial-division primality check per row, at most 4,096 modular powers) and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: pseudoprimeliars took 154, 145 and 143 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 364, 361 and 393 ms in the same environment (the host load was high); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`finitefieldtables` adds the operation tables of finite fields, bringing the current catalog from 1175 to 1176 kinds (1177 gallery choices including plain). Gold rounded squares on a dark navy ground: **the addition and multiplication tables of a finite field GF(q)**, in two rows of two panels: the addition table on the left and the multiplication table on the right; **the top and the bottom row are the same field with two namings of the elements**. The 6 fields are GF(4), GF(8), GF(9), GF(16), GF(5) and GF(7) (q = p^k). An element is a polynomial of degree below k with coefficients mod p, named by the number whose digits in base p are the coefficients, so the names 0 and 1 are the zero and the one of the field; x^k is reduced by the preset (GF(4): x² = x + 1; GF(8): x³ = x + 1; GF(9): x² = 2, that is x² + 1 = 0; GF(16): x⁴ = x + 1; GF(5) and GF(7) are the integers mod a prime). In each row the names 2 to q − 1 are shuffled by hash keys.
