The tone of a cell, 0.2 to 0.95, and its height (0.8 times 0.3 plus 0.7 times) follow "name / (q − 1)", and the panels are parted by wider gaps. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the field and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group (which changes the two shuffles). The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the construction of GF(q) and the irreducible polynomials (x² + x + 1, x³ + x + 1, x² + 1 mod 3, x⁴ + x + 1) are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature — the field axioms in the tests actually verify them. Checked for absence (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): galois, finitefield, gf2 and primitiveroot all gave 0/0; finite = 0/12 and field = 5/36. I read the first part of the entries for `cayleytable` (multiplication tables of groups of order 16, six groups, checking the Latin square, the identity and associativity), `latinsquares` (the complete enumeration of some classes of Latin squares), `projectiveplane` and `walshmatrix` (about 400 characters each, not the whole entries): this material is a field with **both addition and multiplication**, and the tests check distributivity, multiplicative inverses and the cyclic multiplicative group, unlike the one-operation group tables, but both are operation tables (the addition table has a conceptual overlap with the tables of Z_p; I did not compare cell by cell). The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the name solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 36 seeds (6 fields × 6 groups) on every panel pair of both rows: 0 is the additive identity, 1 the multiplicative one, 0 times anything is 0, addition and multiplication are commutative and associative, multiplication distributes over addition, the addition table is a Latin square and the multiplication table without 0 is a Latin square (so every non-zero element has an inverse and there are no zero divisors) — together these **prove that the two tables on the picture really are a field**, whatever algorithm the sampler uses; the characteristic (how many times 1 is added to reach 0) equals p; the multiplicative group is cyclic (an element of order q − 1 exists, the order found by repeated multiplication); (2) the two rows have the same distribution of multiplicative orders (the same field in two namings); (3) the tables of the two rows differ, the pictures of different groups differ (the fraction of lit cells that differ between seeds 0 and 1 is 0.3337249755859375 and between seeds 3 and 9, GF(16), 0.2659454345703125) and one seed repeated gives the same picture; (4) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) seeds 0 and 6 (GF(4)) do not differ in the lit cells (0): GF(4) has only the names 2 and 3 to swap, and both tones are above my 0.5 threshold, so I compared the groups with GF(16); (2) the point-by-point check compares 4668 to 4795 of the 6000 sample points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 4550; (3) 29 valid mutation checks were run on the sampler: 27 caught and 2 equivalent (a `reverse()` before the sort: the comparator is a total order, so the input order does not matter; and reading the table transposed: addition and multiplication are commutative, so the transposed table is the same); 1 more was an invalid mutation I wrote as an identity (`q = prime ** degree - 0 + 0 * degree`) and is not counted; (4) I also replaced the five reduction polynomials in the preset: GF(8) with x³ = x² + x, GF(9) with x² = 1, GF(16) with x⁴ = x² + 1 and GF(4) with x² = 1, **all caught** (reducible polynomials, so the field axioms fail); GF(8) with x³ = x² + 1 (x³ + x² + 1 is also irreducible, so the result is still a field) was caught too, but by the pinned fraction of lit cells and tone statistics, not by the field axioms; (5) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; (6) this block of tests takes about 22 s (with loading); the field-axiom test is the heaviest.

At start-up (per sampler): four q×q `Uint8Array` tables (at most 1,024 B), a sort of the shuffled names (at most 14 elements) and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: finitefieldtables took 349, 277 and 283 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 413, 261 and 337 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`minesweeperboards` adds a solved Minesweeper board, bringing the current catalog from 1174 to 1175 kinds (1176 gallery choices including plain). Coral rounded squares on a dark maroon ground: **a finished game of Minesweeper**, n×n rounded cells, every cell without a mine showing the **number** of mines among its (up to 8) neighbours as pips of a 3×3 dice — filled clockwise along the outer ring from the top left (0 to 8 pips; the middle pip is only lit for a mine) — and a mine showing **all nine pips on a brighter, higher plate**. The mines are the cells with the smallest hash keys (exactly "mines" of them). The 6 boards are 9×9 with 10 mines, 9×9 with 16, 12×12 with 24, 12×12 with 30, 16×16 with 40 and 8×8 with 9. The plate tone is 0.3 (mine 0.55), the plate height 0.3 (mine 0.55) times 0.8, a lit pip has tone 0.95 and 0.4 more height, and an unlit pip is a socket of tone 0.12. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the board and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group (a different hash key, so different mine positions), so seeds 0 to 5 are the six boards of group 0. The gap between cells is 0.05 of a cell and the rounding 0.12; the margin between the pips and the plate is 0.14, the gap between pips 0.025 and the rounding of a pip 0.25 of its half width; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.5 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the rules of Minesweeper (the number is the count of mines among the 8 neighbours) are written from memory and the arrangement of the pips as a 3×3 ring is my own design, not the way the original game draws it. Checked for absence (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): minesweeper, nonogram, hitori, kakuro, slitherlink and sliding all gave 0/0; after writing it I also ran dice = 1/9, domino = 3/15 and pips = 0/2 (mines = 1/1 is this very kind). I read the first part of the entries for `gamedice` (6×6 ivory dice with the standard 1 to 6 pips, thrown by the seed) and `dominoboards` (the enumeration of domino tilings) and scanned the other README entries for "mines": only the literal coincidence in `stringart`; `gamedice` also uses dice pips, but here the pips are **the number of neighbouring mines, up to 8, filled along the outer ring**, on a finished game board with mines rather than thrown dice, so there is a conceptual resemblance but it is not the same thing. The test checks (everything read back from the picture: the plate type solved from the height at the middle of the margin between the plate edge and the pips, and whether each of the nine pips is lit from its tone at its exact middle): (1) for 36 seeds (6 boards × 6 groups): the number of mines is exactly the one for the board, **the lit pips of every cell without a mine are exactly the first "number of mines around" places of the ring** (the number of mines around is computed separately from the **list** of mines read back from the picture, by adding one to each neighbour of every mine rather than by looking around each cell, so it differs from the sampler's algorithm), and a mine has all nine pips lit on the higher plate; (2) the mine positions of groups 0, 1, 2 and 3 all differ, the fraction of lit cells that differ between seeds 0 and 1 (different boards) and between seeds 0 and 6 (same board, different group) is 0.2441864013671875 and 0.18548583984375, and one seed repeated gives the same picture; (3) the tone, height and occlusion of the plate and of every pip are compared point by point (the nine pips tried one by one for the nearest, not with the sampler's clamp; points near an edge are skipped). **Notes (honest)**: (1) on the first run I read the "plate type" at a place too near the plate edge, inside the smoothing zone, and got 0.29 instead of 0.3, so three tests failed; that was a **mistake in the test**, and it passed after I read at the middle of the margin (further than the smoothing half-width from both edges); (2) the point-by-point check compares 3,026 to 3,047 of the 6,000 sample points per seed (those near the edges of pips and plates are skipped, so fewer than before), with the lower bound 2,900; (3) 32 mutation checks were run: 29 caught and 3 not caught: whether the pip mask `socket` is multiplied by `mask` (the pips are entirely within the plate, so equivalent; **I removed that multiplication from the code**), the exclusion of the cell itself (di, dj) = (0, 0) from the neighbour loop (if the cell is not a mine its number is unaffected; if it is a mine it shows 9, so equivalent; **I removed it from the code**), and adding `% 3` to the upper clamp of the nearest-pip index (it only changes the index in the right-hand margin, where the socket is 0; I think it is equivalent but have not proved it); 4 further attempts gave NOMATCH because of stray backslashes in my shell string or prettier's line breaks (2 of the reruns also failed to match the first time), and were rerun against the reformatted text; (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; (5) the mines look randomly scattered in the montage, but I ran no statistical test.

At start-up (per sampler): the n² indices sorted by hash key (at most 256 numbers; the comparator calls `hash` twice per comparison), two `Uint8Array(n²)` (at most 256 B) and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one plate distance, one pip distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: minesweeperboards took 222, 188 and 172 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 387, 294 and 289 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`beattysequences` adds the complementary Beatty sequences, bringing the current catalog from 1173 to 1174 kinds (1175 gallery choices including plain). Aqua rounded squares on a dark teal ground: the consecutive whole numbers are laid out row by row in a w×w grid (the cell (i, j) holds m = 1 + offset + j·w + i), **the first tone (the brightest and highest) marks the terms of the Beatty sequence ⌊kα⌋ and the second tone those of ⌊kβ⌋, with 1/α + 1/β = 1**; by Rayleigh's theorem every whole number is in exactly one of them, so every cell is either bright or dim and there is no third kind. The 6 alphas are the golden ratio φ, √2, 1 + √2, √3, √5 and 2 + √3. The tones are 0.92 (first sequence), 0.4 (second) and 0.12 for a number in neither or both (ruled out by the theorem and never shown); heights are 1, 0.55 and 0.18 times 0.8. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks alpha and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: the group mod 4 picks the width 24, 32, 34 or 40 and (the group divided by 4, rounded down) mod 8 times 997 is the offset of the start, so seeds 0 to 5 are the six alphas with width 24 starting at 1. Because the row length is close to the continued-fraction denominators of alpha, the picture is covered with slanted or nearly vertical quasi-periodic stripes and moiré. The gap between cells is 0.07 of a cell, the rounding 0.15 and the edge smoothing 0.06; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the Beatty and Rayleigh theorems and the partner β of each alpha are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature (I checked 1/α + 1/β = 1 for the six pairs, and the whole-number formulas in the test are written the same way). Checked for absence (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run, before writing the code): sturm, christoffel and beatty all gave 0/0; fibonacciword = 1/3. I read the first part of the entries for `fibonacciword` (the Fibonacci word written row by row into a 55×55 grid, the 1s glowing) and `wythoffnim` (a Grundy table, with the cells with G = 0 cross-checked against ⌊kφ⌋ and ⌊kφ²⌋): **the φ variant of `beattysequences` is the same kind of picture as `fibonacciword`** (the n-th letter of the Fibonacci word marks whether n is in the lower Wythoff sequence), differing only in the width and the display (here both sequences have a colour, the widths are 24/32/34/40 and there is a start offset); the other five alphas (√2, 1 + √2, √3, √5, 2 + √3) and the two-colour complementary display are specific to this material, but **it is not an entirely new concept**. The test checks (read back from the picture, the class solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 192 seeds (6 alphas × 32 groups) the class of every cell equals a separately written test that uses only whole-number arithmetic and exact integer square roots (`⌊k·√2⌋ = isqrt(2k²)`, `⌊k·φ⌋ = ⌊(k + isqrt(5k²)) / 2⌋` and so on, with β written by hand as φ + 1, 2 + √2, 1 + √2/2, (3 + √3)/2, (5 + √5)/4 and (1 + √3)/2), while the sampler uses floating-point `Math.floor(k * alpha)`; (2) **Rayleigh's theorem**: for 39 seeds (every fifth), no cell on the picture is in neither or both of the sequences, and the number of cells of the first sequence differs from N/α by less than 1 (N consecutive whole numbers); (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) on the first run the tone test and the different-views test used a brightness threshold (0.7) that disagreed with the numbers I measured (threshold 0.5), because I forgot to change it when pasting the test; it passed with 0.5; (2) the point-by-point check compares about 4851 points per seed (4849 to 4856), with the lower bound 4700; (3) 22 mutation checks were run: 19 caught and 3 not caught: `last` one too large (the write to an index beyond the Uint8Array is ignored, equivalent), k starting from 0 (⌊0⌋ = 0 is below the start, equivalent), and the tone of the "third kind" `toneOther` replaced by `toneSecond` (a branch the theorem guarantees is never taken, so no input can catch it; I kept it because the test uses it to read "in neither or both" off the picture); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; (5) this block of tests takes about 18.6 s, longer than the previous ones (the cell-by-cell comparison over 192 seeds).

At start-up (per sampler): a `Uint8Array(w²)` (at most 1,600 B) of marks (about N/α and N/β calls of `Math.floor` for the two sequences) and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: beattysequences took 263, 167 and 152 ms (three runs) and talbotcarpet 371, 291 and 272 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`diophantinegrid` adds a grid of Diophantine solutions, bringing the current catalog from 1172 to 1173 kinds (1174 gallery choices including plain). Silver rounded squares on a charcoal ground: 64×64 cells, the cell (i, j) standing for the pair of integers (a, b) = (offset + i + 1, offset + j + 1), **lit when a quadratic form is exactly the square of a whole number c**. The 6 forms are a² + b² = c² (Pythagorean triples), a² + ab + b² = c² (triangles with an angle of 120°), a² − ab + b² = c² (60°), (a² + b²)/2 = c², a² + 3b² = c² and a² − b² = c² (only for a above b, c a positive whole number). A lit cell is of two kinds: a and b coprime (a **primitive solution**) is the brightest and highest, a and b with a common factor dimmer and lower, and a cell that is not lit is a faint low tile (tones 0.12/0.55/0.95, heights 0.18/0.6/1 times 0.8). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the form and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the window: the offset is (⌊seed / 6⌋ mod 8) × 32, so seeds 0 to 5 are the six forms as 64×64 cells starting at (1, 1). The picture looks like a night sky: the non-trivial solutions are scattered stars and trivial ones such as a = b make diagonal streaks (for a² − ab + b², a = b gives c = a). The gap between cells is 0.08 of a cell, the rounding 0.16 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the solutions of the forms and Euclid's formula for Pythagorean triples are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature. Checked for absence (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run, but only after the code was written; I temporarily `git stash`ed the new code so the check saw the original catalog): diophant = 0/0, triple = 0/4, primitive = 0/2, pythagor = 2/9, eisenstein = 1/3, gcd = 1/3. I read the first part of `gcdtable` (gcd(col + 1 + a, row + 1 + b) toned by 1 − 1/gcd, lighting up along lines and diagonals) and `eisensteinprimes` (Eisenstein primes on a triangular lattice); `gcdtable` is likewise a square grid of integer pairs (a, b), so **there is overlap**: this one draws only the sparse subset where a quadratic form is a square and tells primitive from non-primitive, so the picture differs from the line network of gcd; `pythagorastree` (Pythagoras trees; I only read its first sentence) and `pythagoreantiles` (I did not read its entry, I only know its name) are different things. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the class solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 48 seeds (6 forms × 8 windows) the class of every cell equals a separately written test (a set of the squares of 0 to 699 looked up without a square root, and a gcd by subtraction for the primitive ones); (2) **Euclid's formula**: for the 8 windows the set of primitive (a, b) on the picture equals exactly the set made from (m² − n², 2mn) (m > n, coprime, of different parity; both orders) inside the window; a lit cell stays lit when doubled (2a, 2b) (the forms are homogeneous); for the first four (symmetric) forms the lit cells are invariant under swapping a and b; a² − b² is never lit where a ≤ b; (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first version of the test's oracle also counted a = b (c = 0) as a solution of a² − b², which disagreed with the sampler's a > b on 8 seeds; that was a **mistake in the test**, and it passed after the oracle was changed to a > b; (2) the point-by-point check compares 4706 points per seed (the same sample points for all 9 seeds, hence the same number), with the lower bound 4600; (3) 28 mutation checks were run: 26 caught and 2 equivalent (`Math.round(Math.sqrt)` replaced by `Math.floor`: the square root of a perfect square is exact, so the result is the same; and the "sum is even" check of the form (a² + b²)/2: an odd sum halved is a half-integer that cannot be a square, so the check was redundant and **I removed it from the code**, leaving a one-line comment); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; (5) the number of lit cells for seeds 0 to 5 (read back from the sampler, equal to the oracle of the test) is 74, 68, 140, 102, 127 and 54.

At start-up (per sampler): a `Uint8Array(64²)` of 4,096 B for the classes (one square test per cell, at most 4,096 square roots) and the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: diophantinegrid took 549, 248, 205, 174 and 171 ms (five runs) and talbotcarpet 596, 353, 399, 260 and 261 ms in the same environment (both slower in the first two, maybe other load on the host, which I did not measure); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`transformbasis` adds the basis images of a transform, bringing the current catalog from 1171 to 1172 kinds (1173 gallery choices including plain). Pink rounded pixels on a dark violet ground: **the N by N basis images of a two-dimensional transform**, as N by N panels (the panel of the column u and the row v) of N by N pixels: the **cosine transform** (DCT-II: the pixel (x, y) of the panel (u, v) is cos((2x + 1)uπ/2N)·cos((2y + 1)vπ/2N); a JPEG block is made of these images) or the **Haar wavelet transform** (the product of two Haar functions: the first is 1, the others are +1 on the first half of a block of pixels, −1 on the second half and 0 elsewhere, from the whole row down to pairs of neighbours; N a power of 2). A pixel is a rounded tile whose **tone and height follow (value + 1)/2** (tone 0.2 to 0.95, height 0.8·(0.3 + 0.7·(value + 1)/2)), and the panels are parted by wider gaps. The 6 variants are DCT with N = 8 (64 images of 8×8, 64×64 pixels), Haar with N = 8, DCT with N = 6, Haar with N = 4, DCT with N = 5 and DCT with N = 4. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: bit 1 swaps the columns and rows of the panels (the image of (u, v) becomes that of (v, u)) and bit 2 changes the sign of every value, so seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants as written. The gap between pixels is 0.06 of a pixel (0.3 at the edge of a panel), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definitions of the DCT-II and the Haar transform are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature (I use the unnormalised versions, with values between −1 and 1). Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): dct, jpeg, basis, chebyshev, bessel, wavelet and haar all gave 0/0. I read the beginnings of `walshmatrix` (a Walsh–Hadamard matrix of ±1) and `zernikemodes` (Zernike polynomials on discs; about 400 characters each, not the whole entries): this is the separable two-dimensional cosine and Haar basis images, so it is different. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the value solved from the height at the middle of every pixel; the height is deterministic and has no grain, so it is exact): (1) for 24 seeds (6 variants × 4 groups) the value of every pixel differs by less than 1e-9 from the definition (the cosine formula; the Haar matrix built another way, by the recursion "the upper half is the matrix of half the size with every entry twice, the lower half the pairs (1, −1)"), with the panels swapped or the sign changed by the group; (2) on the images read back: the first image is all 1, **all images are mutually orthogonal** (inner products less than 1e-9), the squared norm of every image is the product of the energies of its two one-dimensional functions, the values of the Haar images are only −1, 0 and 1, and **Parseval's identity**: for a test image the sum of the energies of its projections on all the images equals its own energy (N² orthogonal non-zero images in the space of N² pixels are a basis); (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point (the gaps on the four sides of a pixel at the edge of a panel differ). **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 4715 to 4809 of the 6000 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (2) 29 mutation checks were run and all were caught; (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; the DCT with N = 8 has the layout of the 8×8 basis-image charts that are common in explanations of JPEG; (4) the test image of the Parseval check is an integer sequence I made up, and only one is used.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the table of the one-dimensional functions (N×N numbers, N at most 8). At sampling time (per pixel): two table look-ups and a product, one rounded-rectangle distance (the gaps on the four sides differ) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: transformbasis took 163 ms and 145 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 228 ms and 225 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`hanoistates` adds the states of the Tower of Hanoi, bringing the current catalog from 1170 to 1171 kinds (1172 gallery choices including plain). Lime bars on a dark green ground: **every state of the shortest solution of the Tower of Hanoi** (disks[variant] disks from the first peg to the peg targets[variant]; the smaller disks go to the spare peg, the biggest is moved over, and the smaller ones follow it, so there are 2 ^ disks states from the first to the last, one move apart), one panel per state in the order of the solution: a panel has three pegs side by side, the disks of a peg stacked from the bottom, each a bar centred on its peg whose **width, tone and height follow its size** (tone 0.25 to 0.95, height 0.8·(0.4 + 0.6·(size − 1)/(disks − 1))). The 6 variants are 2, 4 and 6 disks to the third peg (2×2, 4×4 and 8×8 panels, 4, 16 and 64 states) and 2, 4 and 6 disks to the second peg. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: bit 1 draws the pegs from right to left and bit 2 puts the panels in the reverse order (the solution backwards), so seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants as written. The margin round a panel is 0.06, a bar is set in by 0.1 of a row above and below, the edge smoothing is 0.05; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the rules of the Tower of Hanoi and the recursion of the shortest solution (2^n − 1 moves being the least) are written from memory, I did not look them up in the literature, and the test does not prove that it is the least but only checks the structure of this solution. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): hanoi, tower and peg all gave 0/0. I looked at `graycode` (a Gray-code rotary encoder disc; about 330 characters of the beginning, not the whole entry); the sequence of disks moved by the shortest solution is related to the order in which a Gray code changes its bits — this is what I remember, I did not check it, and no test checks the relation; this picture draws the disks on pegs, so it is different. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, by whether there is ink at the middle of every stack place of every peg, and the size solved from the height): (1) for 24 seeds (6 variants × 4 groups) the stacks of all panels equal, one by one, a separate recursion (a list of moves [disk, from, to]), there are 2 ^ disks panels, and the group mirrors the pegs and reverses the order; (2) on the solution read back (the 6 variants): every disk appears once in every state, on every peg the bigger disk is under the smaller, the 2 ^ disks states are all different, the first state is all on the first peg and the last all on the target peg, every step changes exactly two pegs (one loses a disk and the other gains one: the top disk moved and landed on the top of the other peg, never on a smaller disk, since every peg goes from big to small), and the disk moved at step t is 1 plus the number of trailing zeros of t; (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 5511 to 5630 of the 6000 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 5400; (2) 29 mutation checks were run: 28 were caught and 1 was an equivalent mutation: the check of the vertical limits of the panel in `inside` (`py >= 0 && py < 1`) could be taken away with every test still passing, because the gap term above and below a bar is already 0 outside the panel; I therefore removed the redundant check from the code (only the tests of the Tower of Hanoi were run again); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; the bars are small (a panel of 6 disks is 64 px); (4) in my first version the widest bar was a little wider than a peg (0.96) and would have been drawn onto the next peg, making a discontinuity at its border; I changed the widest to 0.8 after looking at the formula (I did not run the 0.96 version).

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the table of the stacks of all the states, a `Uint8Array(2 ^ disks × 3 × disks)` of at most 64×3×6 = 1,152 B, and one recursion (63 moves). At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, two smoothed edges and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: hanoistates took 130 ms and 109 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 189 ms and 194 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`euclideanrhythms` adds Euclidean rhythms, bringing the current catalog from 1169 to 1170 kinds (1171 gallery choices including plain). Amber rounded squares on a dark brown ground: the rhythms E(k, n) of **k onsets spread as evenly as possible round a circle of n steps** (an onset at the step i when (i·k) mod n ≥ n − k, a rotation of what Bjorklund's algorithm gives, in which the gaps between neighbouring onsets, round the circle, are n/k rounded down or up). The tile is a grid of n by n cells, the row k (k from 1 to n, row 1 on top) the rhythm of k onsets; **a step with an onset is toned and raised by the gap that follows it** (the shorter or the longer one; when k divides n all are equally long and count as the shorter), and a step without an onset is a faint low tile (tones 0.12, 0.55 and 0.95, heights 0.18, 0.6 and 1 times cellHeight). The 6 variants are n = 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 and 32. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group, which turns row k to the left by group·k steps (mod n), so seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants unturned. The gap between cells is 0.08 of a cell, the rounding 0.16 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; Euclidean rhythms (Toussaint's name), Bjorklund's algorithm and the formula "an onset at (i·k) mod n ≥ n − k" are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): rhythm, bjorklund, sturmian, christoffel and beatty all gave 0/0. I looked at `necklaces` (binary necklaces; about 330 characters of the beginning, not the whole entry): necklaces are all the circular strings, and this is the most even one of them, so it is different. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the class solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 24 seeds (6 variants × 4 groups) every row (n from 8 to 32, k from 1 to n for each n) is a **rotation** of the result of a separately written Bjorklund algorithm (repeatedly pairing the groups of k [1]s and n − k [0]s), the unturned group 0 equals exactly the formula "the floor of (i + 1)·k/n is more than the floor of i·k/n", and the other groups are that turned left by group·k steps; (2) on every row read back: exactly k onsets, gaps round the circle of only the two sizes ⌊n/k⌋ and ⌈n/k⌉, the class of an onset matching the gap after it, n mod k longer gaps, and in every window of the circle of every length 1 to n − 1 the number of onsets differing by at most 1 (the balance property, brute-forced in N³); (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) my implementation of Bjorklund's algorithm is written from memory, and its result is a rotation of the formula's rhythm for all the n and k tested; this is what I saw, not a proof; (2) the point-by-point check compares 4685 to 4708 of the 6000 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (3) 21 mutation checks were run: 20 were caught and 1 was an equivalent mutation: `gap = … || n` changed to `|| 1` (for k = 1 there is one onset and the gap is 0 or n, neither more than the "shorter" n, so the class is 1 either way); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; the picture is a left-right symmetric lens shape, and I did not look into its relation to other mathematical structures (such as the Farey sequence) and say nothing about it.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the class table, a `Uint8Array(n²)` of at most 1,024 B (n = 32), and one O(n) scan per row. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: euclideanrhythms took 147 ms and 139 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 223 ms and 226 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`editdistance` adds the edit distance table, bringing the current catalog from 1168 to 1169 kinds (1170 gallery choices including plain). Teal rounded squares on a dark green ground: **the dynamic programming table of two words of the same length n** — the cell in row i and column j holds the value for the first i letters of the first word and the first j letters of the second (a table of (n + 1) by (n + 1) cells): the **edit distance** (Levenshtein: the least number of insertions, deletions and substitutions, each worth 1) or the **length of the longest common subsequence**; the **tone and height of a cell follow its value over n** (tone 0.2 to 0.95), and the cells of **one optimal path back from the last cell** are bigger and the highest (the rule: the diagonal step if it fits — a match or a substitution, in the longest common subsequence only a match — else up, else left). The 6 variants are the edit distance of intention / execution (9 letters, a 10×10 table, distance 5), of recurrence / occurrence (10 letters, distance 2), of two 16-letter DNA strings ACGTTGCAAGCTTGAC / AGCTTGACCAGTTGCA (distance 7), and the longest common subsequence of the same three pairs (lengths 5, 8 and 12). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: bit 1 reverses both words and bit 2 swaps them (the table is transposed), so seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants as written. The gap between cells is 0.12 of a cell (0.04 on the path), the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the recurrences of the edit distance and of the longest common subsequence, and the priority of the walk back, are my own definitions (the textbook recurrences are written from memory and not looked up in the literature). Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): levenshtein, lcs and editdistance all gave 0/0 (run again after adding, editdistance of course gives 1). I read the beginning of `euclidsteps` (a table of the steps of Euclid's algorithm) and looked at `sortingtraces`: they are tables or traces of other algorithms, not the dynamic programming table of two words. The two DNA strings are 16 letters I wrote by hand and have no biological meaning. The test checks (everything read back from the picture: the value solved from the tone at the middle of every cell, and for cells off the path also from the height): (1) for 24 seeds (6 variants × 4 groups) the whole table equals, cell by cell, a separate recursion (a memoised definition, not a table fill); (2) on the table read back, the first row and column are i + j or 0, every cell fits the recurrence, the edit distance of intention / execution is 5, and swapping the words gives the transposed table; (3) the cells of the path are those of a separately written walk back, and walking the path of the picture (every step diagonal, up or left by one cell) costs (the edit steps, or the matches) the value of the last cell, in n to 2n steps; (4) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point (the gap differs on and off the path). **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first run read a -0 (`Math.round` returns -0 for a value a little below 0), fixed with an absolute value; (2) in the first version the gap of a path cell was 0.03, less than half of the edge smoothing, 0.035, so the mask of a path cell at the cell boundary was not 0 (about 0.015) while the neighbouring cell off the path (gap 0.12) is 0 there, which made a jump, and the C1 test failed with a second difference of 8.5×10⁷; I changed the gap of the path cells to 0.04 (more than 0.035) and the test passed (other cells keep 0.12); (3) the point-by-point check compares 4801 to 4830 of the 6000 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 4700; (4) 27 mutation checks were run: 26 were caught and 1 (changing the `+ 1` of the walk back's "up" condition to `+ 2`) made the loop of the walk back never end (j goes on going down) and ran into the 300 s timeout: an infinite loop, not counted as caught by a test; (5) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the table, an `Int16Array((n + 1)²)` (at most 17² = 289 values), the path in a `Uint8Array` and one walk back. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: editdistance took 122 ms and 97 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 171 ms and 166 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`sortingtraces` adds sorting traces, bringing the current catalog from 1167 to 1168 kinds (1169 gallery choices including plain). Rose squares on a dark plum ground: **the array of a sorting algorithm on 64 values after every step** — row t (row 0 on top) is the array after the step t, and a cell's **tone and height follow its value** (0 to 63, tone 0.2 to 0.95), so the gradient of the sorted array comes out of the mess step by step. The 6 variants are 0 bubble sort (the row t after the pass t, every pass going only up to the sorted tail), 1 insertion sort (after the insertion t), 2 selection sort (after the t-th swap of the least of the rest into place), 3 bottom-up merge sort (after the t-th merge of two neighbouring runs of 1, 2, 4 … elements), 4 quicksort with the last element as the pivot and Lomuto's partition (after each partition, the left part before the right part; the last rows repeat the sorted array if there are fewer than 63 partitions) and 5 heapsort (the row 0 is the max-heap that is built, the row t is after the t-th swap of the greatest to the end and the sifting down of the new top). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the algorithm and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the input: the element i is (a·i + b) mod 64 for a = 2·((5·group + 3) mod 32) + 1 and b = (7·group + 11) mod 64 (so seeds 0 to 5 are the six algorithms on one input, an arithmetic progression mod 64, not a random order). The gap between cells is 0.09 of a cell, the rounding 0.14 and the edge smoothing 0.07; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the steps of the six sorting algorithms and what is sampled at each step are my own definitions (the textbook forms are written from memory and not looked up in the literature). Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): the only catalog name containing sort is `sortingnetwork`; merge, quick, heap, insertion, radix and cocktail have no catalog kinds. I read the beginnings of `sortingnetwork` (a circuit schematic of a 16-wire sorting network) and `permutations` (about 420 characters each, not the whole entries): the former does not depend on the data (the comparators have fixed places), while this draws how a data-dependent array changes in time, so it is different. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the value solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 36 seeds (6 algorithms × 6 inputs) the whole 64×64 grid equals, cell by cell, a separately written trace (bubble sort by whole passes, insertion sort as the sorted prefix with the rest as it was, selection sort by looking the least up with indexOf, merging by sorting the two runs, quicksort with a stack of ranges and heapsort with a recursive sift; not the same form, but the partition of quicksort and the sift of heapsort determine the array at every step, so they could only be written as another form of the same definition); (2) what each algorithm guarantees at every step, checked on what is read back: every row is a permutation of 0 to 63 and the last row is the sorted gradient; after the pass t of bubble sort the t greatest values are at the end; after the insertion t of insertion sort the first t + 1 elements are increasing and the rest is as it was; after the swap t of selection sort the t least values are at the start; after the merges of every width (the 32nd, 48th, 56th, 60th, 62nd and 63rd) every run of that width is increasing for merge sort; for quicksort the number of pivots in their final place (a place s whose value is s and in front of which every value is less) never goes down from row to row, ends at 64, and the rows after it repeat; for heapsort the row 0 is a max-heap and the row t has the t greatest values at the end and a max-heap in front; (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) my first version of the quicksort check was "the number of cells with a[i] = i never goes down", which is wrong (it fell from 4 to 3: a value not yet fixed sat at its own place by chance and was moved away later); the quantity that cannot go down is the number of pivots in their final place, which is what the test uses now; (2) the 256 grid never lands in the middle of a gap between cells, so the least tone in the statistics (0.0708) and the least occlusion (0.6608) are not values of the gap; I check one cell corner separately for no ink and an occlusion of 0.5; (3) the point-by-point check compares 4721 of the 6000 points per seed (the same for all 9 seeds), with the lower bound 4600; (4) 37 mutation checks were run: 33 were caught and 4 were equivalent: the bubble-sort range `i + pass <= size` (the extra comparison with `a[size]`, undefined, is false), `a[i] >= a[i + 1]` and the insertion-sort `a[j] >= value` (the values are all different, so equality never happens) and the selection-sort `j = k` (`a[k] < a[k]` is false); (5) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; the input is an arithmetic progression, so it is not a random order and the picture shows regular stripes.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; an actual run of the sort on 64 values, recording 64 rows (an array of 64×64 integers, 4,096 values; about 2,000 comparisons for bubble and selection sort). At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: sortingtraces took 179 ms and 148 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 245 ms and 269 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`golombrulers` adds Golomb rulers, bringing the current catalog from 1166 to 1167 kinds (1168 gallery choices including plain). Gold dots on a dark brown ground: **optimal Golomb rulers** (every distance between two marks is different, with the least length for the number of marks); the tile is a grid of (length + 1) by (length + 1) cells and a cell (i, j) has a dot if **both i and j are marks**, so every diagonal beside the main one has at most one dot (the differences of the marks are all different); the **tone and height of a dot follow the difference |i − j| over the length** (the main diagonal, difference 0, is the dimmest; tone 0.25 to 0.95). The 6 variants have 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 marks, lengths 11, 17, 25, 34, 44 and 55 (grids of 12, 18, 26, 35, 45 and 56 cells). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group, which picks a ruler by group mod the length of the list: every optimal ruler of a number of marks (both orientations, in the lexicographic order), 4, 8, 10, 2, 2 and 2 of them (found by my search), so seeds 0 to 5 are the first ruler of each variant. The dot radius is 0.45 of a cell and the edge smoothing 0.08; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definition of the Golomb ruler is written from memory, I did not look it up in the literature, and I did not compare the optimal lengths I found with the values in the literature. The rulers were found by a search that I wrote myself (a temporary node script that takes the marks in increasing order, keeps the differences used so far, and tries the lengths from the lower bound m(m − 1)/2 upward, searching every length to the end): 5 marks length 11 (4 rulers), 6 marks 17 (8), 7 marks 25 (10), 8 marks 34 (2), 9 marks 44 (2, 502 ms) and 10 marks 55 (2, 4,699 ms, with the proof that every shorter length has none), the numbers counting both orientations. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): ruler, golombruler and sidon all gave 0/0. I read the beginnings of `costasambiguity` (the displacement-count picture of a Welch Costas array, at most one point for every displacement), `projectiveplane` (the incidence matrix of a Singer perfect difference set) and `nimproduct` (about 360 characters each, not the whole entries): a two-dimensional Costas array, a projective plane and a nim product table, not a one-dimensional Golomb ruler, so this is different. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, by whether there is ink at the middle of every cell): (1) the dots are exactly the cells of (mark) × (mark), the marks taken from the main diagonal; (2) for the variants of 5 to 9 marks (groups 0 to 11 or 0 to 3) the ruler equals, one by one, the list of optimal rulers (lexicographic order) found by a separately written search (a set of the differences, the length from the lower bound upward), and the length of the list (the number of rulers) and the size of the grid are the same too; for 10 marks (the search takes seconds, so it is not repeated in the test) only 10 marks, the grid of 56 and the list are checked; (3) the differences of the marks are all different (m(m − 1)/2 of them), the first mark is 0 and the last is the last cell of the grid, and for every d the diagonal j − i = d has a dot if and only if d is the difference of two marks, and exactly one; (4) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first version of my search script had a bug (it marked `used[L]` as used first, so the last mark could never be placed, every length looked unsolvable and the loop went on upward), and I ran it twice with the whole 250 to 280 s timeout used before I saw it; after the fix the searches for 5 to 10 marks finished in seconds; (2) the first version of the test took 28 s for the group (15.5 s for the one over every ruler alone: it searched the optimal rulers of 10 marks, about 5 s, and had an `expect` per cell), too near the 30 s timeout; I stopped searching for 10 marks in the test, counted the wrong cells and asserted once, and reduced the groups, so the group takes about 16 s (most of it loading and transforming); (3) the point-by-point check compares 5760 to 5969 of the 6000 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 5600; (4) 19 mutation checks were run and all were caught; (5) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5; the dot radius of 0.36 was too small and I changed it to 0.45 and looked at three variants again, without zooming in; the picture looks like sparse braille and the mathematical structure cannot be seen by eye.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the mark table, a `Uint8Array(length + 1)` of at most 56 B. At sampling time (per pixel): two table look-ups, one dot distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: golombrulers took 144 ms and 124 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 226 ms and 233 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`langfordpairings` adds Langford pairings, bringing the current catalog from 1165 to 1166 kinds (1167 gallery choices including plain). Mint bars on a dark green ground: **a row of 2n places in which every number from 1 to n stands twice and the two ends of the number k have k numbers between them** (a Langford pairing, the ends k + 1 places apart) or **the two ends of k are k places apart** (a Skolem sequence); every sequence is a panel (a row of 2n bars) and the **tone and height of a bar follow its number** (tone 0.22 to 0.95, height 0.8·(0.35 + 0.65·(k − 1)/(n − 1))). The panels are in the lexicographic order. The 6 variants are all 2 Langford pairings of n = 3 (1×2 panels), all 2 of n = 4 (1×2), all 6 Skolem sequences of n = 4 (2×3), all 10 of n = 5 (2×5), all 52 Langford pairings of n = 7 (4×13) and the first 64 in the lexicographic order of the 504 Skolem sequences of n = 8 (8×8). A bar is set in by 0.12 of its width on each side (0.2 for the last variant), a panel by 0.07 of its height above and below, with a margin of 0.03 of its width on each side. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group: bit 1 puts the panels in the reverse order and bit 2 reads every sequence from its last place (the reverse of a Langford pairing or a Skolem sequence is another sequence of its kind), so seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants in the lexicographic order. The AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definitions of Langford pairings and Skolem sequences are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature (the test computes them again by another method). Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): langford and skolem both gave 0/0. I read the beginnings of `permutations`, `golombruns`, `alternatingsignmatrices` and `setpartitions` (about 330 characters each, not the whole entries): permutation matrices, Golomb's sequence, alternating sign matrices and set partitions, none of which is a sequence with its pairs a fixed number of places apart, so this is different. The counts come from a temporary node script that enumerated them: Langford pairings of n = 3, 4, 7 and 8 number 2, 2, 52 and 300, Skolem sequences of n = 4, 5, 8 and 9 number 6, 10, 504 and 2656 (n = 12 has 455,936 Skolem sequences and was not used). The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the number solved from the height at the middle of every bar): (1) for 24 seeds (the variants × 4 groups) the panels are equal, one by one, to the sequences of an enumeration written another way (number by number from the greatest down, every place tried for the first end, unlike the sampler's enumeration by the first empty place) sorted in the lexicographic order and reversed in order or each one by the group; (2) in every sequence every number stands exactly twice with the ends k + 1 (Langford) or k (Skolem) places apart, the panels of one picture are all different, a complete variant has 2, 2, 6, 10 or 52 panels (the total 504 of the Skolem sequences of n = 8 is confirmed by the other enumeration, and only the first 64 are shown) and the reverse of every sequence is in the picture too; (3) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 5083 to 5118 of the 6000 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 5000; (2) 30 mutation checks were run: 27 were caught and 3 were equivalent: `to > length` (for `to === length`, `seq[to]` is undefined and `!== 0` skips it anyway), `fill(at)` for `fill(at + 1)` (the while loop of the next call skips the filled place) and `bar >= length` changed to `bar > length` (when `bar` equals the length the edge set-in of the bar makes the ink 0); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; the bars of the variants 4 and 5 are thin (about 9 and 4 px) and look like a barcode, and the pairing of the numbers cannot be seen by eye, only checked from the numbers read back.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the enumeration of all sequences (at most 504 of 16 integers, a recursive search and a sort). At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, two smoothed edges and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: langfordpairings took 119 ms and 93 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 171 ms and 168 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`mondrianpartitions` adds Mondrian partitions, bringing the current catalog from 1164 to 1165 kinds (1166 gallery choices including plain). Blue rectangular blocks on a dark navy ground: **a square cut into integer rectangles no two of which are congruent** (a 3×2 and a 2×3 count as one shape), the **tone and height of every block following its area** (from the least to the greatest area of its variant). The 6 variants are a 5×5 cut into 3 blocks (the greatest and the least area differ by 4), a 6×6 into 7 (differ by 5), a 7×7 into 8 (differ by 5), an 8×8 into 7 (differ by 6) and a 10×10 into 13 (differ by 8), the first five being the partitions with the least spread of the areas that my search found (Mondrian partitions); the sixth is a **perfect squared square** of side 112: 21 squares of different sizes (2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 24, 25, 27, 29, 33, 35, 37, 42 and 50, Duijvestijn's). The lines are a gap inside every block (0.04 of a cell for the first five and 0.17 for the sixth, whose 112 cells need a wider line to be seen). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ mod 8 one of the 8 turns and reflections of the square (bit 4 swaps x and y first; bit 1 makes x the size − x − width; bit 2 makes y the size − y − height), so seeds 0 to 5 are the six partitions as they are. The AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the Mondrian art problem (cutting an n×n into integer rectangles no two congruent so that the greatest and least area differ as little as possible) and the perfect squared square are written from memory, I did not look them up in the literature, and I did not compare the spreads I found with the values in the literature. The partitions were found by a search that I wrote myself (a temporary node script that fills from the bottom up and from the left with a skyline, limits the areas to [least, least + spread] and tries the spread from small to large): 5×5 spread 4 (6 ms), 6×6 spread 5 (38 ms), 7×7 spread 5 (169 ms), 8×8 spread 6 (3,814 ms), 10×10 spread 8 (19,995 ms); for n = 5, 6, 7 and 8 every smaller spread was searched to the end (the limit of 5 million nodes per search was not hit), so, if my search is right, these four are the least spreads; **for n = 10 some searches hit the limit, so 8 is not a proven least value**. (A 9×9 with spread 6 was also found; it resembles the 8×8 partition and is not used.) The 21 sides of the squared square are written from memory (Duijvestijn's of order 21 and side 112); I checked with the skyline fill that they fill the 112×112 (the areas add up to 12544 = 112² and a tiling was found in 21 nodes), and the test reads the sides back from the picture and compares them with this list. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): mondrian, squaredsquare, guillotine, floorplan and treemap all gave 0/0. I read the beginnings of `euclidsteps` (a table of Euclid steps), `trominotiling` and `pentominotiles` (about 420 characters each, not the whole entries), and I know that the catalog has `pythagoreantiles` (two-size square tiles; the README has no entry for it, and I only saw the heading and the first line in ACCEPTANCE); none of them is a partition into rectangles no two alike. The test checks (everything read back from the picture): (1) for 48 seeds (the variants × 8 turns) every block is found from the cells and from whether there is ink at the middle of the edge between neighbouring cells (a gap line has no ink), every block is a rectangle, there are 3, 7, 8, 7, 13 and 21 blocks and the areas add up to the square of the size, the shapes of all blocks differ, the spread of the areas is 4, 5, 5, 6, 8 and 2496, the tone and height rise with the area (the same area, the same tone), the 21 blocks of the sixth variant are squares whose sides are those of the list above, and the edges of the tile have no ink; (2) the blocks of the groups 0 to 7 are those of the group 0 under the same turn and reflection, and group 8 equals group 0; (3) edge smoothing: a quarter of the smoothing width inside and outside the gap line the occlusion equals the smoothstep at 0.75 and 0.25; (4) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 5637 to 5900 of the 6000 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 5500; (2) 27 mutation checks were run and all were caught, but `soft = p.edgeSoft[0]` (the smoothing width 0.12 of the sixth variant changed to 0.03) **was not caught the first time**: the test skips the smoothing zone, so the width of the smoothing was not checked; I added test (3), after which this mutation and another that doubles the smoothing width were caught (the other 25 were not re-run); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the table of the block of every cell, an `Int8Array(size²)` of at most 12,544 B (112×112) and at most 21 blocks. At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, the minimum of four edge distances and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: mondrianpartitions took 106 ms and 88 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 156 ms and 155 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`debruijntorus` adds the de Bruijn torus, bringing the current catalog from 1163 to 1164 kinds (1165 gallery choices including plain). Pale violet rounded squares on a dark violet ground: **a grid of symbols that wraps round its edges (a torus) in which every possible window of symbols appears exactly once** — a de Bruijn torus (a perfect map). The 6 variants (grid size, window size, symbols) are a 4×4 grid with 2×2 windows of 2 symbols, an 8×8 grid with 2×3 windows of 2 symbols, a 4×16 grid with 2×3 windows of 2 symbols, a 9×9 grid with 2×2 windows of 3 symbols, an 8×8 grid with 3×2 windows of 2 symbols and another 9×9 grid with 2×2 windows of 3 symbols; the number of cells is the number of symbols to the power of (window rows times columns) (16, 64, 64, 81, 64, 81), so every window of the grid is a pattern that appears once and only once. Every symbol has a tone (0.22 to 0.95) and a height (0.8·(0.35 + 0.65·symbol/last symbol)); the grid is repeated in the tile to fill 8, 8, 16, 9, 8 and 9 cells on a side (so the cells are square). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group, which moves the grid by 3·group rows and 5·group columns (mod its size) and every symbol on by the group (mod the number of symbols); these changes keep all windows different, so seeds 0 to 5 are the six unchanged grids; the period of the groups depends on the variant, and not every group is different (for the 4×4 binary grid the group 4 equals the group 0). The gap between cells is 0.06 of a cell, the rounding 0.16 and the edge smoothing 0.06; the AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. Read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the idea of a de Bruijn torus (a perfect map) is written from memory and I did not look it up in the literature. The grids were found by a backtracking search that I wrote myself (a temporary node script that fills the cells one by one and checks, after every window is complete, that it is not a repeat); they are not copied from the literature: 4×4 with 2×2 windows of 2 symbols (75 nodes), 8×8 with 2×3 windows (366,843 nodes, 47 ms), 9×9 with 2×2 windows of 3 symbols (2,269,563 nodes, 375 ms), 4×16 with 2×3 windows (2,054,013 nodes, 424 ms), and the other two (the 8×8 grid with 3×2 windows is the transpose of another solution, and the second 9×9 grid) were found again with a random order of the symbols; the searches that did not finish were 16×16 with 2×2 windows of 4 symbols (about 169 million nodes in 60 s), 16×16 with 2×4 windows of 2 symbols, 16×32 with 3×3 windows and 8×32 with 2×4 windows (about 380 to 530 million nodes in 90 s each), **which does not mean that they do not exist**. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): debruijn, perfectmap and pseudorandom all gave 0/0; the only catalog name containing window is `windowpane` (a window pane, unrelated). I read the beginnings of `necklaces`, `graycode`, `latinsquares` and `booleanfunctions` (about 330 characters each, not the whole entries): rings of beads, Gray code, Latin squares and Boolean functions, none of which has a two-dimensional uniqueness of windows, so this is different. The test checks (everything read back from the picture, the symbol solved from the height at the middle of every cell): (1) for 36 seeds (the variants × 6 groups) the tile is the grid repeated, the number of cells is the number of symbols to the power of (rows × columns of a window), the windows of the declared size (wrapping round the edges) are exactly as many different ones as cells, each appearing once (counted by another method with text keys), and the smaller windows a×b all give q^(a·b) different patterns with the same number of occurrences (the balance that follows from the uniqueness); (2) turned a quarter, the windows are no longer all different: the turned windows of variants 1, 2 and 4 give only 39, 41 and 43 different patterns of 64 cells, so the check does not hold for every shape; (3) the grids of groups 1, 2, 3 and 7 are the grid of group 0 moved by (3·group, 5·group) with every symbol on by the group; (4) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point (the distance to a rounded square written piecewise by hand). **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first run read symbols with a -0 (`Math.round` returns -0 for a value a little below 0) and `toBe(0)` failed, a problem of the test, fixed with an absolute value; (2) the point-by-point check compares 4828 to 4839 of the 6000 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 4700; (3) 27 mutation checks were run: 26 were caught and 1 was an equivalent mutation (`rowShift = (3·group) % size` changed to `% width`: the rows are taken mod the row count again later, and the row count divides the width); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the symbol table of the tile, a `Uint8Array(cells²)` of at most 256 B (taken from the grid, at most 16 rows × 16 columns). At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: debruijntorus took 108 ms and 92 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 155 ms and 151 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`kneser` adds the Kneser matrix, bringing the current catalog from 1162 to 1163 kinds (1164 gallery choices including plain). Amber rounded squares on a dark brown ground: **every k-subset of n elements has a row and a column (C(n, k) of them), and the tone and height of a cell follow the number of elements the two subsets have in common** (the Johnson scheme) — the cells of disjoint subsets (the edges of the Kneser graph) are the brightest and the diagonal (a subset with itself, k shared elements) the darkest; the tone runs from 0.22 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8·(0.4 + 0.6·(k − shared)/k). The 6 variants (n, k) are (5, 2) 10×10, (6, 2) 15×15, (7, 2) 21×21, (6, 3) 20×20, (7, 3) 35×35 and (8, 3) 56×56. The gap between cells is 0.07 of a cell, the rounding 0.18 and the edge smoothing 0.08. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group, and the group mod 3 picks the order of the rows and columns: 0 lexicographic, 1 by the sum of the elements (equal sums lexicographic), 2 the revolving-door order (every subset differs from the next by one element), so seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants in the lexicographic order and the groups 3, 4 and 5 repeat the picture of the groups 0, 1 and 2 (with another grain in the tones). The AO is 1 − 0.5·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.45 and metallic 0. The matrix is read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, so the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definitions of the Kneser graph, the Johnson scheme and the revolving-door order are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature (the test computes them again by other methods). Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): kneser, johnson, disjoint, adjacency and cooccur all gave 0/0; subset, intersection, incidence, binomial and combination have no catalog kinds and about 1 README line each. I read the beginnings of the related entries (about 330 characters each, not the whole entries): `projectiveplane` (the point-line incidence matrix of a finite projective plane, 0/1 dots) and `nimproduct` (a nim product table) among them; this draws the matrix of the **number of shared elements** of subsets (k + 1 levels) and its orders, which is different. The test checks: (1) for 18 seeds (the variants × the three orders) every cell is computed again by other methods — the subsets found by counting the bits of the integers, sorted in the three orders (the revolving door by the recursion R(n, k) = R(n − 1, k) followed by R(n − 1, k − 1) reversed with n − 1 added) — and compared with the height read back at the middle of every cell, and there is no ink at the corners where four cells meet; (2) the matrix read back from the picture is symmetric, has k on the whole diagonal, has C(k, i)·C(n − k, k − i) subsets sharing i elements in every row, and **for any two subsets sharing s elements the number of subsets sharing i with the one and j with the other depends only on s** (the intersection numbers of an association scheme, brute-forced in N³); (3) the graph of the disjoint cells: seed 0 is the Petersen graph (10 vertices of degree 3, 15 edges, adjacent vertices without a common neighbour and other pairs with exactly one: strongly regular (10, 3, 0, 1)), seed 3 (3-subsets of 6) has exactly one disjoint subset per subset, its complement, and seed 4 (3-subsets of 7) has 35 vertices of degree 4 and at most one common neighbour for any two (no triangle and no 4-cycle); (4) in the revolving-door order two successive rows share exactly k − 1 elements (8 seeds); (5) ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point (the distance to a rounded square written piecewise by hand). **Notes (honest)**: (1) in my first version the group moved every element on by the group (mod n) before sorting, and the probe showed that the share of lit cells differing between group 0 and 1 was only 0.00014: this was my design error — the set of all k-subsets is the same after renaming the elements, so the sorted matrix is exactly the same and only the grain differs; I changed the group to pick the sorting rule; (2) the second version had the lexicographic order, colex (compared from the greatest element down) and the revolving door, and 32 mutation checks were run on it: 30 were caught and 2 were not: the transpose (`shared[i·size + j]`, an equivalent mutation) and the bit reversal of the sorting key (`1 << e` for `1 << (n − 1 − e)`), which is not a bug sign but a mathematical fact: **the reverse of colex is the lexicographic order after renaming** (e → n − 1 − e), so the lexicographic order sorted by the reverse colex gives exactly the same picture, and the colex picture is the lexicographic one turned by 180 degrees, not a really different arrangement; I therefore replaced colex by "the sum of the elements, equal sums lexicographic" and re-ran the 7 mutation checks that concern the order (all 7 were caught, including the key reversal, because renaming changes the sum inside a group of equal sums); (3) my first list of seeds for the revolving-door test was wrong (2, 8, 14… are not group 2), the group check inside the test caught it and the list is now 12 to 17, 30 and 35; (4) the point-by-point check compares 4486 to 4506 of the 6000 points per seed (9 seeds), with the lower bound 4400; (5) on the final code there are 35 mutations: 34 were caught and 1 was equivalent (the transpose), of which 28 were run on the colex version of the code and the test and were not re-run after the order changed; (6) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 and some other groups without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the bit masks of at most 56 subsets and a `Uint8Array(N²)` of the shared counts, at most 3,136 B (N² bit counts). At sampling time (per pixel): one table look-up, one rounded-square distance and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: kneser took 146 ms and 118 ms (two runs, measured on the colex version; not re-measured after the order rule changed) and talbotcarpet 206 ms and 200 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`lowdiscrepancy` adds low-discrepancy point sets, bringing the current catalog from 1161 to 1162 kinds (1163 gallery choices including plain). Cream dots on a dark navy ground: **the first N points of a low-discrepancy sequence on the torus (the periodic unit square), one dot each**, the **tone and height of a dot following its index in the sequence** (the first point dim and low, the last bright and high; the tone from 0.3 to 0.95 and the height 0.8·(0.35 + 0.65·index/(N − 1))), so one can see how the sequence fills the square step by step. The 6 variants are the 144 points of the Halton sequence (bases 2 and 3), the 64 points of the Hammersley set (i/64 and the radical inverse of i in base 2), the 144 points of the Fibonacci lattice (i/144 and i·89 mod 144 over 144), the 144 points of the Kronecker sequence of the plastic number ρ (the real root of ρ³ = ρ + 1; the points i·(1/ρ, 1/ρ²) taken mod 1), the 80 points of the Halton sequence in the bases 2 and 5 and the 75 points of the Halton sequence in the bases 3 and 5. The dot radius is 0.0141, 0.0085, 0.0141, 0.0141, 0.0141 and 0.0095 respectively (as a fraction of the tile; the Hammersley and Halton sets have pairs of points that are near each other, which is why they have fewer points and smaller dots). **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the group, which moves the whole set on the torus (a Cranley–Patterson rotation: x plus group·0.6180339887498949 and y plus group·0.7548776662466927, mod 1; the group 0 has no shift, so seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of group 0). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. As the points are on a torus and the tile is read with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)`, the pattern is **exactly periodic** (C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the definitions of the Halton, Hammersley, Fibonacci-lattice and (plastic number) Kronecker sequences are written from memory and I did not look them up in the literature (the test computes them again by separate formulas). Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): hammersley, sobol, quasirandom, lowdiscrepancy, stipple and kronecker all gave 0/0. I read the beginnings of the related entries (about 500 characters each, not the whole entries): `poissondisk` (random Poisson-disk sampling by dart throwing, points at least 0.085 apart, a random algorithm) and `vogelspiral` (97 golden-angle disks); this draws **deterministic** low-discrepancy sequences with the tone following the index, which is different from them. The test checks: (1) the points of every variant (groups 0, 1 and 3) are computed again by separate formulas — the radical inverse by "write i as text in that base, reverse it and read it as the digits after the point", the plastic number by Newton's method and the Fibonacci lattice from the Fibonacci numbers — every two points are further apart than twice the radius plus the smoothing (so every dot has a place of its own), the height at the middle of every point is the value computed from its index, and on a grid of 128×128 places there is ink (a height above 0) inside a dot and none outside all the dots (places near the edge of a dot are not compared), which shows that there is no extra point and none missing; (2) the 144 = 16×9 points of the Halton sequence (bases 2 and 3) have exactly one point in every box of 1/16 by 1/9, the 64 = 2⁶ points of the Hammersley set exactly one in every box of 2⁻ᵃ by 2⁻⁽⁶⁻ᵃ⁾ (a from 0 to 6), and the sum of two points of the Fibonacci lattice is a point of it (these are checked on the points of the separate formulas, not on the picture); (3) group 1 has every point of group 0 moved by the same vector; (4) the ink, height, tone and occlusion are compared point by point. **Notes (honest)**: (1) my first version had more points (Hammersley 128, Halton (2,5) 160, Halton (3,5) 135) and bigger dots, and the test "every two points are further apart than twice the radius plus the smoothing" failed (the nearest pair was only 0.011 apart), which made the three tests that go by the nearest point fail as well; I measured the least distance of the sets with a temporary node script (Hammersley 128: 0.0110, Halton (2,5) 160: 0.0080, Halton (3,5) 135: 0.0261; with the new values Hammersley 64: 0.0221, Halton (2,3) 144: 0.0328, Fibonacci 144: 0.0786, Kronecker 144: 0.0678, Halton (2,5) 80: 0.0447, Halton (3,5) 75: 0.0270) and changed the counts and the radii to the values above, after which the tests passed; (2) the first count of boxes was 143 instead of 144 because rounding errors put a point that is exactly on the edge of a box into the next one, so I added a tolerance of 1e-9; (3) the point-by-point check compares 5686 to 5930 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 5500; (4) 31 mutation checks were run: 29 were caught; one was a no-op that I wrote by mistake (1.3 changed to 1.3 + 0), which is not a real mutation, and one was an equivalent mutation (the grid of 24 cells changed to 6, which the 3×3 neighbour cells still cover) (see ACCEPTANCE); (5) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, two `Float64Array`s with the coordinates of the points (at most 144 each) and the counting-sort index of a 24×24 grid (an `Int32Array` of 577 and one of at most 144 items). At sampling time (per pixel): the torus distance to the points in the 9 neighbouring cells (at most 144 points over 576 cells, about 2.25 in 9 cells on average) and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: lowdiscrepancy took 111 ms and 99 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 152 ms and 169 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`hamiltonpaths` adds Hamiltonian paths, bringing the current catalog from 1160 to 1161 kinds (1162 gallery choices including plain). Coral drawings on a dark brown-black ground: **every Hamiltonian path (a path along the edges of a small grid of points that visits every point exactly once, a path and the same path walked the other way counting once) is drawn once**, one path to a small panel. The 6 variants are the 8 paths of a 3×2 grid of points (3×3 panels, 1 slot empty), the 20 of 3×3 (5×4), the 62 of 4×3 (7×9, 1 empty), the 132 of 5×3 (9×15, 3 empty), the 276 of 4×4 (17×17, 13 empty) and the 336 of 6×3 (13×26, 2 empty). A path is a line with round ends (half width 0.1, smoothed over 0.06 units) whose **two ends each carry a bigger dot** (radius 0.2); the **tone and height of a path follow its number of turns** (changes of direction between two steps) over the most there can be (the number of points less 2): the tone runs from 0.4 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.4 + 0.6 times the level). A panel is a box of (width − 1) by (height − 1) units with 0.5 of margin around it, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin, C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the numbers (8, 20, 62, 132, 276, 336) are **not numbers I remember from the literature**: I got them from a temporary brute-force node script I ran before writing the code (depth-first from every start point, keeping the paths whose first point is before the last) and, in the test, by a completely different method (counting over the set of points visited and the last point reached, then dividing by 2); I noticed afterwards that the 276 of the 4×4 grid agrees with a sequence I vaguely recall, but I did not look it up.
