Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): hamiltonpath gave 0/0, hamiltonian 0/3 (string mentions in the README, among them `hamiltoncycle`) and snake 2/2. In this conversation I read the beginnings of the related entries: `hamiltoncycle` (one random Hamiltonian cycle of a 32×32 grid drawn like a labyrinth), `selfavoidingwalks` (every self-avoiding walk of a fixed number of steps, which need not visit every point) and `knightstour`; this draws **every** Hamiltonian path of small grids of points, which is different from them. What the test checks: the path of every panel is read back from the picture (a possible edge of the box is a piece of the path where there is ink at its middle, and the height there gives the level), the pieces form one path through every point (exactly two ends, no branch, connected, covering all the points), the height equals the value for the number of turns of the path read back, and there are no repeats; and **the number of paths drawn equals the number of Hamiltonian paths counted by another method** (dynamic programming) — each path drawn is legal, they are all different and their number equals the total, so the set is complete (unlike the other materials, where two sets are compared one by one, completeness here is shown by legality and counting). **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first run of the test had one failure: I compared the levels rounded to 1/1000, and for a path of the 6×3 grid with 5 turns out of 16 (exactly 312.5) one side gave 313 and the other, with a floating-point error, read 312.4999 and gave 312, which is a rounding boundary of the test and not a fault of the sampler; I changed it to round to 1e-6 and it passed; (2) the point-by-point check compares 5296 to 5578 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 5100; (3) of 32 mutation checks 29 were caught and 3 were equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; in the variants of 276 and 336 paths a unit is only about 7 pixels at 512 pixels, so the lines are thin.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the Hamiltonian paths are found by a depth-first walk (at most 336 are kept, each at most 17 segments of 4 numbers) and shuffled; I did not measure the number of steps of the walk (in my temporary script the searches for 6×3 and 4×4 took about 1 ms each). At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, the distance from the point to at most 17 segments and to two end dots, and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: hamiltonpaths took 118 ms and 104 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 111 ms and 107 ms in the same environment (about the same); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`gridsplits` adds splits of a grid board into two pieces, bringing the current catalog from 1159 to 1160 kinds (1161 gallery choices including plain). Light-green drawings on a dark green-black ground: **every way to split a board of square cells into two regions that are each in one piece (cells joined by their edges) is drawn once**, the region that holds the top left cell having a given number of cells, one split to a small panel. The 6 variants are the 19 splits of a 4×3 board into 6 and 6 cells (4×5 panels, 1 slot empty), the 70 of 4×4 into 8 and 8 (9×8, 2 empty), the 85 of 6×3 into 9 and 9 (7×13, 6 empty), the 245 of 5×4 into 10 and 10 (14×18, 7 empty), the 42 of 4×4 into 6 and 10 (7×6) and the 36 of 5×3 into 7 and 8 (5×8, 4 empty). The cells of a region join without a seam and a gap (0.16, smoothed over 0.1) parts them from the cells of the other region and from the edge of the board; the region of the top left cell is brighter and higher (tone 0.95, height 0.8·1) and the other darker and lower (tone 0.5, height 0.8·0.5). Each panel holds the board (at its top left) with 0.5 of a cell of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the numbers (19, 70, 85, 245, 42, 36) are **not numbers I remember from the literature**: I got them from a temporary brute-force node script I ran before writing the code and from the enumeration written separately in the test. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): gerrymander and district gave 0/0, bisection 0/2, halves 1/1 and split 4/5 (string mentions in the README, which I did not read one by one). In this conversation I read the entries of `dominoboards` (every domino tiling of a small board) and `polyominoes` (shapes); this draws the splits of a whole board into two connected regions, which is different from them. The test checks in two independent ways: the split of every panel is read back from the picture (the height at the middle of a cell has to be that of one of the two regions, no other value; an empty slot shows the ground at every cell), the region of the top left cell has the given number of cells, each region is in one piece, and there are no repeats; the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which grows the connected sets of the wanted size from the top left cell, one neighbouring cell at a time, and keeps those whose other cells are in one piece too (the sampler goes through all the sets of cells of the board as bits, requiring cell 0, the size and the two connectivities); the two sets are identical. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 4812 to 4965 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 4600 (about 17% to 20% of the points are skipped as being near a gap edge); (2) of 35 mutation checks 32 were caught and 3 were equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the 2^(width times height) sets of cells of the board (at most 2^20 = 1,048,576; only those that hold cell 0 and have the right size get the two connectivity checks) are gone through and the splits kept (at most 245, each a `Uint8Array` of at most 20 B) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, one look-up in the board and four neighbour comparisons, four smoothings and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: gridsplits took 114 ms and 96 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 164 ms and 169 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`chorddiagrams` adds chord diagrams, bringing the current catalog from 1158 to 1159 kinds (1160 gallery choices including plain). Silver-white drawings on a dark charcoal ground: **every chord diagram of one kind (a way to join some points on a circle in pairs by straight chords, every point on exactly one chord) is drawn once**, one diagram to a small panel. The 6 variants are all 15 of 6 points (4×4 panels, 1 slot empty), all 105 of 8 points (11×10, 5 empty), the 14 of 8 points with no two chords crossing (4×4, 2 empty), the 18 classes of 8 points under turning the circle (5×4, 2 empty, each panel showing its diagram turned by a multiple of a turn of the points), the 42 of 10 points with no crossing (7×6) and the 105 classes of 10 points under turning (11×10, 5 empty). The points are dots on a circle of radius 1 at equal angles, the first at the top and the others clockwise, and the chords are thin lines (half width 0.045 units, dot radius 0.1). The **tone and height of a diagram** (dots and chords alike) **follow its number of crossings** (two chords cross when their ends alternate round the circle) over the most there can be, pairs·(pairs − 1)/2 for pairs = points/2: the tone runs from 0.4 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.4 + 0.6 times the level). A panel is a box of 2 by 2 units with 0.5 of margin around it, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels and the turn of the classes (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin, C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; that there are (n − 1)!! chord diagrams (15 and 105 for n = 3 and 4 chords) and that those with no crossing are counted by Catalan numbers (14 and 42) are results I remember and did not look up in the literature; the numbers of classes under turning, 18 and 105, are **not** from memory: I got them from a temporary node script before writing the code and from the enumeration written separately in the test. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): perfectmatching gave 0/0, chord 0/4 (mentions in the README, for example the "straight chord" of `woodruffkeys`, unrelated to chord diagrams, which I did not read one by one) and matching 0/3. I read the beginnings of the related entries (about 300 characters each, not the whole entries): `polygondissections` (a polygon cut by diagonals that do not cross, also counted by Catalan numbers, but it draws the pieces the polygon is cut into, not pairings), `dyckpaths`, `spanningtrees` and `hypercube`; this draws pairings of points on a circle, which is different from them. The test checks in two independent ways: the diagram of every panel is read back from the picture (every point has ink at its centre; two points are joined by a chord where there is ink at 15 places along it, from 15% to 85% of the way in steps of 5%, and the height there gives the level), each diagram is of the kind (every point on exactly one chord; no crossing in the variants without crossing), the height of the chords equals the value for the number of crossings counted from the chords read back, and there are no repeats (a class under turning is named by the least name among all its turns); the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which goes through all the sets of pairs of points (chosen among all the pairs, as many as half the points, no two sharing a point) (the sampler joins the least free point to a later free one, prunes the crossing ones in the variants without crossing, and keeps the least name for each class under turning); the two sets are identical. **Notes (honest)**: (1) my first version of the test looked for ink at only two places along a chord (37% and 63%), and for 10 points it read an extra chord that was not drawn (each of its two sample points was covered by a different chord crossing it), so the diagram read back was not a pairing; I changed it to require ink at 15 places along the chord, after which it passed; (2) the point-by-point check compares 5628 to 5770 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 5400; (3) of 30 mutation checks 25 were caught and 5 were equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); one of them is a redundant "lesser end first" conditional in the `name` function of the sampler (the chords are already made that way), which I removed, and after the removal I re-ran only this group of tests (7 passed) and not the other mutations; (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; the panels of 10 points are about 15 pixels per unit at 512 pixels, so the chords are about one pixel wide and harder to see.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the diagrams are listed by a recursion (at most 105 are kept, each at most 5 chords; for the classes under turning all the diagrams (105 of 8 points, 945 of 10) are listed first and only the least of each class kept) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, the distance from the point to at most 5 chords (segments) and to at most 10 dots, and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: chorddiagrams took 130 ms and 116 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 128 ms and 121 ms in the same environment (a small difference); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`stilllifes` adds still lifes of Conway's Game of Life, bringing the current catalog from 1157 to 1158 kinds (1159 gallery choices including plain). Sky-blue drawings on a dark navy-black ground: **every still life (a pattern that the rules leave exactly as it is: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours among its 8 stays alive, a dead cell with exactly 3 is born, and every cell outside the box is dead) in a box of one size is drawn once**, one pattern to a small panel. The 6 variants are the 11 in a 3 by 3 box with at least one live cell (4×3 panels, 1 slot empty), the 27 in a box 3 wide and 4 high (6×5, 3 empty), the 82 in a 4 by 4 box (10×9, 8 empty), the 74 of those whose live cells are joined (also by a corner) (9×9, 7 empty), the 91 in a box 6 wide and 3 high (7×13, none empty) and the 69 of those whose live cells are joined (6×12, 3 empty). A live cell is a flat tile whose **tone and height follow its number of live neighbours**: with 2 neighbours it is lower (tone 0.6, height 0.8·0.55) and with 3 higher (tone 0.95, height 0.8·1); a dead cell shows the ground; a tile has a gap around it (0.16 of a cell, smoothed over 0.1); each panel holds the box (at its top left) with 0.5 of a cell of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the numbers (11, 27, 82, 74, 91, 69) are **not numbers I remember from the literature**: I got them from a temporary brute-force node script I ran before writing the code and from the enumeration written separately in the test. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): stilllife, oscillator and lifelike all gave 0/0, gameoflife 1/6 (the `gameoflife` kind and mentions in the README). I read the `gameoflife` entry: it is one snapshot, not fully settled, of a 64×64 torus started at 38% density and evolved for 250 generations (blocks, beehives, blinkers and gliders), not a catalog of still lifes; this lists every still life in a small box, which is different from it, though it uses the same rules. The test checks in two independent ways: the pattern of every panel is read back from the picture (the height at the middle of a cell is 0 or that of a live cell, and it has to be the value for the number of live neighbours of that cell in the pattern read back), each pattern is a still life by the rules (the next generation computed with a sparse set equals the set), the patterns of the joined variants are joined, and there are no repeats; the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which goes through all the 2^(width times height) patterns of the box and tests each by the rules with a sparse set (the sampler checks cell after cell in an array with a ring of dead cells and neighbour counts); the two sets are identical. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 5525 to 5634 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 5300; (2) of 34 mutation checks 27 were caught and 6 were equivalent mutations; one more (reversing the "not yet seen" condition of the search for joined cells) makes the sampler loop forever, and the test run was stopped by the 600 second time-out, which is not an ordinary assertion failure (see ACCEPTANCE); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the 2^(width times height) patterns of the box (at most 2^18 = 262,144, each scanned in an array with a ring, stopping at the first cell that changes) are gone through and the still lifes kept (at most 91, each a `Uint8Array` of at most 18 B) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, one look-up in the box, four smoothings and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: stilllifes took 87 ms and 69 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 128 ms and 119 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`alternatingsignmatrices` adds alternating sign matrices, bringing the current catalog from 1156 to 1157 kinds (1158 gallery choices including plain). Lime drawings on a dark olive-black ground: **every alternating sign matrix of one kind (a square of 0, 1 and −1 whose every row and column adds up to 1 and, read along it, has its entries that are not 0 alternate in sign, starting and ending with 1) is drawn once**, one matrix to a small panel. The 6 variants are all 7 of order 3 (3×3 panels, 2 slots empty), all 42 of order 4 (7×6), all 429 of order 5 (21×21, 12 empty), the 18 of order 4 with a −1 in them (5×4, 2 empty; the other 24 are the permutation matrices), the 67 of order 5 that equal their transpose (9×8, 5 empty) and the 200 of order 5 with exactly one −1 (15×14, 10 empty). **Only a cell that is 1 or −1 is a flat tile**: a 1 has the tone 0.95 and the height 0.8·1, a −1 the tone 0.5 and the height 0.8·0.45; a 0 shows the ground; a tile has a gap around it (0.16 of a cell, smoothed over 0.1); each panel holds the matrix with 0.5 of a cell of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the numbers of alternating sign matrices of orders 3, 4 and 5 (7, 42, 429) are numbers I remember and did not look up in the literature; the numbers in the test are the results of an enumeration written separately. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): alternatingsign, monotonetriangle and gelfand all gave 0/0 and asm 0/2 (string mentions in the README, which I did not read one by one). I read the beginnings of the related entries (about 330 characters each, not the whole entries): `permutations` (permutation matrices, one per permutation; 24 of the 42 alternating sign matrices of order 4 are permutation matrices, which are the 24 permutations of 4 elements that kind draws, so **there is some overlap**, and what is new here is the matrices with a −1), `latinsquares` and `magicsquares`; this draws alternating sign matrices, which is different from them. The test checks in two independent ways: the matrix of every panel is read back from the picture (the height at the middle of a cell has to be that of a 0, a 1 or a −1, no other value), each matrix is an alternating sign matrix by the definition (along every row and column the entries that are not 0 alternate in sign, start and end with 1) and of the kind, and there are no repeats; the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which goes by the monotone triangles (n rows of 1 to n strictly increasing numbers, each between its neighbours in the rows above and below, the last row being 1 to n) turned back into matrices (the sampler fills cell after cell and keeps the sums along the row and down the column at 0 or 1); the two sets are identical. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 5602 to 5653 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 5400; (2) of 29 mutation checks 4 were not caught, all equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); one is a redundant "every column sum ends at 1" check in the sampler (every row adds up to 1 and every column to at most 1, so it always holds), which I removed with its comment updated, and after the removal I re-ran only this group of tests (7 passed) and not the other mutations; another is the symmetry check skipping one sub-diagonal, which made no difference in the tests of order 5 (an experimental result, not a proof; I kept the full check); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the matrices are listed by a recursion that fills cell after cell (at most 429, each an `Int8Array` of at most 25 B), with the sums along the row and down the column held between 0 and 1, and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, one look-up in the matrix, four smoothings and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: alternatingsignmatrices took 76 ms and 63 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 122 ms and 120 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`polysticks` adds polysticks, bringing the current catalog from 1155 to 1156 kinds (1157 gallery choices including plain). Teal drawings on a dark teal-black ground: **every polystick of one size (a connected shape made of unit sticks, the edges of the square lattice) is drawn once**, one shape to a small panel. The 6 variants are the **free** polysticks (a shape and its turns and mirror images count once, and every panel draws its shape with one of the 8 turns and flips) of 3, 4 and 5 sticks, 5, 16 and 55 of them (3×2 panels with 1 slot empty, 4×4 with none, 8×7 with 1 empty), and the **fixed** polysticks (shapes that differ by moving them only) of 3, 4 and 5 sticks, 22, 88 and 372 of them (5×5 with 3 empty, 10×9 with 2 empty and 20×19 with 8 empty). A stick is a line with round ends (half width 0.1, smoothed over 0.06 units), so sticks that meet join without a seam; the **tone and height of a shape follow its symmetry** (the number of the 8 turns and flips that map it onto itself, 1, 2, 4 or 8, the levels 0, 1/3, 2/3, 1): the tone runs from 0.4 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.4 + 0.6 times the level). A panel is a box of n by n units with the shape at its top left and 0.5 of margin around it, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels and the turn of every free shape (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin, C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the numbers of free polysticks of 3, 4 and 5 sticks (5, 16, 55) and of fixed polysticks of 3, 4 and 5 sticks (22, 88, 372) are numbers I remember and did not look up in the literature; the numbers in the test are the results of an enumeration written separately. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): polystick and polyedge both gave 0/0. I read the beginnings of the entries `polyominoes` (square cells with the same free/fixed and symmetry-level approach as here) and `selfavoidingwalks` (self-avoiding walks on the lattice points, each drawn as one path) (about 450 characters each, not the whole entries) and the beginning of the `matchsticks` preset (an object material, a heap of matchsticks, not shapes on the lattice); this draws any connected shape of lattice edges, which can branch and can close into a loop, which is different from those. The test checks in two independent ways: the shape of every panel is read back from the picture (a possible lattice edge of the box is a stick of the shape where there is ink at its middle, and the height there gives the symmetry level), each shape has exactly n sticks and is connected, and there are no repeats (a free shape is named by the least of its 8 turns and flips, a fixed one by the shape moved to the corner); the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which goes through all the sets of n edges of the window of the lattice from 0 to n in both directions and keeps the connected ones (the turns and flips are written with matrices; the sampler grows the shapes stick by stick and removes repeats by the least name under moving and the 8 turns); the two sets are identical; the test also checks that the symmetry level read from the picture equals the number of symmetries counted in the test, and which levels occur in each variant; the point-by-point check judges the ink from the distance to the nearest stick read back. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first run of the test had two failures, because I had put placeholder values for the symmetry levels and for the number of compared points in the test to be measured, and I filled in the measured values afterwards (the levels are in the test, the compared points are 5873 to 5927 with the lower bound 5700); (2) of 25 mutation checks 3 were not caught, all equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); one of them is a redundant last term in the sort comparison of the sampler (at one first end there are only a horizontal and a vertical stick, whose second ends differ in y), which I removed, and after the removal I re-ran only this group of tests (8 passed) and not the other mutations; (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; the picture is sparse (the lit lines are only 1.4% to 1.8% of a 256² sampling) and dark.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the shapes are produced by growing stick by stick and removing repeats by the least name under the 8 turns and flips (at most 372, each at most 5 sticks of 4 numbers) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, the distance from the point to at most 5 sticks and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: polysticks took 134 ms and 126 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 156 ms and 161 ms in the same environment (a small difference, and the machine load varies); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`polyhexes` adds polyhexes, bringing the current catalog from 1154 to 1155 kinds (1156 gallery choices including plain). Violet drawings on a dark purple-black ground: **every polyhex of one size (a shape made of hexagonal cells joined by their edges) is drawn once**, one shape to a small panel. The 6 variants are the **free** polyhexes (a shape and its turns and mirror images count once, and every panel draws its shape with one of the 12 turns and flips) of 4, 5 and 6 cells, 7, 22 and 82 of them (3×3 panels with 2 slots empty, 5×5 with 3 empty and 9×10 with 8 empty), and the **fixed** polyhexes (shapes that differ by moving them only) of 3, 4 and 5 cells, 11, 44 and 186 of them (3×4 with 1 empty, 7×7 with 5 empty and 14×14 with 10 empty). The cells of a polyhex join without a seam and a gap (0.16, smoothed over 0.1, in units of the distance between cell centres) parts them from cells next to them that are not of it; the **tone and height of a shape follow its symmetry** (the number of the 12 turns and flips that map it onto itself, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12 from the least to the most, the levels 0, 1/5, …, 1): the tone runs from 0.4 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.4 + 0.6 times the level). A panel holds rows of pointy-topped hexagons one unit apart between centres, every other row shifted by half a unit, in a box n + 0.5 wide and (n − 1)·√3/2 + 2/√3 high with the shape at its top left, and 0.5 of margin around it, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels and the turn of every free shape (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin, C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the numbers of free polyhexes of 4, 5 and 6 cells (7, 22, 82) and of fixed polyhexes of 3, 4 and 5 cells (11, 44, 186) are numbers I remember and did not look up in the literature; the numbers in the test are the results of an enumeration written separately. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): polyhex and polyiamond both gave 0/0. In this conversation I read and adapted my own earlier `polyominoes` (square cells, the same free/fixed and symmetry-level approach) sampler and test; this one has hexagonal cells (12 turns and flips, six neighbours, hexagon cell look-up and distances) and is different from it; I did not read the entries of the other hexagon materials in the catalog (for example `hexagontiles`) to compare. The test checks in two independent ways: the shape of every panel is read back from the picture (a cell of the box is part of the shape where there is ink at its centre, and the height there gives the symmetry level), each shape has exactly n cells and is connected, and there are no repeats (a free shape is named by the least of its 12 turns and flips, a fixed one by the shape moved to the corner); the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which goes through all the sets of n cells of a window of n by n cells (a connected shape of n cells spans at most n values of q and of r, so the window is large enough), keeps the connected ones and names them again with turns and flips written in cube coordinates (the sampler grows the shapes cell by cell and removes repeats by the least name under moving and the 12 turns); the two sets are identical; the test also checks that the symmetry level read from the picture equals the number of symmetries counted in the test, and which levels occur in each variant. In the point-by-point check the cell of a point is the one with the nearest centre in the test (the sampler uses rounding in cube coordinates). **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first run of the test had two failures, because I had put placeholder values for the symmetry levels and for the number of compared points in the test to be measured; both were expected measuring steps, and I filled in the measured values afterwards (the levels are in the test, the compared points are 4855 to 5465 with the lower bound 4600); (2) in the point-by-point check about 9% to 19% of the points were skipped as being near a gap edge; (3) all 40 mutation checks were caught; (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; the picture is sparse (the lit cells are only 2.6% to 6.5% of a 256² sampling) and, like `polyominoes`, rather dark.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the shapes are produced by growing cell by cell and removing repeats by the least name under the 12 turns and flips (at most 186, each a `Uint8Array` of size² at most 25 B) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, one rounding in cube coordinates, up to six neighbour look-ups with distances and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: polyhexes took 115 ms and 87 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 155 ms and 142 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`compositions` adds integer compositions, bringing the current catalog from 1153 to 1154 kinds (1155 gallery choices including plain). Blue-violet drawings on a dark navy-black ground: **every composition of one kind (a way to write an integer as an ordered sum of positive integers) is drawn once, as a strip cut into parts** — a strip of n cells is cut into pieces by the parts of the composition, the cells of a piece join without a seam and a gap parts a piece from the next — one composition to a small panel. The 6 variants are all the compositions of 8, 128 (2^(n − 1), 5×26 panels, 2 slots empty), all of 9, 256 (7×37, 3 empty), those of 10 with no part above 2, 89 (4×23, 3 empty), those of 12 with no part above 2, 233 (6×39, 1 empty), those of 12 with only odd parts, 144 (5×29, 1 empty) and those of 12 with all parts different, 101 (4×26, 3 empty). The numbers of compositions with no part above 2 and with only odd parts are Fibonacci numbers. The **tone and height of a piece follow its length**: the shortest is the darkest and the longest there can be (8, 9, 2, 2, 11, 12) the brightest; the tone runs from 0.3 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.3 + 0.7 times (length − 1) / (longest − 1)); a gap is 0.16 of a cell, smoothed over 0.1; each panel holds the strip with 0.5 of a cell of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; that there are 2^(n − 1) compositions of n and that those with no part above 2 and those with only odd parts are counted by Fibonacci numbers are results I remember and did not look up in the literature; the numbers in the test (128, 256, 89, 233, 144, 101) are the results of an enumeration written separately. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): composition gave 0/6 (mentions in the README, which I did not read one by one), and no kind has compos in its name. I read the beginnings of the related entries (about 450 characters each, not the whole entries): `dominoboards`, `dominotiling` and `trominotiling` (tilings); a composition with no part above 2 is a strip of n cells tiled by pieces of length 1 and 2, which is different from these two-dimensional tilings, and no other kind draws integer compositions. The test checks in two independent ways: the composition of every panel is read back from the picture (the strip is cut where the height at the seam between two neighbouring cells is 0, and the height at the middle of every cell of a piece must be that of the length of the piece; an empty slot shows the ground at every cell), each composition is of the kind by the definitions (the parts add up to n; no part above 2, only odd parts, or all parts different) and there are no repeats; the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which goes through all the 2^(n − 1) ways to cut or not cut each of the n − 1 seams of a strip of n cells and filters each by the definition (the sampler recursion chooses the length of the next part one after the other and prunes while doing so); the two sets are identical. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 5153 to 5348 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 5000; (2) of 30 mutation checks 2 were not caught, both equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the compositions of the kind are listed by a recursion that chooses the length of the next part (at most 256, each two `Uint8Array`s of at most 12 B; the restrictions to parts of at most 2, odd parts and different parts prune the recursion) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, one look-up in the strip, four smoothings and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: compositions took 74 ms and 59 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 113 ms and 115 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`setpartitions` adds set partitions, bringing the current catalog from 1152 to 1153 kinds (1154 gallery choices including plain). Amber drawings on a dark plum-black ground: **every partition of a set of n elements into blocks of one kind is drawn once, as its restricted growth string** — the element i (counting from 0) is the column i and its block the row j, the blocks numbered in the order of their first elements, exactly one lit tile in every column — one partition to a small panel. The 6 variants are all the partitions of 3 elements, 5 (3×2 panels, 1 slot empty), of 4 elements, 15 (4×4, 1 empty), of 5 elements, 52 (8×7, 4 empty), the **noncrossing** partitions of 5 elements, 42 (7×6), of 6 elements, 132 (12×11), and all the partitions of 6 elements, 203 (15×14, 7 empty). The numbers of all the partitions are the Bell numbers (5, 15, 52, 203) and of the noncrossing ones (no a < b < c < d with a and c in one block and b and d in another) the Catalan numbers (42 and 132). The **tone and height of a lit tile follow the size of its block**: a block of one element is the darkest and one of all the elements the brightest; the tone runs from 0.3 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.3 + 0.7 times (size of the block − 1) / (n − 1)); the other cells show the ground; a tile has a gap around it (0.16 of a cell, smoothed over 0.1); each panel holds the n by n table (at its top left) with 0.5 of a cell of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the Bell numbers (5, 15, 52, 203) and the Catalan numbers of the noncrossing partitions (42, 132) are numbers I remember and did not look up in the literature; the numbers in the test are the results of an enumeration written separately. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): setpartition, noncrossing and rgs gave 0/0, bell 2/1 (`bellpepperslices` and `brassjinglebells`, unrelated) and partitions 0/4 (mentions in the README). I read the beginnings of the related entries (about 380 characters each, not the whole entries): `youngdiagrams` (partitions of an integer drawn as Young diagrams), `standardtableaux`, `polygondissections` (Catalan numbers too), `permutations` (permutation matrices, which also have one lit cell in every column, but those are permutations whereas these are set partitions with the blocks numbered by first elements and the height following the size of the block) and `partitionmod5` (a table of the partition numbers p(n) mod 5); this draws partitions of a **set**, which is different from them. The test checks in two independent ways: the partition of every panel is read back from the picture (every column must have exactly one lit tile, and its row is the block of that element; the height of the lit tile must be that of the size of the block; an empty slot shows the ground at every cell), each partition is of the kind by the definitions (the blocks numbered in the order of their first elements; for the noncrossing kind no a < b < c < d with a and c in one block and b and d in another) and there are no repeats; the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which goes through all the n^n maps from the elements to labels, renumbers them in the order of the first elements, keeps the distinct ones and filters by the definition (the sampler recursion adds each element to a block that is there or opens a new one and prunes while doing so); the two sets are identical. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the point-by-point check compares 5686 to 5783 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 5550; as most points are ground the check tests mostly that the ground is flat, and the contents of the lit tiles are guarded mainly by the partition and height read back; (2) of 28 mutation checks 3 were not caught, all equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); (3) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in; the picture is sparse (the lit tiles are only 6% to 8% of a 256² sampling) and, like `permutations`, rather dark.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the partitions of the kind are listed by a recursion that adds element after element (at most 203, each two `Uint8Array`s of at most 6 B; the noncrossing restriction prunes the recursion) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, one look-up in the column, four smoothings and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: setpartitions took 90 ms and 67 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 149 ms and 127 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`booleanfunctions` adds Boolean functions, bringing the current catalog from 1151 to 1152 kinds (1153 gallery choices including plain). Mint-green drawings on a dark green-black ground: **every Boolean function of one kind is drawn once, as its truth table** — the cell number k of the table (counting along the rows) is the value for the inputs given by the bits of k (the lowest bit the first variable), a lit cell for 1 and a dim one for 0 — one function to a small panel. The 6 variants are all the functions of 2 variables, 16 (a 2×2 table, 4×4 panels), the **monotone** functions of 3 variables (the value never goes from 1 to 0 when an input bit goes from 0 to 1), 20 (a 4×2 table, 5×4 panels), the **self-dual** functions of 3 variables (the opposite inputs give opposite values), 16 (4×4), all the functions of 3 variables, 256 (16×16), the monotone functions of 4 variables, 168 (a 4×4 table, 13×13, 1 slot empty) and the self-dual functions of 4 variables, 256 (16×16). The numbers 20 and 168 of monotone functions are the Dedekind numbers and that of self-dual ones is 2 to the power 2^(n − 1). Every cell is a flat tile: a lit cell has the tone 0.95 and the height 0.8·1, an unlit one the tone 0.25 and the height 0.8·0.25; a tile has a gap around it (0.16 of a cell, smoothed over 0.1); each panel holds the truth table (at its top left) with 0.5 of a cell of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the number of monotone Boolean functions (the Dedekind numbers 20 and 168) and of self-dual ones (2 to the power 2^(n − 1)) are numbers I remember and did not look up in the literature; the numbers in the test are the results of an enumeration written separately. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): boolean, truthtable, dedekind, monotone and selfdual all gave 0/0, and no kind has boolean or truth in its name. This is the first material on Boolean functions, so there was no other entry to compare with. The test checks in two independent ways: the truth table of every panel is read back from the picture (the height at the middle of a cell has to be that of a lit or an unlit cell, no other value; an empty slot shows the ground at every cell), each function is of the kind by the definitions (monotone: f(x) ≤ f(y) whenever the set bits of x are among those of y; self-dual: f of the opposite input = 1 − f of the input) and there are no repeats; the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which goes through all the 2^(2^n) tables and tests each by the definition (the sampler fills input after input with a recursion and prunes while doing so); the two sets are identical. **Notes (honest)**: (1) my first reader for the test handled an empty slot wrongly (after the first cell read the ground, the later cells failed an "nothing before" check), so I changed it to count the ground cells and require that all or none are ground; (2) the point-by-point check compares 4616 to 5449 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 4400; (3) of 22 mutation checks 2 were not caught, both equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the functions of the kind are listed by a recursion that fills input after input (at most 256, each a `Uint8Array` of at most 16 B; the monotone and self-dual restrictions prune the recursion) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, one look-up in the truth table, four smoothings and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: booleanfunctions took 92 ms and 77 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 147 ms and 146 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`latinsquares` adds Latin squares, bringing the current catalog from 1150 to 1151 kinds (1152 gallery choices including plain). The 6 variants are all the Latin squares of order 3, 12 (4×3 panels), the **reduced** Latin squares of order 4 (whose first row and first column read 0, 1, 2, …), 4 (2×2), the **diagonal** Latin squares of order 4 (whose two long diagonals also hold every symbol), 48 (7×7, 1 slot empty), the reduced Latin squares of order 5, 56 (8×7), the **Sudoku squares** of order 4 (every 2×2 box too holds every symbol), 288 (17×17, 1 empty) and all the Latin squares of order 4, 576 (24×24). Every cell is a flat tile whose **tone and height follow its symbol**: 0 is the darkest and n − 1 the brightest; the tone runs from 0.2 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.3 + 0.7 times symbol / (n − 1)); a tile has a gap around it (0.12 of a cell, smoothed over 0.08); each panel holds the square with 0.4 of a cell of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the numbers of Latin squares, reduced Latin squares and Sudoku squares (12 of order 3, 576 of order 4, 4 reduced of order 4, 56 reduced of order 5 and 288 Sudoku squares of order 4) are numbers I remember and did not look up in the literature; the numbers in the test are the results of an enumeration written separately. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): shidoku gave 0/0, latin 1/23 (`graecolatin`) and sudoku 1/3 (`sudoku`). I read the related entries: `sudoku` (a newspaper 9×9 Sudoku grid with digits placed at random, **not** a legal Sudoku), `graecolatin` (one 13×13 Graeco-Latin square), `cayleytable` (the multiplication table of a group of order 16, a special case of a Latin square) and `magicsquares`; this draws **all** the Latin squares of small orders, which is different from them. The test checks in two independent ways: the picture of every panel is read back (the symbol of a cell comes from the height at its middle and must be close to an integer), and each square is a Latin square (every row and every column a permutation of 0 to n − 1), in the reduced variants the first row and first column read 0 to n − 1, in the diagonal variant both long diagonals hold every symbol, in the Sudoku variant every 2×2 box does too, and there are no repeats; the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test: all the permutations are listed as possible rows, rows are chosen one after the other so that no symbol repeats in a column, and only then the restriction of the kind is applied (the sampler fills cell after cell checking row, column and box at the same time); the two sets are identical; the numbers read from the picture also satisfy 576 = 4!·3!·(the number of reduced squares) = 24·6·4. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the mutation checks showed that for order 4 it is enough to check the main diagonal to get the same 48 "diagonal" squares as checking both diagonals, so the check of the other diagonal is redundant at order 4 (an experimental result, not a proof); I kept it because the variant is defined by "both diagonals" and the difference would show at higher orders; (2) the point-by-point check compares 4760 to 5269 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 4600; (3) of 24 mutation checks 5 were not caught, all equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the squares are listed by a recursion that fills cell after cell (at most 576, each a `Uint8Array` of at most 25 B) and shuffled. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: latinsquares took 158 ms and 119 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 234 ms and 217 ms in the same environment (the machine load varies, so the comparison is only rough); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`dominoboards` adds domino boards, bringing the current catalog from 1149 to 1150 kinds (1151 gallery choices including plain). Amber drawings on a dark brown-black ground: **every domino tiling of a small board is drawn once** — the board covered by dominoes of two cells, with no cell left open and none sticking out — one tiling to a small panel. The 6 boards (width × height) are 6×2 with 13 tilings (3×5 panels, 2 slots empty), 4×3 with 11 (3×4, 1 empty), 4×4 with 36 (6×6), 6×3 with 41 (5×9, 4 empty), 5×4 with 95 (9×11, 4 empty) and 6×4 with 281 (14×21, 13 empty); the numbers come from Kasteleyn's formula. The two cells of a domino join without a seam and are parted from other cells by a gap (0.16 of a cell, smoothed over 0.1); **a horizontal domino is brighter and higher than a vertical one**: the tone is 0.85 against 0.45 and the height 0.8 times (1 against 0.6). Each panel holds the board (at its top left) with 0.5 of a cell of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the board and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; Kasteleyn's formula (the product over all j up to m and k up to n of (4 cos²(πj / (m + 1)) + 4 cos²(πk / (n + 1))) to the power 1/4 for an m by n board) was written from memory and not looked up in the literature; the numbers 13, 11, 36, 41, 95 and 281 are counted by an enumeration written separately in the test and checked against this formula, not only remembered. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): kasteleyn gave 0/0 and domino 2/9, dominoes 1/6 and matching 0/3 (README mentions); the kinds with domino in the name are `dominotiling` and `dominoes`. I read the entry of `dominotiling`: it is **one** random tiling of a 32×32 torus reached by flips, horizontal dominoes sand and vertical ones slate grey; for `dominoes` I found no separate README entry with my entry pattern, so what I read is its preset in `materials.ts` (a domino game tile with pips and a divider), a different thing. This draws **all** the tilings of small boards, close to the first in visual vocabulary (two tones for horizontal and vertical) but different in content, and I did not compare them pixel by pixel. The test checks in two independent ways: the tiling of every panel is read back from the picture (the height at the middle of a cell says whether it belongs to a horizontal or a vertical domino, and at the middle of each side between it and a neighbour the ground is seen where there is a seam and the domino where there is none) and each cell is joined to exactly one neighbour, the joining is mutual, the direction agrees with the height and there are no repeats; the set is compared with an enumeration written separately in the test, which covers the last free cell with a domino to the left or above (the sampler covers the first free cell with a domino to the right or below); the two sets are identical and the number equals Kasteleyn's formula (worked out by adding logarithms). **Notes (honest)**: (1) the first version of the point-by-point check also marked the gap region as "near a border" and skipped it, so it compared only points far from a gap and would have missed the gap itself; I changed it to skip only the smoothing zone (from half the gap to half the gap plus the smoothing) so that the gaps (a distance not above half the gap) and the insides of cells are both compared; (2) the point-by-point check compares 4919 to 5392 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 4800; (3) of 23 mutation checks 1 was not caught, an equivalent mutation (see ACCEPTANCE); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the tilings are listed by a recursion (at most 281, each a `Uint8Array` of at most 24 B) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, one look-up in the board, four smoothings and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: dominoboards took 62 ms and 50 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 95 ms and 95 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`rootedtrees` adds rooted trees, bringing the current catalog from 1148 to 1149 kinds (1150 gallery choices including plain). Lime-green drawings on a dark green-black ground: **every rooted tree with n nodes is drawn once up to renaming the nodes (one for each isomorphism class)**, one tree to a small panel. The 6 variants are all the rooted trees of 5, 6, 7 and 8 nodes, 9, 20, 48 and 115 of them, in 3×3 (9), 5×4 (20), 7×7 (49, 1 slot empty) and 11×11 (121, 6 empty) panels, and the rooted trees of 8 and 9 nodes with at most 2 children to a node, 46 and 98 of them, in 7×7 (49, 3 empty) and 10×10 (100, 2 empty) panels. The drawing: the root is at the top, the children of a node hang from a bar half a unit below it, a node is right above its first child and the leaves are one unit apart from left to right; a node is a dot (radius 0.18) whose **tone and height follow its number of children** over the most it could have, n − 1: the tone runs from 0.3 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.4 + 0.6 times the fraction); the lines have the half width 0.07 (tone 0.5, height 0.8·0.25) below the dots, smoothed over 0.04. Each panel holds a box of (n − 2) by (n − 1) units (the tree at its top left) with 0.5 of a unit of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the lines and dots are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the numbers of rooted trees 9, 20, 48 and 115 (A000081) and "46 and 98 with at most 2 children to a node (the same as the Wedderburn–Etherington numbers)" are numbers I remember and did not look up in the literature; the numbers in the test are the results of an enumeration written separately. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): rootedtree, rootedtrees, dendrogram, arborescence, wedderburn and cayleytree all gave 0/0; the kinds with tree in the name are `htree` and `pythagorastree` (fractals) and `spanningtrees`. I read the entries of `spanningtrees` (every spanning tree of small graphs, a listing of the trees of one graph) and `graphatlas` (the isomorphism classes of small graphs); this is the isomorphism classes of the trees themselves, drawn as tree diagrams. The test checks in two independent ways: the tree of every panel is read back from the picture (the nodes are the lattice points where a dot is seen; for each node the half line below it, the bar and the half lines above the children are read at the middles of the unit pieces, where the height is that of a line (present) or 0 (absent), no other value; the children of a node are the nodes that hang from its bar; the height of a dot gives a number of children that has to equal the number of children read, and the number of nodes reached has to equal the number of dots seen in the panel), and then the class is named in the AHU way (the names of the subtrees sorted and put in brackets) and compared with a result written separately in the test: all the lists of parents (the node k has a parent with a number smaller than k; 8! = 40,320 lists for n = 9) are tried and the distinct names are taken (the sampler instead builds the trees recursively as multisets of smaller trees, picking by size and place in the list without going back); the two sets of classes are identical and no two panels are alike. **Notes (honest)**: (1) my first version had a line half width of 0.05 and a dot radius of 0.14; after looking at the montage I found the lines too thin and changed them to 0.07 and 0.18 (the middle of a unit piece is 0.25 from a dot, still more than the radius of a dot plus half the smoothing, so reading back is not affected); (2) I looked at 512×512 crops of seeds 1 and 3 at full size: in the variant of 8 nodes with 115 trees the lines are about a pixel wide at 512 pixels and look dotted, hard to make out, while the smaller variants are clear; (3) the point-by-point check compares 5852 to 5908 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 5700; (4) the point-by-point check uses the unit pieces and dots read back from the picture (not the long segments inside the sampler) as the ideal shape, so a long segment is split into small pieces and more points near their joints may be skipped as near a border than is necessary.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the isomorphism classes are listed by a recursion (at most 115, each a list of subtrees, n ≤ 9), shuffled, and for each the nodes (at most 9) and segments (about 3n at most) are worked out. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, the distance to up to about 27 segments with smoothing, the distance to up to 9 dots with smoothing and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: rootedtrees took 204 ms and 192 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 131 ms and 133 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`graphatlas` adds a graph atlas, bringing the current catalog from 1147 to 1148 kinds (1149 gallery choices including plain). Sky-blue drawings on a dark navy-black ground: **every graph of one kind is drawn once up to renaming its vertices (one for each isomorphism class)**, with the vertices on a regular polygon (the first at the top) and the edges as straight lines, one graph to a small panel. The 6 variants are all the graphs of 4 vertices, 11 (4×3 panels, 1 slot empty), the connected graphs of 5 vertices, 21 (6×4, 3 empty), all the graphs of 5 vertices, 34 (7×5, 1 empty), the connected graphs of 6 vertices, 112 (12×10, 8 empty), all the graphs of 6 vertices, 156 (13×12) and the graphs of 6 vertices with exactly 7 edges, 24 (6×4). A vertex is a dot (radius 0.1 of the polygon radius) whose **tone and height follow its degree** (the number of edges at it) over the most it could have, n − 1: the tone runs from 0.3 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.4 + 0.6 times the fraction); an edge is a line of half width 0.03 (tone 0.5, height 0.8·0.25) below the dots, smoothed over 0.03. The polygon has the radius 1 and is centred in its slot at one scale with 0.2 of margin. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the lines and dots are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the numbers of graphs up to renaming (1, 2, 4, 11, 34, 156), of connected graphs (21 and 112) and "24 graphs of 6 vertices with 7 edges" are numbers I remember and did not look up in the literature; in the test the number of all the graphs is also computed by Pólya's counting (the mean over all renamings of 2 to the number of cycles that the renaming makes of the pairs of vertices) and the other numbers are results of the enumeration. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): graphatlas, atlas, isomorphism, isomorphic, nonisomorphic and graphs gave 0/0 everywhere, and the kinds with graph in the name are `fareygraph`, `gabrielgraph`, `graphpaper` and so on (other things). I read `gabrielgraph` (the Gabriel graph of a Poisson-disk point set), `fareygraph` (the semicircular arcs of the Farey graph), `spanningtrees` (every spanning tree of the small graphs K4, K(2,4), wheels, K(3,3) and K5, a listing of the trees of one graph) and `sortingnetwork`; this is an atlas of all the small graphs, which is different. The test checks in two ways: the picture of every panel is read back (at a probe point of each pair of vertices, far enough from all the other segments and the dots, a height above 0 means the edge is there; the height of a dot gives the degree, which has to equal the number of edges read at that vertex) and compared with a result written separately in the test: all the isomorphism classes are found by **marking orbits** (going through all the 2^(n(n−1)/2) labelled graphs and, at one that is not yet marked, marking all its renamings as seen, one edge list per class; the sampler instead builds the classes from those with one vertex fewer by joining the new vertex to every subset and keeps the least number among the renamings), and the classes are compared by a name for the class, the least edge list written as a string over all renamings; the two sets of classes are identical, no two panels are alike and the number of all the graphs equals Pólya's count. **Notes (honest)**: (1) the sampler keeps the classes found for each number of vertices in a module-level cache (`graphClassCache`), because for 6 vertices it tries 34 classes × 32 subsets × 720 renamings and doing that for every sampler created would be too slow; (2) the point-by-point check compares 5321 to 5743 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 5200; (3) of 28 mutation checks 3 were not caught, all equivalent mutations (see ACCEPTANCE); (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 without zooming in and did not check each panel by eye.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain; the classes of graphs are looked up in the module-level cache and found the first time (for 6 vertices: from the 34 classes of 5 vertices, each joined to the 32 subsets, 1,088 candidates, each tried with 720 renamings for the least) and stored, so that the same number of vertices is not worked out again; each class keeps its edge list (at most 15) and the degrees of the vertices. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, the distance to up to 15 segments with smoothing, the distance to up to 6 dots with smoothing and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: graphatlas took 202 ms and 191 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 145 ms and 179 ms in the same environment (the machine load varies, so the comparison is only rough); the time of the first search for the classes was not measured separately; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`standardtableaux` adds standard Young tableaux, bringing the current catalog from 1146 to 1147 kinds (1148 gallery choices including plain). Mint-green drawings on a dark green-black ground: **every standard Young tableau of a shape is drawn once** — the numbers 1 to n written into the cells of a Young diagram (English notation) so that they increase along every row from left to right and down every column — one filling to a small panel. The 6 shapes (row lengths) are (3, 2, 1) with 16 tableaux (4×4 panels), (5, 3) with 28 (4×7), (3, 3, 3) with 42 (7×6), (4, 3, 1) with 70 (8×9, 2 slots empty), (4, 3, 2) with 168 (13×13, 1 empty) and (4, 4, 2) with 252 (14×18); the numbers come from the hook length formula (n! over the product of the hook lengths). Every cell is a flat tile whose **tone and height follow its number**: 1 (at the top left corner) is the darkest and n the brightest; the tone runs from 0.2 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.3 + 0.7 times (number − 1) / (n − 1)). A tile has a gap around it (0.16 of a cell, smoothed over 0.1); each panel holds the box of the diagram (width by height cells, the diagram at its top left) with 0.5 of a cell of margin, drawn at one scale and centred. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; standard Young tableaux and the hook length formula are described from memory and were not looked up in the literature (the numbers 16, 28, 42, 70, 168 and 252 are counted by an enumeration written separately in the test and checked against the hook length formula, not only remembered). Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): standardtableaux, hooklength and robinson gave 0/0, tableaux 0/1 (a README mention), tableau 1/7 (the one kind is `excitableautomata`, whose name happens to contain those letters, a different thing) and young 1/7 (`youngdiagrams`). I read the entry of `youngdiagrams`: it draws every partition of an integer n (a Young diagram) with each cell toned by its hook length, and mentions that n!/∏h, the number of standard tableaux, is an integer, but it does not draw the tableaux; this draws all the fillings of one shape, a different object. The test checks in two ways: the picture of every panel is read back (a cell with a height above 0 is in the diagram and its number is computed from the height, and has to be close to an integer), and each tableau has the shape, the numbers 1 to n once each, increasing along every row and down every column, no repeats, and the set equals a list written again in the test, which goes the other way round: n goes into a corner of the diagram (a row longer than the next) and the rest is a tableau of the smaller diagram (the sampler writes 1, 2, … into cells that can be added); the counts equal the hook length formula. Limitation (honest note): although the two enumerations go in opposite directions, both are recursions on the shape of the diagram, so they are not entirely independent algorithms; the agreement of the counts with the hook length formula is a further support, but the formula itself is from memory. **Notes from the work**: (1) my first layouts of the panels ((5, 3) in 7 columns by 4 rows, (4, 4, 2) in 16 by 16) did not match the proportions of the boxes of the diagrams and left large empty areas, so I changed them to columns and rows closer to the box proportions (4×7, 14×18 and so on) and measured again; (2) on backtracking the sampler first cleared a cell to 0, but every cell is overwritten before a complete filling is copied, so that line was redundant; the mutation checks did not catch it, so I removed it (the output is unchanged; afterwards I re-ran only the tests); (3) the point-by-point check compares 4953 to 5247 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 4800; (4) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 and 512×512 crops of seeds 1 and 3 at full size.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the standard tableaux are listed by a recursion (at most 252, each a `Uint8Array` of at most 4×3 = 12 B, about 3 KB in all) and shuffled. At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, one look-up in the grid of the tableau, four smoothings and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: standardtableaux took 74 ms and 67 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 113 ms and 140 ms in the same environment (the load of this machine varies, so the comparison is only rough); the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`polygondissections` adds polygon dissections, bringing the current catalog from 1145 to 1146 kinds (1147 gallery choices including plain). Amber drawings on a dark maroon-black ground: **every way of cutting a regular polygon by diagonals that do not cross is drawn once**, one cut to a small panel. The 6 variants are the triangulations (as many diagonals as possible, n − 3, cutting the polygon into triangles; Catalan numbers) of the hexagon, 14 (4×4 panels, 2 slots empty), the heptagon, 42 (7×6) and the octagon, 132 (12×11), and the dissections (any number of diagonals, none included; little Schröder numbers) of the pentagon, 11 (4×3, 1 empty), the hexagon, 45 (7×7, 4 empty) and the heptagon, 197 (15×14, 13 empty). Every piece is a flat tile parted from the others by a gap (0.07 of the radius wide, smoothed over 0.05) along the diagonals and the sides of the polygon. **The tone and height of a piece follow the fraction of its sides that are sides of the polygon** (an ear of a triangulation has 2 of 3, a triangle in the inside none): the tone runs from 0.35 to 0.95 and the height is 0.8 times (0.4 + 0.6 times the fraction). The polygon has the radius 1, the first vertex at the top, and is centred in its slot at one scale with 0.12 of margin. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps around the pieces are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the relation between triangulations of a polygon and the Catalan numbers, the little Schröder numbers for dissections and the formula for the number of cuts with k diagonals, C(n − 3, k) C(n + k − 1, k) / (k + 1) (Kirkman–Cayley), are described from memory and were not looked up in the literature (I checked it by hand for the pentagon: k = 0, 1, 2 give 1, 5, 5, which add up to 11). Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): triangulations, dissection, dissections and schroder gave 0/0, triangulation 0/1 (a README mention, `delaunay`), catalan 0/4 (README mentions), polygon 2/14 (the 2 kinds are `polygonoffsets` and `pursuitpolygons`, other things) and ear 8/87 (mostly pieces of other words). I read the related entries: `delaunay` (the Delaunay triangulation of a Poisson-disk point set, one random triangulation), `dyckpaths` (Dyck paths, which also have the Catalan numbers 14, 42 and 132) and `permutations` (the 132 permutations that avoid 231, the same Catalan number); this draws all the ways of cutting a regular polygon, which is different from them, and only the numbers are the same (there are one-to-one correspondences between these objects, which is also from memory). The test checks in two independent ways: the diagonals of every panel are read back from the picture (at a probe point on each diagonal that is far enough from the other diagonals and the sides of the polygon the ground is seen, height 0 in the gap, where the diagonal is cut, and a tile is seen where it is not), giving the set of diagonals of each panel, and the sets are compared with a list written separately in the test: all the subsets of the diagonals are tried with a bit mask and whether two diagonals cross inside is decided from the coordinates of the vertices (the sampler uses the alternation of the end numbers and a recursion that chooses diagonal after diagonal); the lists are identical, the counts equal the sum of the Kirkman–Cayley formula and every triangulation has at least two ears (vertices whose two neighbours are joined by a diagonal). In the point-by-point check the piece of a point is told by the vertices that no cut separates from the point (unlike the sampler, which cuts one diagonal after the other), and the distances to the sides of the piece are computed from them. **Notes (honest)**: (1) my first version toned a piece by its number of sides, but all pieces of a triangulation are triangles, so every tone was the same (the lit fraction and the unlike fraction were both 0), and I changed it to the fraction of its sides that are sides of the polygon; (2) my first test used a fixed place 0.3 along each diagonal as the probe, but where a diagonal that is not cut crosses one that is, the probe could fall near the gap of the other and be read as cut, so I changed it to choose for each diagonal a place farther than half a gap plus 0.01 from all the other diagonals; (3) a mutation check showed that the second clause of the crossing test was not caught by any test, and I found that it is dead code (the earlier diagonal never starts after the later one, so the second clause can never hold); I removed it (the output is unchanged; afterwards I re-ran only the tests, not all the mutations); (4) the point-by-point check compares 4987 to 5596 of the 6000 points per seed, with the lower bound 4900; (5) I looked at the montage of previews of seeds 0 to 5 and 512×512 crops of seeds 0 and 3 at full size.

At start-up (per sampler): the `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B for grain, and all the sets of diagonals that do not cross are listed by a recursion (at most 197 sets, each with at most 4 diagonals; for the octagon the choosing is pruned by the crossing test) and each is cut into its pieces (at most 6). At sampling time (per pixel): one slot look-up, for each piece of that set (at most 6) the distances from its sides (at most 8) to the point, the smoothing for the first piece that has the point and one grain look-up. I measured single-threaded maps generation of 512×512 in Bun: polygondissections took 146 ms and 131 ms (two runs) and talbotcarpet 118 ms and 117 ms in the same environment; the time in a browser Worker was not measured.

`lozengetilings` adds lozenge tilings, bringing the current catalog from 1144 to 1145 kinds (1146 gallery choices including plain). Cyan-blue drawings on a dark teal-black ground: **every lozenge tiling of a hexagon with the sides a, b, c, a, b, c is drawn once**, which is the same as every plane partition in an a by b by c box (a stack of unit cubes in the corner of the box, seen along the diagonal), one tiling to a small panel. The three kinds of lozenge are the top, right and left faces of the cubes (and of the floor and the two walls behind them), in three tones, the top brightest. The 6 variants (boxes [a, b, c]) are [1, 2, 3] with 10 tilings (4×3 panels, 2 slots empty), [2, 2, 2] with 20 (5×4), [2, 2, 3] with 50 (8×7, 6 empty), [2, 2, 4] with 105 (11×10, 5 empty), [2, 3, 3] with 175 (14×13, 7 empty) and [1, 3, 4] with 35 (7×5). Every lozenge has a gap around it (0.08 of the side of a lozenge wide, smoothed over 0.06); the tone is 0.95 for a top face, 0.62 for a right face and 0.35 for a left face; the height is 0.8 times (1 for a top face, 0.75 for a right face and 0.5 for a left face); the AO is 1 − 0.45·(1 − ink); roughness is 0.4 and metallic 0. Each hexagon is centred in a square slot of side span, all drawn at one scale, with 0.35 of a unit of margin. **The seed is split in two**: seed % 6 picks the variant and ⌊seed / 6⌋ the order of the panels (Fisher–Yates shuffled; seeds 0 to 5 are the six variants of one group). The pattern wraps with `fract(u)` and `fract(v)` and is **exactly periodic** (every panel has a margin and the gaps around every lozenge are combined from product masks, so it is C1).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; MacMahon's formula for the number of plane partitions (the product of (i + j + k − 1) / (i + j + k − 2) over the box) and the one-to-one correspondence between lozenge tilings and plane partitions are described from memory and were not looked up in the literature; the numbers 10, 20, 50, 105, 175 and 35 were computed by the enumeration in the test and checked against this formula, not only remembered. Checked for absence before adding (`/tmp/absent.sh` actually run): planepartition, isometric, cubes and macmahon gave 0/0, lozenge 0/1 (the README mention is the stepped-lozenge weave of `kilimdiamonds`), rhombus 0/5 (rhombus tilings such as Penrose), rhombille 2/6 and hexagon 6/27 (several hexagonal tile materials). I read the related entries: `kisrhombilletiles` (README, a V4.6.12 tiling of triangles), `kilimdiamonds` (a stepped-lozenge weave) and the Penrose and Ammann families (aperiodic rhombus tilings); for `rhombille` I found no separate README entry with my entry pattern, so what I read is its preset in `materials.ts` (3 columns, 4 rows, three shades): it is a **fixed periodic** "tumbling blocks" pattern, close to this one in visual vocabulary but not the same as a poster that lists all the tilings of a hexagon, and I did not compare them pixel by pixel.
