`radicaltable` adds a radical table, bringing the current catalog from 1002 to 1003 kinds (1004 gallery choices including plain). It is a 48×48 grid of squares in which cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row·48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned by `ln(rad(n)) / ln(n)`, where `rad(n)` is the product of all distinct prime factors of n (the radical): squarefree numbers (1400 of them; n = 1 is defined as ratio 1) have ratio 1 and are brightest; prime powers `p^k` have ratio `1/k` (for example 4 gives 1/2, 8 gives 1/3 and 2048 gives the smallest, 1/11); the ratio is then squared to widen the differences; multiples of 4, 8 and 9 leave dark stripes and diagonals, in pale sage green on dark green. The cells are rounded raised squares showing gaps through height and AO, and the seed shifts the whole table around the torus. It shares the cell shape with number-theory tables such as `divisorcount` and `totienttable`, only the values and tones differ. It only shows the radical ratios of the first 2304 positive integers; it does not prove or illustrate the abc conjecture.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the toneExponent of 2, the toneFloor of 0.14, the toneSpan of 0.7, the sage green and dark green tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). The cell shape and tone combination reuse the divisorcount parameters and were not retuned for the radical. The tests passed on the first run with no need to adjust ranges. Most cells are bright (squarefree numbers are about 61% of the table), so the whole is on the bright side; this follows from the way values are assigned and is not a defect. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0296).

At start-up a sieve computes the radical for `n ≤ 2304` (set `rad(n) = 1`, and for every prime `q` that has not yet been multiplied into itself — that is, `rad(q) = 1` at that point — do `rad(m) *= q` for each multiple `m`) and precomputes each cell's tone `0.7·(ln(rad(n)) / ln(n))^2` (n = 1 is treated as ratio 1); at sampling time every cell uses one compact-support rounded-square kernel (a quartic superellipse through smoothstep, exactly zero before the cell boundary, so the cell lookup never jumps and the field is C1): color is `0.04 + (0.14 + tone − 0.04)·mask + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·dome·(0.88 + 0.12·tone) + 0.08·grain`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.4·(1 − mask)`, roughness is fixed at 0.4 and metallic is 0; the cache totals a `Float64Array(2305)` (radicals) of 18,440 B plus a `Float64Array(2304)` (tones) of 18,432 B plus a `Float64Array(128²)` of 131,072 B, 167,944 B in all, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample does a constant number of operations; I did not measure the time, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run): up to 2304 there are 1400 squarefree numbers, `rad(4) = 2` gives the ratio 1/2, `rad(2048) = 2` gives the smallest ratio 1/11, and `rad(2304) = 6`; on a 256² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff) the lit area (color>0.5) covers 60.65%–60.87%, color is 0.0255–0.0257 to 0.8542–0.8545 with a mean of 0.5278–0.5308, the lowest AO is 0.6 (equal to `1 − 0.4`) and height is at most 0.8472–0.8483 relief; on a 512² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7) the lit area covers 60.26%–60.57%, color is 0.0251–0.0254 to 0.8547–0.8549 with a mean of 0.5278–0.5290 and height is at most 0.8493–0.8505 relief; for each seed exactly one torus shift (seed 0: (46, 4), 1: (4, 7), 0xffffffff: (17, 42), 7: (30, 23)) makes the colours at the 2304 cell centres match the tones that the test rewrites independently by trial division, within a maximum error of 0.0150 (the error comes from the grain; the test's threshold is 0.03); between seeds 0 and 1, 64.3% of the cell centres differ in colour by more than 0.05, and the light masks (512²) differ on 19.8% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (123.0, 137.3, 101.8), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0296 and the minimum z component is 253. I viewed the preview (seed 7): pale sage rounded squares on dark green, interspersed with dark vertical streaks and diagonal dark dots. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`goldbachtable` adds a Goldbach partition table, bringing the current catalog from 1001 to 1002 kinds (1003 gallery choices including plain). It is a 48×48 grid of squares in which cell (col, row) stands for the even number `n = 2·(row·48 + col + 2)` (4, 6, 8, …, 4610) and is toned by its number of Goldbach partitions `g(n)` (the number of primes `p ≤ n/2` for which `n − p` is also prime): using g(n) directly would brighten steadily with n and show a hard colour step at the table's seam, so I first multiply by `ln(n)²/n` to remove the overall growth, then divide by the largest value in the table and raise it to the power 0.75; what is left is the band structure of the so-called Goldbach comet, where multiples of 6 and 30 are brighter than their neighbours (brightest at n = 2310 = 2·3·5·7·11), in violet on dark purple. The cells are rounded raised squares showing gaps through height and AO, and the seed shifts the whole table around the torus. It shares the cell shape with number-theory tables such as `divisorcount` and `totienttable`, only the values and tones differ. It only shows the partition counts of the first 2304 even numbers; it does not prove or illustrate the Goldbach conjecture.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the toneExponent of 0.75, the toneFloor of 0.14, the toneSpan of 0.7, the violet and dark purple tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. Adjustment record: the first version toned by g(n) divided by its maximum, and the preview showed a dark upper half, a bright lower half and a horizontal band at the table's seam (because g(n) grows with n), so I changed it to multiply by `ln(n)²/n` first; in the second preview the seam shows only a few darker cells (near n = 4) and there is no large colour step overall. I did not keep the test and probe numbers of the first version, and the documentation and tests use only the second version. I did not write claims such as 'numbers just above a power of 2 have few partitions' because I did not verify them. The tests passed on the first run with no need to adjust ranges. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0280).

At start-up a sieve marks the composite numbers up to `4611`, and for every even `n` the code checks every `q = 2 … n/2` for `q` and `n − q` both being prime to count the partitions (about 2.7 million checks; I measured the sampler build only three times: about 76 ms (first), 17 ms and 16 ms, which is not a benchmark), computes `g(n)·ln(n)²/n`, normalises by the maximum and precomputes each cell's tone `0.7·(ratio/maximum)^0.75`; at sampling time every cell uses one compact-support rounded-square kernel (a quartic superellipse through smoothstep, exactly zero before the cell boundary, so the cell lookup never jumps and the field is C1): color is `0.04 + (0.14 + tone − 0.04)·mask + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·dome·(0.88 + 0.12·tone) + 0.08·grain`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.4·(1 − mask)`, roughness is fixed at 0.4 and metallic is 0; the cache totals a `Uint8Array(4611)` of 4,611 B plus two `Float64Array(2304)` (ratio and tone) plus a `Float64Array(128²)`, 172,547 B in all, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample does a constant number of operations; I did not measure its time. Measured (tool-run): g(4) = 1 (2 + 2), g(10) = 2 (3 + 7 and 5 + 5), every even number in the table has at least one partition, the largest g is 171, g(4610) = 72, and the maximum of `g(n)·ln(n)²/n` is at n = 2310; on a 256² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff) the lit area (color>0.5) covers 26.77%–29.34%, color is 0.0257–0.0261 to 0.8451–0.8511 with a mean of 0.3765–0.3830, the lowest AO is 0.6 (equal to `1 − 0.4`) and height is at most 0.8347–0.8425 relief; on a 512² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7) the lit area covers 27.77%–29.11%, color is 0.0252–0.0255 to 0.8463–0.8527 with a mean of 0.3803–0.3826 and height is at most 0.8418–0.8461 relief; for each seed exactly one torus shift (seed 0: (33, 9), 1: (21, 40), 0xffffffff: (8, 0), 7: (11, 34)) makes the colours at the 2304 cell centres match the tones that the test rewrites independently by trial division, within a maximum error of 0.0150 (the error comes from the grain; the test's threshold is 0.03); between seeds 0 and 1, 39.7% of the cell centres differ in colour by more than 0.05, and the light masks (512²) differ on 9.1% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (98.0, 63.3, 111.8), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0280 and the minimum z component is 253. I viewed the second-version preview (seed 7): violet rounded squares on dark purple with bright and dark fine vertical streaks and no obvious horizontal band. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`totienttable` adds an Euler totient table, bringing the current catalog from 1000 to 1001 kinds (1002 gallery choices including plain). It is a 48×48 grid of squares in which cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row·48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned by the totient ratio `φ(n)/n`: the smallest ratio in the table (at n = 210, 48/210) maps to 0 and the ratio 1 (n = 1; primes are only just below 1) to the top, raised to the power 1.5, so primes and numbers with only large prime factors are brightest; even numbers have a ratio of at most 1/2 and multiples of 3 or 5 are pushed down as well, and the table shows distinct vertical stripes (the width 48 is even, so the parity of every column is fixed and the odd columns are brighter), in amber gold on dark brown. The cells are rounded raised squares showing gaps through height and AO, and the seed shifts the whole table around the torus. It shares the cell shape with number-theory tables such as `divisorcount` and `abundantnumbers`, only the values and tones differ. It only shows the function values of the first 2304 positive integers; it does not prove or illustrate any theorem of number theory.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the toneExponent of 1.5, the toneFloor of 0.14, the toneSpan of 0.7, the amber gold and dark brown tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). The cell shape and tone combination reuse the divisorcount parameters and were not retuned for the totient. I did not check whether the vertical stripes are too monotonous: the preview shows clear vertical stripes (because the table width of 48 is even), which is a property of this way of assigning values and not a defect, and I did not break them up by changing the table width. The tests passed on the first run with no need to adjust ranges. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0296).

At start-up a sieve computes `φ(n)` for `n ≤ 2304` (set `φ(n) = n`, then for every prime `q` and every multiple `m` do `φ(m) −= φ(m)/q`), takes `least = min φ(n)/n`, and precomputes each cell's tone `0.7·((φ(n)/n − least)/(1 − least))^1.5`; at sampling time every cell uses one compact-support rounded-square kernel (a quartic superellipse through smoothstep, exactly zero before the cell boundary, so the cell lookup never jumps and the field is C1): color is `0.04 + (0.14 + tone − 0.04)·mask + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·dome·(0.88 + 0.12·tone) + 0.08·grain`, `occlusion = 1 − 0.4·(1 − mask)`, roughness is fixed at 0.4 and metallic is 0; the cache totals an `Int32Array(2305)` of 9,220 B plus a `Float64Array(2304 + 128²)` of 149,504 B, 158,724 B in all, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Each sample does a constant number of operations; I did not measure the time, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run): n = 210 is the first integer to reach the smallest ratio 48/210, there are 342 primes up to 2304, and the largest ratio among all even numbers is 0.5; on a 256² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff) the lit area (color>0.5) covers 22.23%–23.72%, color is 0.0255–0.0259 to 0.8527–0.8529 with a mean of 0.3109–0.3183, the lowest AO is 0.6 (equal to `1 − 0.4`) and height is at most 0.8459–0.8471 relief; on a 512² grid (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7) the lit area covers 22.13%–22.78%, color is 0.0252–0.0254 to 0.8536–0.8542 with a mean of 0.3114–0.3142 and height is at most 0.8486–0.8500 relief; for each seed exactly one torus shift (seed 0: (39, 33), 1: (23, 23), 0xffffffff: (19, 33), 7: (42, 4)) makes the colours at the 2304 cell centres match the `φ(n)/n` tones that the test rewrites independently by counting coprime numbers, within a maximum error of 0.0150 (the error comes from the grain; the test's threshold is 0.03); between seeds 0 and 1, 78.5% of the cell centres differ in colour by more than 0.05, and the light masks (512²) differ on 23.6% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (96.6, 80.1, 37.3), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0296 and the minimum z component is 253. I viewed the preview (seed 7): amber rounded squares on dark brown laid out in distinct vertical stripes, the brightest columns being the odd ones. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`spirographtable` adds a spirograph curve table, bringing the current catalog from 999 to 1000 kinds (1001 gallery choices including plain). It is a 6×6 table in which cell (col, row) draws the hypotrochoid made by a wheel of radius `a = col + 1` rolling inside a ring of radius `b = row + 7`, with the pen `0.8·a` from the wheel's centre; a runs from 1 to 6 and b from 7 to 12, so a is always below b; the curve is scaled to lie at most `0.4` cell widths from the cell centre and then rotated as a whole by an angle set by the seed (0 to 0.5 radians), each cell drawing one closed curve, which looks like copper curves with a faint glow on a dark oxblood ground. Where the curve passes over itself a Gaussian sum (not a minimum of distances) is used, so no crease appears. In 13 of the 36 cells a and b have a common factor and the curve closes in fewer than `a` turns; I draw only one closed period and do not retrace. It is only a table of integer ratios of `a` and `b`, not a comparison of pen distances (the pen ratio is fixed at 0.8), and not a real spirograph toy.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the pen ratio of 0.8, the amplitude of 0.4, the line width of 0.016, the glow radius of 0.1 and the copper and dark oxblood tones are authored choices (I looked at two previews: the first used `t ∈ [0, 2π·a)`, which retraces the same curve in cells where a and b have a common factor and doubles its strokes, so I changed it to `t ∈ [0, 2π·a / gcd(a, b))`; the second preview showed no obvious difference to the eye, I made no quantitative comparison and only changed it because it is the mathematically correct closed period). The first preview was only a visual judgement, not a quantitative check. The tests passed after that change; I did not keep the test results from before it, so I make no before-and-after comparison. The relief reuses 0.0008 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0495).

It uses the same soft union as the rose table (rhodoneatable): each of the 36 cells has a precomputed closed polyline of 360 points (stored in a `Float64Array` in cell widths relative to the cell centre), and at sampling time only the 360 segments of the cell containing the point are walked, computing `Σ exp(−d²/0.016²)` (d is the distance from the point to the segment) and squashing it with `1 − exp(−4·sum)` into the line strength, plus a compact smoothstep glow (radius 0.1; because the curve is at most 0.4 from the cell centre, the glow is exactly zero at the cell boundary and neighbouring cells never jump into each other); color is `0.04 + 0.74·line + 0.12·glow·(1 − line) + 0.02·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·line + 0.2·grain`, roughness drops by 0.2 on lines, AO is always 1 and metallic is 0; the cache totals 2×36×360 + 128² = 42,304 Float64 values / 338,432 B, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Every sample walks 360 segments; I measured a single 512² maps generation (seed 7) at about 444 ms, which is one measurement, not a benchmark, and I did not compare it with other materials. Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 19.06%–19.20%, color is 0.0303–0.0304 to 0.7892–0.7898 with a mean of 0.2033–0.2035, roughness is 0.2–0.4, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9919–0.9984 relief; on a 512² grid the lit area covers 19.07%–19.10%, color is 0.0301–0.0302 to 0.7898–0.7899 with a mean of 0.2034–0.2035 and height is at most 0.9975–0.9992 relief; the maximum color at the four cell corners (0.02 cell widths from the corner) is 0.0487–0.0495; for each of the four seeds, 25–29 of 101 rotation angles (0 to 0.5 radians) put all 36 cells × 96 independently computed curve points on bright pixels (color>0.5), with a best minimum brightness of 0.7702–0.7704 (so the curves really are the hypotrochoids of this table and not a generic bright texture); the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 18.5% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (72.6, 43.4, 29.2), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0495, and the AO and alpha checks found nothing wrong. I viewed the preview (seed 7): copper stars, polygons and thin ellipses laid out in a regular grid on dark oxblood, with a faint glow on the edges. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`dodecagridfilled` adds a filled twelve-grid tiling, bringing the current catalog from 998 to 999 kinds (1000 gallery choices including plain). The same twelve-fold patch as `dodecagridtiling` (the same six grids and offsets; 151 tiles, 330 edges, 180 vertices, Euler characteristic 1, vertex valences 2 to 10), but with a tone inside every tile: 30° rhombi are darkest (0.10), 60° rhombi are in the middle (0.18) and squares are brightest (0.26), while the edges are thin pale lime lines, giving lime lines on a dark forest-green ground. The weight of the tone is the same as in `penrosefilled` (a product of one smooth step per edge, C1). The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 30° (12 choices). It is only a small patch, not an infinite tiling, and the tone depends only on the tile shape — it is not a real colouring rule. It shares the tile-filling feature of the multigrid sampler branch with `penrosefilled`, `ammannfilled` and `heptagridfilled`, and only the preset differs.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the three tile tones of 0.10/0.18/0.26, the rim width of 0.15, the interior height gain of 0.05, the line tone of 0.7, the lime and forest-green tones and the 0.5 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). Having learned from `heptagridfilled`, I first worked out which tile shape each fill class `k − j − 1` gets from the direction angle `(k − j)·30°` (classes 0 and 4 are 30°, classes 1 and 3 are 60°, class 2 is the 90° square) and only then wrote `fills`, so it was not reversed again. The crease problem of the tile-filling feature had already been fixed in `penrosefilled`, and the C1 test passed on the first run. `ammannfilled` adds a filled Ammann–Beenker tiling, bringing the current catalog from 996 to 997 kinds (998 gallery choices including plain). It shares the tile-filling feature of the multigrid sampler branch with `penrosefilled`, and only the preset differs.

`penrosefilled` adds a filled Penrose tiling, bringing the current catalog from 995 to 996 kinds (997 gallery choices including plain). The same Penrose rhombus patch as `penrosetiling` (the same pentagrid offsets, 149 rhombi, 323 edges and 175 vertices), but with a tone inside every rhombus: fat rhombi (72°) are brighter and thin rhombi (36°) darker, while the edges remain pale thin lines, giving cream lines and brown-purple rhombi on a dark purple ground. The tone of a rhombus follows the product over its four edges of a weight that tends to 0 (with zero slope) near an edge and is 1 beyond 0.15 edge lengths from every edge, so the tones of neighbouring rhombi never jump and the lines cover the seams. The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 36° (10 choices). It is only a small patch, not an infinite tiling, and the tone depends only on the two rhombus shapes — it is not a real colouring scheme (it obeys no matching rules, for example). It shares the multigrid sampler branch of `penrosetiling` and the other kinds and adds the fields `fills` (the interior tone per grid-pair class), `fillRim` and `fillHeight`; the `fills` of all other materials are 0, so their behaviour is unchanged.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the fat-rhombus tone of 0.2, the thin-rhombus tone of 0.1, the rim width of 0.15, the interior height gain of 0.05, the line tone of 0.7, the cream and dark purple tones and the 0.5 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at two previews: the first before, the second after the fix described next). The relief reuses 0.0007 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0335). Error record: the first version weighted the interior tone with a smooth step of the minimum of the four edge distances, and the C1 test failed (largest second-difference ratio 51.8) — the minimum has a crease along the bisector of the acute corners where it is still below 0.15, so the tone has a slope discontinuity there; after changing to the product of one smooth step per edge the C1 test passed, and the statistics changed with it (the brightest value dropped from 0.79 to 0.77), so I updated the test's value ranges from the corrected probe output. I wrote the documentation and verification only for the corrected version.

It reuses the multigrid sampler branch (which now serves `penrosetiling`, `penrosestar`, `ammannbeenker`, `heptagridtiling`, `dodecagridtiling` and `penrosefilled`) and adds tile filling: at build time, besides the edges, every rhombus keeps its rotated four corners, its centre, the sign of its area and its class `k − j − 1`; at sampling time, for every rhombus within 1.2 of the point, the weight is `Π over the four edges smooth(clamp(signed distance to the edge / 0.15))` (outside the rhombus one edge has a negative signed distance and the weight is 0; the product is 0 on every edge with zero slope there, so it is C1, whereas a minimum creases at acute corners), the tone gains `fills[class]·weight` (0.2 for fat-rhombus classes 0 and 3, 0.1 for thin-rhombus classes 1 and 2) and the height gains `0.05·weight`; materials whose `fills` are all 0 skip this loop. Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile and 0.0007 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Every sample walks the 323 edges and the 149 rhombi (skipping those beyond 1.2 of their centre); I did not measure the time, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 11.16%–11.28%, color is 0.0455–0.0461 to 0.7718–0.7734 with a mean of 0.1933–0.1934, roughness is 0.3–0.4, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9329–0.9424 relief; on a 512² grid the lit area covers 11.24%–11.25%, color is 0.0452–0.0453 to 0.7732–0.7742 with a mean of 0.1933–0.1934 and height is at most 0.9390–0.9451 relief; at exactly one rotation step per seed (steps 3, 0, 0 and 4) the colours at every third vertex and every third rhombus centre (interior tone included) match the independently rewritten model of the test (maximum error below 0.03, which is the test's threshold); the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 5.9% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (68.7, 51.1, 60.0), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0335 and the minimum z component is 253. The structure (149 rhombi, 323 edges, 175 vertices, Euler characteristic 1, 95 fat and 54 thin) is the same as penrosetiling. `dodecagridtiling` adds a dodecagrid tiling, bringing the current catalog from 994 to 995 kinds (996 gallery choices including plain). Thin pale violet lines on a dark blue-violet-black ground draw a patch of an aperiodic tiling with approximate twelve-fold rotational symmetry: de Bruijn's multigrid construction with six grids, unit vectors the first six twelfth roots of unity (0°, 30°, …, 150°) and offsets `(0.13, −0.31, 0.22, 0.07, −0.19, 0.08)` (summing to 0), every grid crossing being one rhombus or square — 151 tiles in three kinds by acute angle (41 rhombi of 30°, 70 rhombi of 60° and 40 squares of 90°), 330 unit-length edges and 180 vertices with vertex valences from 2 to 10; the patch is a simply connected disc (Euler characteristic 1); its radius is 6.2 edge lengths and it sits in the middle of a tile with a period of 16 edge lengths, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles. The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 30° (12 choices). It is only a small patch, not an infinite tiling and not a periodic one; its twelve-fold symmetry is approximate. It shares the multigrid sampler branch of `penrosetiling`, `penrosestar`, `ammannbeenker` and `heptagridtiling` and only the preset differs.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the six offsets are a set I picked by hand (summing to 0, with no scan of other offsets), the patch radius of 6.2, the line radius of 0.09, gain 1.6, the pale violet and dark blue-violet tones and the 0.5 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). The relief reuses penrosetiling's 0.0007 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0401). I did not check how this tiling relates to twelve-fold quasicrystal tilings in the literature (for example the Stampfli or Socolar tilings), so I only call it a "dodecagrid tiling" and do not claim it is any of them. The structural checks (counts, Euler characteristic, edge length, vertex valences, numbers of the three tile kinds) are checks of the consistency of the construction, not a formal proof.

`ammannbeenker` adds an Ammann–Beenker tiling, bringing the current catalog from 992 to 993 kinds (994 gallery choices including plain). Thin mint lines on a dark green-black ground draw a patch of the Ammann–Beenker eight-fold aperiodic tiling, built with de Bruijn's multigrid construction — four grids, unit vectors the first four eighth roots of unity (0°, 45°, 90°, 135°), offsets `(0.13, −0.31, 0.22, −0.04)`, every grid crossing being one square (90°) or one rhombus (45°/135°) — 148 tiles in all (62 squares and 86 rhombi, about 1.39 rhombi per square; the infinite tiling has the ratio √2 ≈ 1.41), 322 unit-length edges and 175 vertices with vertex valences from 2 to 8 (8 at the eight-pointed stars); the patch is a simply connected disc (Euler characteristic 1); its radius is 6.2 edge lengths and it sits in the middle of a tile with a period of 16 edge lengths, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles. The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 45° (8 choices). It is only a small patch, not an infinite tiling and not a periodic one. It shares the multigrid sampler branch of `penrosetiling` and `penrosestar` and only the preset differs (a new `roots` field; the number of grids follows the number of offsets).

The structural checks (counts, Euler characteristic, edge length, vertex valences, numbers of squares and rhombi) are checks of the consistency of the construction, not a formal proof, and I did not verify that the rhombus-to-square ratio of a patch must converge to √2. `penrosestar` adds a Penrose star, bringing the current catalog from 991 to 992 kinds (993 gallery choices including plain). Thin peach lines on a dark purple-black ground draw a patch of the Penrose rhombus tiling that is close to five-fold rotationally symmetric: the same de Bruijn pentagrid construction as `penrosetiling`, but with the five grid offsets near zero, `(0.011, −0.006, 0.004, −0.013, 0.004)` (summing to 0), so the tiling is close to the singular (five-fold symmetric) case — 160 rhombi (95 fat and 65 thin, about 1.46 : 1), 345 edges and 186 vertices with vertex valences from 2 to 7, a simply connected disc (Euler characteristic 1); 258 of its 345 edges (75%) land on another edge when the patch is turned by 72°, whereas the generic-offset patch of `penrosetiling` has only 72 of 323 (22%). The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 36° (10 choices); because the patch is nearly symmetric the rotated versions differ little. It is only a small patch, not an infinite tiling, and not exactly five-fold symmetric (75%, not 100%). It shares the sampler branch of `penrosetiling` and only the preset differs.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the offsets `(0.011, −0.006, 0.004, −0.013, 0.004)` are values near zero that I picked by hand (I tried only this set and did not scan other offsets), the remaining numbers follow penrosetiling (patch radius 6.2, line radius 0.09, gain 1.6, 0.5 m nominal tile, relief 0.0007 without further tuning; maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0401) and the peach and dark purple tones are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). The first time, a probe measured a 72° coincidence rate of 63% (it rounded the coordinates first and then parsed them, losing precision); the test now uses exact coordinates and gets 258/345 (75%), and I confirmed 72/323 (22%) for the generic-offset penrosetiling; the documentation uses the exact-coordinate numbers. The structural checks in the test (numbers of rhombi, edges and vertices, Euler characteristic, edge length, vertex valences, numbers of fat and thin rhombi) are again checks of the consistency of the construction, not a formal proof.

It reuses the `penrosetiling` pentagrid sampler branch (which now serves `penrosetiling` and `penrosestar`): the offsets are `(0.011, −0.006, 0.004, −0.013, 0.004)` and the construction and sampling are otherwise the same — the five unit vectors are the fifth roots of unity, for every pair of grids and integers `(r, s)` (−6 to 6) the crossing is solved and `ceil(x·e_l − offsets[l])` gives the four corners of a rhombus, rhombi whose centre lies within 6.2 of the origin are kept and shared edges de-duplicated by a coordinate key (345 of them), and the whole patch is turned by the seed (0 to 9 times 36°); every sample takes the point-to-segment distance to each edge, sums the weights `(1 − d²/r²)²` (r = 0.09, C1) and squashes by `1 − exp(−1.6·sum)`; color is `0.06 + 0.78·thread + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.85·thread + 0.15·grain`; roughness drops by 0.1 on lines; AO is always 1; metallic is 0; the cache totals 345×4 + 128² = 17,764 Float64 values / 142,112 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile and 0.0007 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Every sample walks the 345 edges; I did not measure the time, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 12.35%–12.36%, color is 0.0453–0.0457 to 0.8515–0.8528 with a mean of 0.1507–0.1509, roughness is 0.3–0.4, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9857–0.9919 relief; on a 512² grid the lit area covers 12.30%–12.32%, color is 0.0451–0.0453 to 0.8525–0.8540 with a mean of 0.1507–0.1509 and height is at most 0.9916–0.9968 relief; at exactly one rotation step per seed (steps 4, 8, 9 and 5) the colours at every third vertex of the patch match the independently rewritten model of the test (maximum error below 0.03, which is the test's threshold); the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on only 2.9% of pixels (a 144° rotation of a nearly symmetric patch); in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (63.9, 38.1, 43.0), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0401 and the minimum z component is 252. `penrosetiling` adds a Penrose tiling, bringing the current catalog from 990 to 991 kinds (992 gallery choices including plain). Thin pale blue lines on a dark navy-black ground draw a patch of the Penrose aperiodic rhombus tiling, built with de Bruijn's pentagrid construction in which every grid crossing is one rhombus: 149 rhombi (95 fat ones of 72°/108° and 54 thin ones of 36°/144°, about 1.76 : 1), 323 unit-length edges and 175 vertices, with vertex valences from 2 to 7; the patch is a simply connected disc (Euler characteristic V − E + F = 1); its radius is 6.2 edge lengths and it sits in the middle of a tile with a period of 16 edge lengths, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles; the vertices where edges meet are brighter because their weights add up. The seed only turns the whole patch by a multiple of 36° (10 choices). It is only a small patch of the Penrose tiling, not an infinite tiling and not a periodic one; on the torus it is a separate disc.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the five grid offsets `(0.13, −0.31, 0.22, 0.07, −0.11)` (summing to 0), the patch radius of 6.2, the line radius of 0.09, gain 1.6, the pale blue and dark navy tones and the 0.5 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). The offsets are fixed, so different seeds only change the rotation, not the tiling itself. At relief 0.0012 the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps was 0.1000 (minimum z component 248); lowering it to 0.0007 gave 0.0378 (253). The test confirms the structure with a separately rewritten pentagrid program (149 rhombi, 323 edges, 175 vertices, Euler characteristic 1, all edge lengths 1, vertex valences 2 to 7, 95 fat and 54 thin rhombi); these properties are an independent check that the construction is consistent, but not a formal proof that this is the genuine Penrose tiling.

A dedicated sampler: at build time the patch is generated with the pentagrid construction — the five unit vectors `e_j` are the fifth roots of unity, grid `j` is the set of lines `x·e_j = integer + offsets[j]`, and for every pair `(j, k)` and every integer pair `(r, s)` (−6 to 6) the crossing `x` of the two lines is solved, the other three indices are `ceil(x·e_l − offsets[l])` and the indices of `j` and `k` are `r`, `r+1` and `s`, `s+1`, giving the four corners `Σ K_l e_l` of one rhombus; only rhombi whose centre lies within 6.2 of the origin are kept, shared edges are de-duplicated by a coordinate key (323 of them) and the whole patch is then turned by the seed's rotation; every edge is stored as a midpoint and a half-length vector (four Float64 arrays). Every sample converts its coordinates to tiling units (period 16), takes the point-to-segment distance to every edge, sums the weights `(1 − d²/r²)²` (r = 0.09, value and slope zero at the boundary, C1) and squashes the sum by `1 − exp(−1.6·sum)`; color is `0.06 + 0.78·thread + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.85·thread + 0.15·grain`; roughness drops by 0.1 on lines; AO is always 1; metallic is 0; the cache totals 323×4 + 128² = 17,676 Float64 values / 141,408 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM; the crossing and de-duplication tables exist only during construction). Defaults are a 0.5 m nominal tile and 0.0007 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Every sample walks the 323 edges (skipping those out of reach) and construction walks 1,690 grid crossings; I measured neither, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 11.54%–11.60%, color is 0.0454–0.0458 to 0.8512–0.8520 with a mean of 0.1450–0.1453, roughness is 0.3–0.4, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9811–0.9872 relief; on a 512² grid the lit area covers 11.54%–11.55%, color is 0.0451–0.0452 to 0.8526–0.8538 with a mean of 0.1451–0.1453 and height is at most 0.9887–0.9967 relief; at exactly one rotation step per seed (steps 4, 3, 2 and 1) the colours at every third vertex of the patch match the independently rewritten model of the test (maximum error below 0.03, which is the test's threshold; I did not record the actual maximum per seed); the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 12.7% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (31.5, 44.6, 62.7), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0378 and the minimum z component is 253. `kagome` adds kagome, bringing the current catalog from 989 to 990 kinds (991 gallery choices including plain). Thin pale straw lines on a dark olive-green ground draw the kagome lattice: joining the midpoints of the six edges of every honeycomb hexagon in order gives three families of crossing straight lines that form a lattice of alternating hexagons and triangles (the weave of a bamboo basket); 7 columns × 8 rows (56 honeycomb cells, 336 segments in all) with horizontal and vertical periods in the ratio `7√3 : 12` (about 1.04% stretch, so the hexagons and triangles are not regular). The vertices where two segments meet are brighter because their weights add up. The seed only shifts the whole pattern around the torus (in steps of 1/64 of the tile). It is a schematic lattice, not a photograph of a real bamboo basket, and it does not show the over-and-under weaving. It shares the honeycomb-segment sampler branch of `tulle` and `kikko`, and only the preset differs (new `outer` and `innerDegrees` fields).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the inner hexagon radius `√3/2` (which reaches exactly the edge midpoints), the 30° rotation, the line radius of 0.12, gain 1.8, the straw and olive-green tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices (I looked at only one preview). The relief reuses kikko's 0.0009 without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0323). The shared branch gained the fields `outer` (1 or 0, whether to draw the outer edges) and `innerDegrees` (the rotation of the inner hexagon): `tulle` has `outer 1`, `innerDegrees 0` and `inner 0`, `kikko` has `outer 1` and `innerDegrees 0`, so their segments and behaviour are unchanged and the `Tulle as` and `Kikko as` tests still pass after this change.

`vermiculation` adds vermiculation, bringing the current catalog from 987 to 988 kinds (989 gallery choices including plain). A pale tan stone surface carries curving, branching, separate dark worm-like grooves, in the manner of the vermiculated rustication of architectural stone: the pattern comes from periodic Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion in the "worms" regime at `feed 0.078` and `kill 0.061`; the grooves cover about 35% of the area as roughly 20 to 30 separate worms in one connected stone surface; the grooves are darker, rougher (0.85 → about 0.93) and lower, and the stone has a fine grain. The seed changes the initial perturbation of the reaction-diffusion, so every seed lays the worms out differently. It shares the sampler branch of `turingmaze` and only the preset differs (plus a new `baseHeight` field). It is a schematic stone texture, not a photograph or scan of real stone.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; `feed 0.078` and `kill 0.061` come from the commonly quoted Gray-Scott "worms" regime, and I first scanned 12 seeds (0 to 9, 0xffffffff and 12345) with a survey script at 96×96, `seedCells 8`, 6000 and 9000 steps, which gave 35%–37% bright area, 24 to 31 connected components and nearly identical results at 6000 and 9000 steps; the other values (stone colours, groove depth, grain, the 0.4 m nominal tile and relief 0.0015) are authored choices. To make the grooves lower than the stone I added a `baseHeight` field to the shared sampler: `height = baseHeight + ridgeHeight·ridge + grainHeight·grain`, with `baseHeight` set to 0 for `turingmaze`, so its behaviour is unchanged and the `Turing maze as` tests still pass after this change. The maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps is 0.0512 (I did not tune the relief). I only scanned this one parameter pair and did not compare other regimes (for example coral, `feed 0.0545` and `kill 0.062`, which gave a single connected network in the 64×64 scan).

It reuses the `turingmaze` sampler branch (which now serves `turingmaze` and `vermiculation`): at build time `grayScott(96, 8, 0.078, 0.061, 6000, seed)` runs 6000 reaction-diffusion steps on a 96×96 torus grid (only additions, subtractions and multiplications, so it is bit-identical across engines; the result is normalised to [0, 1]) and `latticeField` turns it into a C1 interpolation field; each sample warps its position slightly with 5×5 noise (amplitude 0.05), looks the pattern up and cuts the grooves with `0.5 + 0.5·tanh(9·(pattern − level))` (`level = 0.5 + 0.24·(7×7 noise − 0.5)`) with `ink = ridge·(0.85 + 0.15·7×7 noise)`; color is `0.9 − 0.75·ink + 0.06·(160² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.7 − 0.55·ridge + 0.3·grain`; roughness increases by 0.08 in grooves (base 0.85); AO is always 1; metallic is 0; the cache totals 96² + 5² + 7² + 7² + 160² = 34,939 Float64 values / 279,512 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM; the reaction-diffusion scratch arrays exist only during construction). Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile and 0.0015 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff on a 256² grid: grooves (color<0.5) cover 34.76%–36.02%, stone (color>0.8) covers 58.33%–59.48%, the grooves form 22–28 4-connected regions, the stone is exactly 1 connected region, 4,418–4,610 neighbouring pairs straddle a groove edge, color is 0.1270–0.1331 to 0.9293–0.9297 with a mean of 0.6455–0.6528, roughness is 0.85–0.9297 and height is at most 0.9978–0.9990 relief; the groove masks (256²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 46.8% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (161.0, 146.5, 121.9), 36.3% of pixels have r<128, the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0512 and the minimum z component is 252. Single measurements (bun on this machine): building the sampler (including the reaction-diffusion) took about 110–132 ms per seed and the 512² maps about 157 ms — one run for four seeds and one maps run, not a benchmark. I viewed the preview (seed 7): dark curving worm-like grooves on pale tan stone with soft edges. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`minkowskisausage` adds a Minkowski sausage, bringing the current catalog from 986 to 987 kinds (988 gallery choices including plain). A thin pale blue line on a dark navy-black ground traces the order-2 quadratic Koch island (also called the Minkowski sausage): starting from `F+F+F+F` (a square) and replacing every `F` by `F+F−F−FF+F+F−F` twice gives a simple closed loop of 256 unit steps and 256 distinct lattice points (the end returns to the start); its bounding box is about 27×27 cells on a 36×36-cell torus, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles; the line is a third of a cell wide with a faint glow outside it. The seed only shifts the whole curve around the torus. It is a schematic fractal trace, not a real sausage or a map. It shares the trace sampler branch of `dragoncurve`, `peanocurve` and `levycurve`; only the vertex list differs.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the order 2, the 36×36-cell torus, the one-third-cell line width, the tanh sharpness of 8, the pale blue and dark navy tones and the 0.25 m nominal tile are authored choices. Order 3 would have 2,048 steps and a bounding box of about 107×107 cells, which exceeds the torus sizes this trace branch uses, so I stopped at order 2. The relief reuses dragoncurve's 0.0008 without further tuning (the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps is 0.0492). I first checked the replacement rule with a small independent script for the number of steps, distinct points and bounding box of order 2, and then chose the torus size.

It reuses the trace sampler branch (which now serves `dragoncurve`, `peanocurve`, `levycurve` and `minkowskisausage`): in Minkowski mode the turtle string `F+F+F+F` has every `F` replaced twice by `F+F-F-FF+F+F-F`, where `F` advances one cell, `+` turns left by 90° and `−` turns right by 90°, giving 257 vertices (the last one back at the start); on a 108×108 lattice the cell points sit at every third coordinate (256 of them) and two connector nodes between consecutive cells fill the gap (512 of them), for 768 lit nodes in total; the curve coordinates get a fixed offset of (7, 7) plus the seed's torus shift; after that it is identical to dragoncurve: `latticeField` blends with the C1 smoothstep and re-sharpens with `0.5 + 0.5·tanh(8·(pattern − 0.5))`, color is `0.06 + 0.76·line + 0.1·glow·(1 − line) + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·line + 0.2·grain`, roughness drops by 0.2 on the line (base 0.4) and metallic is 0; the cache totals 108² + 9² + 128² = 28,129 Float64 values / 225,032 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.25 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7 on a 256² grid: the lit area (color>0.5) covers 6.38%–6.43%, color is 0.0458–0.0460 to 0.8331–0.8335 with a mean of 0.1113–0.1114, roughness is 0.2001–0.3999, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9887–0.9918 relief; each seed's 108×108 node map equals the curve the test writes independently by block recursion at exactly one torus shift ((28, 24), (31, 33), (30, 32) and (30, 29); 768 lit nodes each); the node maps of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 9.8%; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (26.2, 31.2, 55.1), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0492 and the minimum z component is 252. The test also checks that the independent curve has 257 vertices, ends where it starts and has 256 distinct lattice points (a simple closed loop). I viewed the preview (seed 7): a pale blue jagged cross-shaped island outline on navy, repeated over the torus. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`pisanotable` adds a Pisano table, bringing the current catalog from 985 to 986 kinds (987 gallery choices including plain). 48×48 rounded-square tiles; cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row × 48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned by the Pisano period `π(n)` of the Fibonacci numbers modulo `n` relative to its upper bound `6n`: `0.7·(π(n)/6n)^0.5` — `π(n)` reaches the bound `6n` only for `n = 2·5^k` (10, 50, 250 and 1250 up to 2304, the brightest), and `n` with a short period are dim; the first periods are 1, 3, 8, 6, 20, 24, 16, 12, 24, 60, 10, 24. The whole looks like noise but is a tile mosaic determined by number theory. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic number-theory pattern, not a real material.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the 48×48 grid, the tone `0.14 + 0.7·(π(n)/6n)^0.5` (the exponent 0.5 was my up-front choice and I did not compare other exponents), the coral tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. The relief reuses the 0.0008 of the existing table kinds without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0280). In the preview the whole is mid-toned with low contrast and looks like noise. The seed-difference test only asserts that more than 20% of the cells of two seeds' tables differ in tone by more than 0.05, and I did not measure the actual fraction. At build time every `n` steps through the Fibonacci pairs modulo `n` until it returns to (0, 1) (at most `6n` steps); I did not measure this build time, so no performance number is claimed.

It follows the table-tile sampler (the same shape as `mobiustable`): at build time, for every `n ≤ 2304`, the pair `(F_k, F_{k+1})` of the Fibonacci numbers modulo `n` is stepped until it returns to `(0, 1)`, giving the period `π(n)`, and the tone table (Float64) holds `0.7·(π(n)/(6n))^0.5`; every cell owns one compact-support rounded-square kernel (a quartic superellipse through smoothstep with a half width of 0.46 cell, exactly zero before the cell boundary, C1), color is `0.04 + (0.14 + tone − 0.04)·mask + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.8·dome·(0.88 + 0.12·tone) + 0.08·grain`; gap AO is 0.6; roughness is a constant 0.4; metallic is 0; the cache totals 48² + 128² = 18,688 Float64 values / 149,504 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 11.48%–11.56%, color is 0.0257–0.0258 to 0.8505–0.8537 with a mean of 0.2850–0.2854, the lowest AO is 0.6 and height is at most 0.8312–0.8380 relief (seeds 0/1/0xffffffff); on a 512² grid the lit area covers 11.38%–11.55%, color is 0.0252–0.0255 to 0.8526–0.8540 with a mean of 0.2853–0.2859, roughness is a constant 0.4, the lowest AO is 0.6 and height is at most 0.8349–0.8448 relief; the colours at the 2,304 tile centres match the period table written independently in the test by generating the pair sequence, at exactly one torus shift ((41, 2), (9, 30), (12, 32) and (22, 22); maximum error about 0.0149–0.0150, roughly the amplitude of the fine grain); the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 19.3% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (91.3, 48.5, 41.4), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0280 and the minimum z component is 253. The test also checks the first 12 periods and the `n` that reach the bound `6n` (10, 50, 250 and 1250). `mobiustable` adds a Möbius table, bringing the current catalog from 984 to 985 kinds (986 gallery choices including plain). 48×48 rounded-square tiles; cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row × 48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned in three classes by the Möbius function `μ(n)`: `μ = 0` when a square divides `n` (dark, 904 of them), `μ = +1` when `n` is a product of an even number of distinct primes (bright violet, 699, including `n = 1`) and `μ = −1` for an odd number (middle grey-violet, 701); because each row has 48 cells, a multiple of 4, the columns holding multiples of 4 are all dark and form dark vertical bars. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic number-theory pattern, not a real material.

`abundantnumbers` adds an abundant-numbers table, bringing the current catalog from 983 to 984 kinds (985 gallery choices including plain). 48×48 rounded-square tiles; cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row × 48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned in three classes by comparing `σ(n)` (the sum of all positive divisors of `n`) with `2n`: deficient numbers (`σ(n) < 2n`, 1,732 of them) are dim, abundant numbers (`σ(n) > 2n`, 569 of them) are brighter and perfect numbers (`σ(n) = 2n`: 6, 28 and 496, 3 of them) are the brightest; because each row has 48 cells, a multiple of 12 and of 6, abundant numbers (12, 18, 20, 24, …) line up in conspicuous bright vertical bars while the remaining scattered bright dots are other abundant numbers. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic number-theory pattern, not a real material.

`xortable` adds an XOR table, bringing the current catalog from 982 to 983 kinds (984 gallery choices including plain). 64×64 rounded-square tiles; the tone of tile (row, col) is proportional to `row XOR col` (bitwise exclusive or) over 63: the main diagonal (`row = col`, result 0) is darkest and the larger `row XOR col` is the brighter the tile, the brightest being yellow-green (lime); the binary digits form nested, Sierpinski-like blocks (the classic "XOR texture", the nim-sum table). The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic mathematical pattern, not a real material.

`paleytable` adds a Paley table, bringing the current catalog from 981 to 982 kinds (983 gallery choices including plain). 61×61 rounded-square tiles; tile (row, col) is the Legendre symbol of `col − row` modulo the prime 61 (the Paley construction): a difference of 0 (the diagonal) takes the middle tone, a nonzero square modulo 61 (a quadratic residue; there are 30 of them) takes bright rose pink and a non-residue takes dark plum; because 61 ≡ 1 (mod 4) the symbol is symmetric, and since the table depends only on `col − row` the whole table shows parallel diagonal bands and repeats seamlessly on the torus. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus, and only `(sx − sy) mod 61` of that shift makes a difference. It is a schematic number-theory pattern, not a real material.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the 61×61 grid, the residue / non-residue / zero tones `0.14 + 0.7` / `0.14 + 0.1` / `0.14 + 0.4`, the rose and plum tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. The relief reuses the 0.0008 of the existing table kinds without further tuning (maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps 0.0378). I first expected exactly one matching torus shift per seed; the probe showed 61 (the table depends only on `col − row`), so the test now asserts that structure: the `sx − sy` of all 61 shifts is the same, and the `(sx − sy) mod 61` of the four seeds all differ. `hadamardmatrix` adds a Hadamard matrix, bringing the current catalog from 980 to 981 kinds (982 gallery choices including plain). 64×64 rounded-square tiles; tile (row, col) is entry (row, col) of the Sylvester Hadamard matrix: +1 (bright cool white) when the number of 1 bits in the bitwise AND of `row` and `col` is even and −1 (dark blue-grey) when it is odd; row 0 and column 0 are all +1 and every other row has equally many +1 and −1 entries (2,016 of the 4,096 entries are −1), and the whole is built from nested 2×2 blocks. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a schematic mathematical-matrix pattern, not a real material.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the 64×64 grid, the +1/−1 tones `0.14 + 0.7` / `0.14 + 0.1`, the cool white and dark blue tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. `levycurve` adds a Lévy curve, bringing the current catalog from 979 to 980 kinds (981 gallery choices including plain). A thin mint-green line on a dark teal-black ground traces the order-9 Lévy C curve: 512 unit steps in which step `k` heads in direction `i^popcount(k)` (`popcount` is the number of 1 bits in `k`; the directions cycle east, north, west, south), with 416 distinct lattice points and 462 distinct edges — 50 steps retrace an edge already walked, so some segments are drawn twice; its bounding box is about 39×39 cells on a 48×48-cell torus, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles; the line is a third of a cell wide with a faint glow outside it. The seed only shifts the whole curve around the torus. It is a schematic fractal trace and the curve is not closed. It shares the trace sampler branch of `dragoncurve` and `peanocurve`; only the vertex list differs.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the order 9, the 48×48-cell torus, the one-third-cell line width, the tanh sharpness of 8, the mint and dark teal tones and the 0.25 m nominal tile are authored choices. The relief reuses dragoncurve's 0.0008 without further tuning (the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps is 0.0543). I first checked the direction rule with a small independent script for the vertex and edge counts (order 9: 416 distinct points, 462 distinct edges, bounding box x −7 to 31, y −15 to 23) and then chose the torus size and offsets.

It reuses the `dragoncurve` sampler branch (which now serves `dragoncurve`, `peanocurve` and `levycurve`): in Lévy mode the walk starts at (0, 0) and step `k` (`k = 0 … 511`) advances one cell east, north, west or south according to `popcount(k) mod 4`; on a 144×144 lattice the cell points sit at every third coordinate (416 of them) and two connector nodes between consecutive cells fill the gap (a retraced edge is simply marked again, 924 nodes), for 1,340 lit nodes in total; the curve coordinates get a fixed offset of (8, 16) plus the seed's torus shift; after that it is identical to dragoncurve: `latticeField` blends with the C1 smoothstep and re-sharpens with `0.5 + 0.5·tanh(8·(pattern − 0.5))`, color is `0.06 + 0.76·line + 0.1·glow·(1 − line) + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`, height is `0.8·line + 0.2·grain`, roughness drops by 0.2 on the line (base 0.4) and metallic is 0; the cache totals 144² + 9² + 128² = 37,201 Float64 values / 297,608 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.25 m nominal tile and 0.0008 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7 on a 256² grid: the lit area (color>0.5) covers 7.08%–7.12%, color is 0.0457–0.0459 to 0.8328–0.8339 with a mean of 0.1109–0.1112, roughness is 0.2001–0.3999, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9872–0.9944 relief; each seed's 144×144 node map equals the Lévy curve the test writes independently with bit counting at exactly one torus shift ((26, 39), (12, 40), (40, 7) and (29, 40); 1,340 lit nodes each); the node maps of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 11.3%; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (16.8, 46.0, 43.5), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0543 and the minimum z component is 252. The test also checks the independent curve's 416 distinct points and 462 distinct edges. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`tulle` adds tulle, bringing the current catalog from 978 to 979 kinds (980 gallery choices including plain). A hexagonal honeycomb net knitted from fine ivory threads on a dark purple-black ground: pointy-top hexagons of circumradius 1, 7 columns × 8 rows (56 hexagons, 168 segments with each shared edge stored once) filling the tile; each thread is a compact-support quartic profile and the knots where three threads meet are brighter because the profiles add up. To let the honeycomb tile the square torus evenly, the horizontal and vertical periods are in the ratio `7√3 : 12`, which stretches the hexagons by about 1.04% (they are not regular). The seed only shifts the whole net around the torus (in steps of 1/64 of the tile). It is a schematic net textile, not a photograph of real tulle, and it is not translucent (the dark ground is just the colour behind the mesh).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the 7 columns × 4 row pairs, the thread radius of 0.15, gain 1.8, the ivory and dark purple tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. Tuning record: the first version used a thread radius of 0.2 and gain 1.5, the threads looked too thick in the preview, and I adopted 0.15 and 1.8 (I only looked at those two previews); at relief 0.0015 the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps was 0.0643, and lowering it to 0.0012 gave 0.0424 (minimum z component 251 → 252). The first version of the probe's independent model had a bug (a wrong key in the edge de-duplication produced 176 segments instead of 168) and for seed 0xffffffff it found no matching shift; after fixing the de-duplication all four seeds had matching shifts.

A dedicated sampler: at build time, on a pointy-top honeycomb (width `√3`, row spacing 1.5), every hexagon contributes its east, north-east and north-west edges (each stored as a midpoint and a half-length vector, 168 of them, in four Float64 arrays); every sample converts its coordinates to honeycomb units (horizontal period `7√3`, vertical period 12), takes the point-to-segment distance to the nearest torus image of every segment, sums the weights `(1 − d²/r²)²` (r = 0.15, value and slope zero at the boundary, C1) and squashes the sum by `1 − exp(−1.8·sum)`; color is `0.08 + 0.78·thread + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.85·thread + 0.15·grain`; roughness drops by 0.1 on threads (base 0.65); AO is always 1; metallic is 0; the cache totals 168×4 + 128² = 17,056 Float64 values / 136,448 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0012 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Every sample walks the 168 segments (skipping those out of reach); I did not measure the time, so no performance number is claimed. Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 19.57%–19.59%, color is 0.0651–0.0657 to 0.8686–0.8695 with a mean of 0.2215–0.2217, roughness is 0.5505–0.65, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.9827–0.9866 relief (on a 512² grid the lit area covers 19.65%–19.66%); each seed matches the independently rewritten honeycomb model of the test at 48 sample points for exactly 8 of the 64 × 64 candidate torus shifts (maximum error 0.0113–0.0138, roughly the amplitude of the fine grain), and these 8 shifts are the honeycomb's own translation symmetry (x mod 32 and y mod 8 fixed); the light masks (512²) of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 33.8% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (74.7, 69.8, 74.3), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0424 and the minimum z component is 252. I viewed the preview (seed 7): a regular ivory honeycomb of fine threads on a dark ground with slightly brighter knots. `sacksspiral` adds a Sacks spiral, bringing the current catalog from 977 to 978 kinds (979 gallery choices including plain). On a dark navy-black ground the integers 1 to 500 are laid out as dots on a Sacks spiral: the integer `n` sits on an Archimedean spiral at radius `0.45·√(n/500)` (in tile units) and angle `2π√n`, so the perfect squares line up along one ray; primes (95 of them) are bright gold dots and composites are dim gold-brown dots, with the primes particularly dense along a few curved arms. The spiral is centred in the tile and does not reach the tile edge, so tiles do not overlap; on the torus every tile holds one disc-shaped spiral. The seed only turns the whole spiral by a whole number of degrees (0 to 359). It is a schematic number-theory pattern, not a star chart or a photograph.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the 500 integers, the radius of 0.45, the dot radius of 0.014, the gold and navy tones and the 0.4 m nominal tile are authored choices. Tuning record: the first version (dot radius 0.012, prime tone 0.7, composite tone 0.2, gain 2, relief 0.0008) had dots that looked small and dim in the preview, and the probe measured a brightest value of 0.667, a mean of 0.077 and a maximum normal tilt² of only 0.0048 in the 512² maps; after changing to a dot radius of 0.014, prime tone 0.85, composite tone 0.3, gain 3 and relief 0.002 the brightest value is 0.871, the mean 0.111 and the maximum tilt² 0.0441, and the rotation fit (exactly one whole degree per seed) was the same for both versions.

A dedicated sampler: at build time trial division decides whether each `n = 1 … 500` is prime, and the position of every integer is stored in two Float64 arrays (plus a Uint8 prime flag); every integer owns one compact-support quartic dot (weight `(1 − d²/r²)²` with radius 0.014, value and slope both zero at the boundary, C1); primes and composites are summed separately and squashed into [0, 1) by `1 − exp(−3·sum)`; color is `0.05 + 0.85·prime dots + 0.3·composite dots·(1 − prime dots) + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.6·prime dots + 0.25·composite dots·(1 − prime dots) + 0.1·grain`; roughness drops by 0.15 on primes (base 0.4); AO is always 1; metallic is 0; the cache totals 500×2 + 128² = 17,384 Float64 values (139,072 B) plus a 500 B prime flag array, all lattice arithmetic (not total RAM). Every sample walks the 500 integers (skipping those beyond the radius); I did not measure how long this takes at 512², so no performance number is claimed. Defaults are a 0.4 m nominal tile and 0.002 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7: on a 256² grid the lit area (color>0.5) covers 2.93%–2.96%, color is 0.0355–0.0358 to 0.8670–0.8696 with a mean of 0.1114–0.1115, roughness is 0.2575–0.4, AO is always 1 and height is at most 0.6547–0.6647 relief (on a 512² grid the lit area covers 2.94%–2.95%); at exactly one whole-degree rotation per seed (298°, 161°, 4° and 107°) the colours at the centres of all 500 dots match the independently rewritten model in the test (maximum error 0.0143–0.0148, roughly the amplitude of the fine grain); in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (33.7, 32.8, 37.1), the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0441 and the minimum z component is 252. I viewed the preview (seed 7): gold spiral discs on navy with clearly curved bright arms, one disc per tile. No new API or dependency; Worker, cache and texture ownership follow the existing paths; this paragraph does not claim browser gallery verification.

`peanocurve` adds a Peano curve, bringing the current catalog from 976 to 977 kinds (978 gallery choices including plain). A thin pink line on a dark navy-black ground follows the order-3 Peano space-filling curve: each of the 27×27 cells is visited exactly once (728 steps, 2,185 lit nodes), winding from one corner (0, 0) to the opposite corner (26, 26), on a 32×32-cell torus with a 5-cell empty margin so it does not join neighbouring tiles; the line is a third of a cell wide with a faint glow outside it. The seed only shifts the whole curve around the torus. It is a schematic fractal trace, not a real circuit board, and the curve is not closed. It shares the trace sampler branch of `dragoncurve`; only the vertex list differs.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the order 3, the 32×32-cell torus, the one-third-cell line width, the tanh sharpness of 8, the pink and navy tones and the 0.25 m nominal tile are authored choices. The relief reuses dragoncurve's 0.0008 without further tuning (the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps is 0.0468).

`divisorcount` adds a divisor-count table, bringing the current catalog from 975 to 976 kinds (977 gallery choices including plain). 48×48 rounded-square tiles; cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row × 48 + col + 1` (1 to 2304) and is toned by the number of divisors `d(n)`: primes (`d = 2`, 342 of them) are dim, composite numbers with many divisors (highly composite numbers) glow, and the largest `d` in the table is 40 (at `n = 1680`); because each row has 48 cells, a multiple of 12, the columns holding multiples of 12 form conspicuous bright vertical bars, with fainter bars for multiples of 6, 4 and so on. The seed only moves the whole table around the torus, so the statistics stay the same and only the position changes. It is a schematic number-theory table, not a mineral or a photographed material.

`dragoncurve` adds a dragon curve, bringing the current catalog from 974 to 975 kinds (976 gallery choices including plain). A thin golden line on a dark purple-black ground traces the order-9 Heighway dragon curve: 512 unit steps whose turns follow the regular paper-folding sequence (step `k = 2^m(2j+1)` turns left for even j and right for odd j); the curve touches itself at lattice points but never shares an edge (361 distinct lattice points, 512 edges); its bounding box is about 27×32 cells on a 40×40-cell torus, so there is empty space around it and it does not join neighbouring tiles; the line is a third of a cell wide with a faint glow outside it. The seed only shifts the whole curve around the torus. It is a schematic fractal trace, not folded paper, and it is not closed.

`juliatiles` adds Julia tiles, bringing the current catalog from 973 to 974 kinds (975 gallery choices including plain). A mosaic of a Julia set (`c = −0.8 + 0.156i`) made of 64×64 rounded-square tiles: cell (col, row) takes the complex number at its centre (real and imaginary parts both from −1.6 to 1.6) as `z₀` and iterates `z → z² + c`, and its tone is the escape iteration count (`|z| > 2`, at most 64) over 64 under a square root, from dark red-brown (fast escape) to bright orange (many iterations before escaping, near the set boundary); cells that never escape (404 of them, about 9.9%) are the darkest brown-black. The tiles are raised and the gaps darker with occlusion (AO), and the seed only moves the whole table around the torus. With only 64×64 resolution it is a pixel-art Julia set; it shares the sampler branch of `mandelbrottiles` and differs only in the start point and the constant.

`rhodoneatable` adds a rose-curve table, bringing the current catalog from 971 to 972 kinds (973 gallery choices including plain). A pink-neon table of rhodonea curves: 6×6 cells, where cell (col, row) draws `r = cos(k·θ)` with `k = (col + 1)/(row + 1)` (θ from 0 to 2π·(row + 1), so every rational k closes), from single circles through three- and four-petal roses and many-petal flowers to tangled rings, with a faint glow on a dark purple-black ground; the seed only rotates all the roses by one angle (0 to 0.5 radians). It is a mathematical pattern and not a real neon tube (no tube width variation, end electrodes or reflections). The diagonal cells with k = 1 are a small circle through the cell centre.

`primesieve` adds the sieve of Eratosthenes, bringing the current catalog from 969 to 970 kinds (971 gallery choices including plain). A 32×32 grid of rounded-square tiles standing for the integers 1 to 1024: primes (172 of them) are bright gold, 1 is dim, and a composite is toned `0.4·(1 − 1/p)` by its smallest prime factor `p` (multiples of 2 are darkest and composites with larger factors slightly brighter), so the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 leave regular vertical bars and diagonals on an olive ground with the primes scattered among them. The tiles are raised and the gaps darker with occlusion (AO), and the seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is a number-theory pattern, not any real material; the contrast between composites is low, so it reads as gold dots on an olive ground.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the 32×32 grid, 1 to 1024, the prime tone of 0.8, the composite tone span of 0.4, the gold and olive tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. My first version used a prime tone of 0.92, which would have pushed the colour sum above 1 (about 1.06); I changed it to 0.8 before the first run and changed nothing else.

A dedicated sampler: at build time a sieve of Eratosthenes gives the smallest prime factor of every integer from 1 to 1024 and the tone table (Float64) is 0.1 for 1, 0.8 for a prime and `0.4·(1 − 1/smallest factor)` for a composite; every cell owns one compact-support rounded-square kernel (a quartic superellipse through smoothstep with a half width of 0.46 cell, exactly zero before the cell boundary, the same as the modulartable family, C1); color is `0.05 + (0.14 + tone − 0.05)·mask + 0.03·(128² fine grain − 0.5)`; height is `0.8·dome·(0.88 + 0.12·tone) + 0.08·grain`; gap AO is 0.6; roughness is a constant 0.45; metallic is 0; the cache totals 32² Float64 values (the tone table) + a 128² fine grain = 17,408 Float64 values / 139,264 B of lattice arithmetic (not total RAM; building also uses one 1,025-entry Int32 sieve table as scratch). Defaults are a 0.3 m nominal tile and 0.0012 UV-relative relief (not metric displacement). Measured (tool-run) at seeds 0/1/0xffffffff/7 on a 512² grid: the light area (color>0.5) covers 15.9%–16.0%, color is 0.0351–0.0352 to 0.9545–0.9547 with a mean of 0.3573–0.3576, roughness is a constant 0.45, the lowest AO is 0.6 and height is at most 0.8579–0.8595 relief; the colours at the 1,024 tile centres match the smallest prime factors rewritten independently in the test by trial division (172 of them primes), with exactly one torus shift per seed ((18, 21), (0, 10), (10, 29) and (18, 23) for the four seeds) and a maximum error of 0.0150 (the amplitude of the fine grain); the light masks of seeds 0 and 1 differ on 19.1% of pixels; in the seed-7 512² maps mean r/g/b is about (106.5, 89.3, 55.2) and the maximum normal tilt² is about 0.0399. `collatzsteps` adds Collatz stopping times, bringing the current catalog from 967 to 968 kinds (969 gallery choices including plain). A 32×32 grid of rounded-square tiles where cell (col, row) stands for the integer `n = row·32 + col + 1` (1 to 1024) and its tone is the number of Collatz steps (halve an even n, triple an odd n and add 1) needed to reach 1 divided by 178 (the longest below 1025 is 178 steps for n = 871), varying continuously from dark purple to warm orange. The tiles are raised and the gaps darker with occlusion (AO), and the seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It looks like structured noise (neighbouring integers have subtly related step counts, but the whole is close to random); it is not any real material, only a mathematical pattern.

The seed only moves the whole table around the torus. It is not any real material, only a mathematical pattern.

`modulartable` adds a modular multiplication table, bringing the current catalog from 965 to 966 kinds (967 gallery choices including plain). A mosaic of 31×31 rounded-square tiles where the tone of cell (col, row) comes from the mod-11 multiplication-table residue `((a + col)·(b + row)) mod 11` (11 steps from dark purple to golden yellow, with the seed choosing the offsets a and b), the tiles raised and the gaps darker with occlusion (AO). Because a residue of 0 occurs whenever `a + col` or `b + row` is a multiple of 11, whole rows and columns turn into bands of dark tiles, and the rest shows the symmetric multiplication-table pattern. It is not any real mosaic or tiling, only a mathematical pattern.

`elementaryautomata` adds elementary cellular automata, bringing the current catalog from 964 to 965 kinds (966 gallery choices including plain). Four Wolfram elementary automata side by side on an amber LED matrix (each band 32 rows by 128 columns with the columns joined on a ring): rule 30 (the chaotic triangle from a single live cell), rule 90 (the Sierpinski triangle), rule 110 (a complex asymmetric structure) and rule 184 (diagonal traffic-flow stripes from a repeating "110" start pattern); the seed only rotates the columns of the whole picture and the pattern itself is fixed. Each cell is a rounded-square LED and unlit LEDs stay dark brown. Because the columns form a ring, the triangles of rules 30, 90 and 110 do not reach the edge within 128 columns, so they look the same as on an infinitely wide row.

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or photograph cited and no photograph compared; the 128 columns, the 32 rows per band, the four rules and start patterns, the amber tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. It was adopted from the first preview; the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps is only 0.0038 (relief 0.001) and was not adjusted.

`gameoflife` adds Conway's Game of Life, bringing the current catalog from 963 to 964 kinds (965 gallery choices including plain). A Conway soup on a dark blue-green LED matrix: a 64×64 torus started from a seeded random 38% density and evolved for 250 generations, where bright green live cells form blocks, beehives, blinkers and gliders. **The evolved board has not fully settled** (gliders and blinkers still move; in the next 12 generations about 4%–9% of the cells still change each generation) and is only a static snapshot. Each cell is a rounded-square LED, and unlit LEDs stay dark.

The Game of Life runs once when the sampler is built, which took about 30 ms.

`hilbertcurve` adds a Hilbert curve, bringing the current catalog from 962 to 963 kinds (964 gallery choices including plain). One cyan circuit trace on a dark navy ground follows an order-4 Hilbert space-filling curve: each of the 16×16 cells is visited exactly once, and the end is joined to the start across the tile seam to close the loop (the start and end of a Hilbert curve are neighbouring cells on a torus); the line is about half a cell wide with a faint glow outside it. The seed picks one of the eight square symmetries (mirror and transpose) and shifts the curve around the torus, so the statistics stay the same and only the orientation and position change. It is not a real circuit board (no pads, vias or multiple layers).

This material is an authored schematic with no specific source or circuit-board photograph cited and no photograph compared; the order of 4, the half-cell line width, the tanh sharpness of 8, the cyan tones and the 0.2 m nominal tile are authored choices. At relief 0.002 in the first version the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps was 0.0901; lowering it to 0.0015 gave 0.0512 (before and after values from the same probe).

`quasicrystal` adds a quasicrystal-style interference pattern, bringing the current catalog from 961 to 962 kinds (963 gallery choices including plain). Five plane waves with integer wave vectors at nearly 72° steps interfere into a blue-and-white pattern that looks five-fold symmetric: dark blue dots, pentagon rings and star-like shapes over a pale blue ground. Because every wave vector is an integer, the pattern is **exactly periodic over the tile**, so it is an approximation by five-wave interference and not a true quasicrystal or Penrose tiling (the vector lengths are 14 and about 13.6 and the angles are 0°, 72.9°, 144.0°, 216.0° and 287.1°, only approximating equal 72° steps); the seed changes only the wave phases and the statistics stay the same.

This material is an authored schematic that cites no quasicrystal literature or measured diffraction image and has no photograph comparison; the five integer wave vectors (14, 0), (4, 13), (−11, 8), (−11, −8) and (4, −13), the tanh contrast of 1.5, the tones and the 0.3 m nominal tile are authored choices. At relief 0.004 the maximum normal tilt² of the 512² maps was 0.358; lowering it to 0.0015 gave 0.0716 (before and after values from the same probe).
